What a business model is

How a product creates value, delivers it, and captures a share of it — and why the three must be checked against each other rather than described one at a time.

1. Two decisions, three days apart

On Tuesday 6 October 2026 Ritika Behere, chief product officer of Indali Clinic Cloud, had a one-page memo on her desk in Pune and no settled view about it. Indali sells practice-management software — NABL-format report templates, PM-JAY claim files — to diagnostic centres in tier-two cities, per seat per month; in the quarter ended Wednesday 30 September 2026 it billed 24,000 seat-months at ₹1,400 each. CFO Rochana Bodhankar's memo proposed abandoning seats for ₹2.80 per report, forecasting that seat-months would then rise 30.0 per cent, because a clinic running eighty reports a day stops rationing logins. Behere's objection was not that the forecast was wrong, but that she could not say what the company would be optimising if it agreed.

Three days later, on Friday 9 October, Rutvij Burte faced the inverse in Bengaluru. Iktara Instruments makes the IK-2, a logger reporting cold-room temperature excursions to a dashboard. It sells the device to cold-chain distributors at ₹18,000 against ₹14,220 of materials, assembly and warranty provision — a margin of 21.0 per cent — and the dashboard to the cold-storage operator at ₹900 per device-month against ₹270 of connectivity, cloud and support. Channel head Rujul Barhate wanted to give the device away at cost and let the subscription carry everything. What the arithmetic hid was that Iktara would then fund its installed base out of working capital, and that payer and beneficiary sit in different companies.

2. The idea, and the schools that disagree about it

A business model is the architecture by which a firm creates value for a defined customer, delivers it, and captures a share — in enough detail that the three can be checked against one another. Creation, delivery and a price list are three documents; the model makes them answerable to each other.

The core is an identity. For one unit of what the customer buys, let W be willingness to pay, C the incremental cost of serving it and P the price. Value created is W − C, delivered W − P, captured P − C:

W − C = (W − P) + (P − C)

Everything else is an argument about estimating those terms and moving the split. Indali's own split, for one seat-month, is below.

Note what the exhibit exposes: Indali's gross margin on this unit is 840 / 1,400 = 60.0 per cent, its capture ratio — the share of created value kept — 840 / 2,040 = 41.2 per cent. Same firm, month and unit, 18.8 points apart because the denominators differ.

The term predates the internet that popularised it: a 1957 operations-research paper by Bellman and colleagues, a 1960 accounting article by Jones, Drucker's 1994 theory of the business as ancestor. It became urgent around 1998–2001, when firms giving products away needed a vocabulary for how that ends in cash; Timmers (1998) wrote the first taxonomies.

Activity-system (Amit and Zott, 2001): interdependent activities spanning firm boundaries, creating value through novelty, lock-in, complementarities and efficiency. Would sign two firms with identical products, prices and costs can have different models. It would not sign the model is the revenue model.

Narrative (Magretta, 2002): a story about how the enterprise works, categorically different from strategy, which is doing what rivals do not. Would sign a model can be internally perfect and still lose, because it names no competitor; Porter's 2001 critique is the hard edge, that the term lets managers skip competitive advantage. Not choosing a model is choosing a strategy.

Choices and consequences (Casadesus-Masanell and Ricart, 2010) denies that separation: a model is a firm's choices and their consequences, strategy is the choice of model, the residue tactics. The clean line, they would sign, is between model and tactics.

Operationalising (Johnson, Christensen and Kagermann, 2008; Osterwalder and Pigneur's canvas, 2010; Blank's repeatable-model search): a finite set of blocks a team changes one at a time. Would sign a model is decomposable, which makes it teachable. Not that interdependence makes it irreducible.

Appropriability (Chesbrough and Rosenbloom, 2002, on the Xerox PARC spin-offs; Teece, 2010): a model matters only once it says how value is held. Would sign absent an isolating mechanism, a good model gives everything it creates to customers and imitators. Not a model is a description.

3. Mechanics in depth

Experts do not fill in a canvas. They run seven steps, the last three checks, and expect one to fail. One: name the unit at which the customer experiences value — not the unit you bill. For Indali it is a dispatched report; for Iktara, a cold-room-day without an unnoticed excursion. Two: estimate a distribution of willingness to pay, not a point: Indali's median was ₹2,600, its upper quartile ₹3,400, and that spread makes tiering possible. Three: lay out the incremental cost of serving the unit, apart from step-fixed costs. Four: choose the capture mechanism — who pays, on what meter, how often, who signs.

Then the checks. (i) Capture consistency: the band between cost and willingness to pay must be non-empty for the segment you mean to serve, price inside it; Indali's band on a seat-month runs ₹560 to ₹2,600, a width of ₹2,040. (ii) Delivery consistency: the capture mechanism's own cost must fit inside that band, and is usually left implicit. Metering reports rather than seats raises Indali's cost to serve from ₹560 to ₹620 — 2.9 per cent of the band. At a ₹300 band the same ₹60 is 20.0 per cent of the surplus, which is why thin-band firms keep crude meters. (iii) Reinvestment consistency: this period's capture must fund next period's proposition. A model failing only (iii) looks healthy for a year.

The second-order effects are where expertise shows. A meter changes behaviour: seat pricing produces shared logins, per-call pricing caching, per-report pricing report-splitting. It changes the signatory: a per-seat contract is signed by the clinic owner against a fixed budget, a per-report contract by the operations manager against a variable line — lengthening the first sale, shortening each renewal. And it changes the firm: usage billing needs revenue assurance licence billing does not.

4. When it applies, and when it misleads

Four conditions, each falsifiable, each applied to both protagonists. There is an observable unit at which the customer experiences value. Indali passes: the report is counted and already NABL-audited. Iktara fails partially, because what the operator values is a non-event. Willingness to pay can be bounded above by something the customer already pays. Iktara passes cleanly: a cold room holding ₹42 lakh of stock at an observed 1.4 per cent annual spoilage rate loses ₹58,800 a year against a first-year cost, at full pass-through, of ₹18,000 plus twelve months at ₹900, or ₹28,800 — a ratio of 2.04. If the logger prevents half that loss, ₹29,400, the first-year surplus is ₹600 and the second, carrying only ₹10,800 of subscription, ₹18,600: a statement about contract length, not price. The meter's cost is small against the band — Indali's 2.9 per cent, and one monthly line per device for Iktara. The party receiving the value can pay. Indali passes inside one firm, Iktara across two.

It misleads in four situations. Where value creation is genuinely joint, as in a regulated utility, policy sets capture. Where the firm is not the unit of analysis — a cross-subsidised product inside a conglomerate — a standalone model is a fiction kept for reporting. Where the product changes willingness to pay, as habit and network goods do, W is an outcome, not a parameter. And before product-market fit there is no distribution to estimate, so a canvas manufactures precision where honesty means guesses.

5. Hard edge cases

Multi-product. Indali's claims module would serve the same clinic from a different budget line, and its meter can break the first product: priced per filing, it rewards batching, degrading the turnaround the licence was sold on.

Two-sided. Rochet and Tirole's result is that price structure matters independently of level: you subsidise the side that is more own-price elastic and generates the larger cross-side externality. The test is quantitative. Indali's 24,000 seat-months over three months is 8,000 seats a month across 2,000 clinics — 4.0 each — so a clinic carries 4.0 × 12 × ₹840 = ₹40,320 of captured value a year under A. Vendors pay about ₹1,100 per clinic-year for placement: at most 2.7 per cent of that. Indali is not two-sided, and saying so saves a quarter.

Regulated. Where a third party reimburses — PM-JAY for a procedure, an insurer for a panel — W belongs to a payer not in the room, and the meter must be one that payer's rules recognise: a permissible meter can be commercially wrong, an ideal one unbillable.

Hardware plus software. Iktara's at-cost proposal moves the installed base onto the balance sheet. Distributors pay 90 days after dispatch, so Iktara funds ₹14,220 a unit until they do: ₹255.96 lakh across 1,800 devices, ₹383.94 lakh across 2,700, a difference of ₹127.98 lakh. Exhibit 4 plots contribution, not cash: the device cost returns at invoice under both policies.

AI-native. Where cost to serve rises with use, gross margin is a property of the price structure, not the technology, and a flat per-seat price shorts your own success.

At the seams. Pricing sits with finance, the meter with engineering, the proposition with product; the model alone spans all three. Mature firms say they run a pricing council; most run an analyst's spreadsheet.

6. Eight things that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

The model is not the revenue model. The tell is an answer to "what is our business model?" that is a pricing page. Two firms with identical price lists can have opposite cost structures and opposite answers on whether growth helps.

The billing unit is not the unit of value, and the gap is the main design variable. The tell is a workaround rational under the meter, irrational under the value: shared logins, cached calls, batched filings. The obvious reading polices them; experts read the gap.

Margin and capture ratio answer different questions. Indali's 60.0 per cent margin says how much of each rupee billed it keeps; its 41.2 per cent capture ratio, how much of the value created. Carrying only one, a team reads a price rise as a value rise.

Changing the meter changes the customer. The tell is that the signatory moves. A revenue-neutral change looks like a non-event, but reroutes the deal through a different budget and approver: the sales motion moves though no price did.

The model's inputs are often endogenous to it. The tell is a willingness-to-pay figure in a current deck, measured before the product existed. Where the product creates the habit, W is partly an output, and fixing it imports last year's product into this year's choice.

Creation needs no moat; capture does. Teece's point, and among the most skipped. The tell is an excellent model beside an isolating mechanism that is a feature, not a position. Without one, competition pushes P towards C and the band goes to customers.

Operating leverage is a property of the model, not of scale. The tell is revenue growing faster than gross profit. Ikshu Intelligence's revenue rose 256.1 per cent in the eleven months to March 2026 while gross profit rose 50.8 per cent; growth would not have cured that.

Reinvestment consistency is the condition everyone forgets. The tell is a stable gross margin beside a starving roadmap. A model can clear capture and delivery and still not fund next year's proposition, so a firm posts four good quarters then finds W decayed.

7. Across product types and company stages

Two things do the real work across product types: where the payer sits, and the shape of the cost curve. They surface as different units of value and different binding checks. In consumer advertising the unit of value is an attention-minute and the payer a third party with its own W; in B2B software, a workflow completed, the meter drifting from value; in enterprise, a contracted outcome, capture negotiated rather than listed; in marketplaces, a matched transaction, structure binding before level; in hardware, a device-day in service, capture and cash out both front-loaded; in AI products, a task completed, cost to serve usage-elastic. What does not differ is the identity: Indali's ₹2,040 splits into ₹1,200 delivered and ₹840 captured, and an advertising impression splits whatever it creates the same way. Claims that platforms obey different economics usually reduce to claims that their W is hard to observe.

Stage matters more than frameworks admit. Pre-fit the model is a hypothesis whose only honest form is a list of statements that would falsify it. In early scale the meter is chosen for billability rather than fit — correct then, an unpriced liability later. In growth, meter-to-value drift is the biggest cheap lever. At maturity the model is load-bearing for the org chart, compensation and revenue recognition, so mature firms add tiers instead of changing meters.

8. Three worked examples

Indali, where structure beat level. Mechanism B holds the price level where A had it — ₹2.80 × 500 reports is ₹1,400 — yet forecast seat-months rise 30.0 per cent. Because the level does not move, that 30.0 per cent is no elasticity but a structure effect: the removal of a rationing incentive seat pricing created. C does move the level, by 35.7 per cent, for a forecast 45.0 per cent fall in seat-months — a two-point ratio of 1.26, a forecast pair, not an estimated elasticity. So B keeps the least per unit, 39.4 per cent, and the most in the quarter, ₹243.36 lakh.

Iktara, where the balance sheet was the model. Barhate's proposal forgoes ₹3,780 of device margin on each of the 1,800 devices Iktara expects to place at ₹18,000 — ₹68.04 lakh — for 900 extra placements at ₹900 − ₹270 = ₹630 a month, ₹5.67 lakh a month in all. Those 900 sell at cost: nothing upfront, nothing negative. Payback is ₹68.04 lakh / ₹5.67 lakh = 12.0 months, and turns on the margin's rupee value, not its percentage.

Ikshu Intelligence, where the model failed and was rebuilt. Ragini Balsekar's Hyderabad company sells AI contract review to in-house legal teams. In April 2025 a seat-month cost ₹1,125 to serve and was priced at ₹7,500: an 85.0 per cent margin, and at 410 seats ₹26.14 lakh of monthly gross profit. Eleven months later: 1,460 seats, ₹39.42 lakh, a 36.0 per cent margin.

The cause was not cost inflation but its opposite. Documents per seat-month rose from 25 to 160, and cost per document fell from ₹1,125 / 25 = ₹45.00 to ₹4,800 / 160 = ₹30.00, a 33.3 per cent gain engineering reported proudly. Cost per seat-month rose 326.7 per cent over the same window: the seat was the billing unit, the document the unit of value.

The rebuild, effective Wednesday 1 July 2026, was a two-part tariff: ₹3,000 per seat-month including 40 documents, then ₹60 per document. At 160 documents that is ₹3,000 + ₹60 × 120 = ₹10,200, a 36.0 per cent increase on ₹7,500. Of 1,460 seats, 1,180 renewed — 80.8 per cent — and 280 lapsed. Level and structure moved together — a ₹3,000 base against the old ₹7,500, a marginal ₹60 against a marginal ₹30 — so neither alone explains the margin. The base covers the 40 included documents (₹1,200) with ₹1,800 over.

9. Failure modes and their early diagnostics

Meter drift. Sign: usage per billing unit rising faster than price. Ask whether cost per billing unit moved while cost per unit of value fell. Ikshu caught it eleven months late, at 49.0 points of margin, 85.0 to 36.0.

Capture without creation. Sign: healthy margin, high churn, renewals about discount rather than scope. Ask what the customer loses if the product vanishes on Friday, in rupees they budget. Late, renewal is already a price negotiation.

Creation without capture. Sign: delighted customers, flat revenue. Ask who else holds the surplus — a channel, an integrator, a platform. Late, that holder has already capitalised it.

Payer and beneficiary in different firms. Sign: a channel partner negotiating price while the end user talks reliability — Iktara's position. Ask who signs the order and who bears the spoilage. Caught late, the contract reopens, not the price.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Is a model distinct from strategy, or a substitute for it? Magretta says distinct, Porter distinct and dangerous: a model describes a system, a strategy explains how you beat rivals, and conflating them lets a team feel rigorous while naming no rival. Casadesus-Masanell and Ricart say it is artificial, because real choices — a meter, a channel, a cost structure — are at once model and strategy. The first camp is wrong if model choices settle competitive outcome alone; the second, if identical model choices diverge on positioning.

Is a model decomposable? The canvas schools say yes, pointing to a decade of teachability and block-by-block experimentation. The activity-system school says value lies in the interdependence, so testing blocks singly measures the wrong thing. It is settleable: if single-block changes predicted outcomes as well as joint ones, the canvas wins. No large-scale test has been published.

Designed or discovered? Chesbrough and Rosenbloom's Xerox evidence — the same technologies under different models to very different ends — supports design; the base rate of pivots supports search. Both hold if design is what you do with the model you discovered.

Does the capture ratio matter, or only absolute profit? Exhibit 3 cuts both ways: B keeps the smallest share of created value and the largest rupee amount. The ratio camp says the share forecasts where competition will attack; the absolute camp, that shareholders do not receive ratios.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this asks for the unit of value before the price, and notices a billing unit in disguise. They carry both denominators and name the one they use. They can state what would have to be false for the model to stop working, and know which check binds now, because it is rarely all three. They treat the meter as a product decision, not a finance approval. And they will say a difference does not bind: Indali's vendor side at most 2.7 per cent of clinic-side capture is not two-sided, and the expert move is to say so.

12. The decisions, and three questions

On Thursday 12 November 2026 Behere took mechanism B to Indali's board, staged: new clinics from January, the rest at renewal, under a twelve-month guarantee. Her reasoning was that the seat-month forecast is the larger of Exhibit 3's two unobserved inputs, so the cheapest way to buy the decision is to observe it on a cohort. Burte declined Barhate's proposal for a year — not over the 12.0-month payback, which he accepted, but over the ₹127.98 lakh of working capital against a subscription life his records bound only from below.

  1. Which of mechanism B's two figures should the board grade Behere on, and what would make the answer the other one?
  2. Iktara's distributor pays for a device whose value accrues to the operator. Does Iktara have one business model or two, and what evidence would settle it?
  3. Ikshu's engineers cut cost per document 33.3 per cent while cost per seat-month rose 326.7 per cent. Which figure belongs in the business model, and which in the operating plan?

13. Going deeper

  1. Unit economics — supplies the C term.
  2. Business Model and Lean Canvas — the decomposability claim as an artefact.
  3. Revenue models — the catalogue of capture mechanisms.
  4. Cost structure and operating leverage — growth answered two ways.
  5. Changing a business model — why meters move under pressure.
  6. Subscription economics — reinvestment consistency made measurable.
  7. Advertising business models — payer and beneficiary at their furthest.
  8. Marketplace economics — where the structure test binds.
  9. Freemium as a business model — deliberate zero capture.
  10. Hardware business models — Iktara's cash problem, generalised.
  11. Licensing, OEM and white-label — capture by handing delivery away.

What a Business Model Is

How a product creates, delivers and captures value

1. The offer on the Monday

At 7:40 on Monday, 12 October 2026, Pranoti Ambekar was watching boxes move down the line in the central kitchen of Halad, the Pune lunch-box subscription company she founded in 2023. Fourteen cooks were closing roughly 1,470 boxes for desks in Hinjewadi and Baner. Each held a home-style meal and cost the subscriber ₹150. Halad had 1,800 subscribers averaging 18 meals a month, and after fixed costs of ₹8,10,000 a month it earned an operating profit of ₹3,56,400.

The previous Friday, Pradnyesh Angal, head of people at Zunjar Software, a Hinjewadi firm with 640 employees, had made an offer. Zunjar would pay Halad ₹135 a meal as a staff benefit for up to 375 enrolled employees at 20 meals each, invoiced monthly and delivered in one drop to the lobby. Pranoti's adviser and early investor, Purushottam Awati, put it bluntly: "Do not mistake this for a new customer. It is a new company with the same kitchen." Pradnyesh wanted an answer by Friday 16 October.

Pranoti could not settle it by asking whether ₹135 was a good price. The larger question was what Halad is, and what it keeps. That is the question a business model answers.

2. The idea

A business model is an account of how an organisation creates value for a customer, delivers it, and captures a share of it as money it keeps after cost. Each verb names a separate problem. Creating value means giving someone something worth more to them than their next-best alternative. Delivering means the activities, assets and partners needed to bring it to them. Capturing means who pays, for what, how often, and what remains after the cost of delivery.

The idea has several parents. Peter Drucker wrote in 1994 of a "theory of the business", the assumptions about what a company is paid for. During the internet boom, firms with little revenue needed some way to explain why revenue might one day exceed cost, and "business model" became the phrase, often as an excuse. Joan Magretta's 2002 Harvard Business Review article restored discipline with two tests: the story must make sense, and the numbers must work. Alexander Osterwalder, in a doctoral thesis completed in 2004 and a 2010 book with Yves Pigneur, turned it into nine boxes called the canvas. David Teece's 2010 paper stated the create, deliver and capture formulation used here.

Pranoti could repeat the point in a meeting without sounding glib: we make a lunch worth more to the customer than it costs us to make and carry, and we have a way of keeping a share of the difference. The module's shorthand is that a business model is unit economics plus how value is captured. Unit economics is the profit or loss on one unit sold. The model adds who pays, when, and why they keep paying.

3. How it works

Walk the steps through Halad. Step one names the customer and the job: an engineer in Hinjewadi who wants a lunch cooked to home standards, arriving hot, with no decision to make each morning. Step two sizes the value created, which is the most the customer would pay less what it costs to produce. A survey of 140 subscribers gave a median stated maximum of ₹190 a meal. That is a stated figure, not a revealed one, and a later section returns to it.

Step three is delivery: the Wakad kitchen, the cooks, a rider network and a subscription app. Step four prices the unit, meaning what one more box costs. Step five is capture: Halad charges the subscriber per box, ₹150, collected through the app before each week begins.

Practitioners usually leave three further steps implicit. Who carries the risk of an uneaten box? Halad does. When does cash move relative to cost? Here money arrives before the meals are cooked. And what happens to margin as volume grows? That depends on how far fixed costs spread, which the worked example tests. Step six closes the loop: does what is captured fund the delivery system that creates the value? If not, the model is a subsidy, however good the product.

4. A worked example

Table 1 prices one box. Every figure is per meal, in rupees. Contribution is the price less the costs that rise with each additional meal, and it is what each box contributes toward fixed costs.

Table 1. Halad's current model, per meal (₹)
Item₹ per meal
Ingredients58
Cooks (per-meal share of a largely fixed wage bill)24
Packaging7
Delivery22
Payment fees (2% of ₹150)3
Total variable cost114
Price charged150
Contribution per meal36

The contribution margin is 36 over a revenue base of 150, or 24.0 per cent. Over a month of 22 working days, 1,800 subscribers at 18 meals give 32,400 meals, about 1,470 boxes a day. Revenue is ₹48,60,000, variable cost ₹36,93,600 and contribution ₹11,66,400. Fixed cost of ₹8,10,000 covers kitchen rent, supervisors and the app team, leaving ₹3,56,400. Break-even is fixed cost divided by contribution per meal: 8,10,000 ÷ 36 is 22,500 meals, or 1,250 subscribers at 18 meals.

Table 2 changes one input. In the monsoon, rider incentives lift delivery from ₹22 to ₹28 a meal, with volume, price and fixed cost held.

Table 2. One input changed: delivery cost per meal (monthly, 32,400 meals)

A rise of ₹6 on a ₹114 cost, 5.3 per cent, cuts profit by ₹1,94,400, which is 54.5 per cent of ₹3,56,400, because fixed cost does not move. The thinness of the unit margin, not its 24.0 per cent level, is what the example exposes.

5. Seven nuances

Created is not captured

Halad creates ₹76 of value a meal: the customer's stated ₹190 less the ₹114 cost. The subscriber keeps ₹40 (190 less 150), Halad captures ₹36, and 36 over 76 is 47.4 per cent. That is a share of value created. The 24.0 per cent margin is a share of revenue. They answer different questions and must not be quoted as if one were the other.

A model is not a strategy

The model says how the money works. Strategy says why a rival cannot copy it. Any Pune kitchen can sell a ₹150 box. Halad needs something beyond the model, such as delivery density in two business parks, that a rival cannot quickly match. A model can be sound and still be easy to imitate, and a model that is easy to imitate rarely holds its margin for long.

A revenue model is one box

A revenue model describes how money comes in: per box, monthly plan, commission. It covers only the capture half. Two firms with the same revenue model can differ completely in delivery and cost. Halad and a canteen contractor both charge per meal, yet one carries riders and an app and the other carries none. Pricing is a decision inside the model, not the model itself.

Unit economics is necessary, not sufficient

Two models can share a ₹36 contribution and still differ in who carries the unsold-box risk, when cash arrives, and what keeps customers from leaving. The unit figure is a result of the model and cannot stand in for it.

Fixed cost decides what the unit figure means

₹36 a meal sounds comfortable until it meets ₹8,10,000 of fixed cost. Below 22,500 meals each extra meal narrows a loss; above it each adds profit. This is why the same ₹6 cost rise in Table 2 did far more damage than its size suggests: fixed cost converts a small change in unit margin into a large change in profit.

Stated value is not revealed value

The ₹190 came from 140 people who already subscribe. Those who declined are missing, and stated willingness to pay often exceeds what people accept at a checkout. Treat ₹190 as an upper estimate until a price test shows otherwise.

Where it applies, and what it cannot tell you

The framework presumes a repeatable unit and a payer. Before the first customers, a model is a hypothesis, not a measurement. Even a sound one cannot say whether demand will persist or rivals respond. Ask before relying on it: who pays, per what unit, what does one more unit cost, and what would make them stop?

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace

The same three verbs get different answers by product type. In a consumer product the user pays, and cash arrives early but churn is constant. In B2B the payer and the user differ: Zunjar's head of people is buying retention while the engineer is buying lunch, so value must satisfy both. A marketplace such as Swiggy or Zomato must create value for two sides at once and captures through a take rate, the share of each order's value the platform keeps.

Table 3. Capture by product type
TypeWho paysCharged perCash timing
Consumer (Halad today)SubscriberBoxBefore the week
B2B (Zunjar offer)EmployerEnrolled meal30 days after invoice
MarketplaceBuyer, with seller commissionOrderAt the order

The timing column carries a cost. At 7,500 meals and ₹102 of variable cost, Halad would fund ₹7,65,000 of a month's cooking and delivery, for up to two months before the first rupee returned. The consumer model never asks for that.

Stage matters too. An early company is testing whether any model works, and a large one is defending or optimising one. Halad, at 1,800 subscribers, sits between the two: its unit economics are measured, but whether employers will pay is not.

7. Common mistakes

Table 4. Three mistakes, how they show, and the cheapest check
SymptomMisunderstandingCheapest diagnostic
A founder says "we keep 24 per cent of the value".Revenue margin read as share of value created.Name both denominators: revenue (150) and value created (76).
Subscribers rise while profit falls.Revenue growth taken as proof the model works.Compare contribution per meal this month with last.
A price rise brings unexpected churn.Survey value treated as proven pricing power.Test the new price on a slice of new sign-ups.

All three come from the same habit: quoting a figure without saying what it is measured against.

8. What good looks like

Handled well, Pranoti's Thursday would produce that page. It would set both offers in the same measure, contribution per meal and per month, name the meals that merely move from one channel to another, show what happens when a cost input rises, and end with a test whose failure would be visible.

9. The decision, and what to learn next

On Thursday 15 October Pranoti accepted the Zunjar contract as a second channel, not a replacement, capped at 7,500 meals a month. Of these, 3,000 would replace meals now sold to 150 existing subscribers who, as office regulars, average 20 meals; each such meal moves from ₹36 to ₹33 of contribution (the Zunjar price of ₹135 less ₹102 of variable cost, with delivery at ₹12 for a single drop and ₹1 for invoice settlement, the rest as in Table 1), a loss of 3,000 × 3 = ₹9,000. The other 4,500 are new at ₹33, adding ₹1,48,500. Net gain is ₹1,39,500, less ₹54,000 a month for an account manager, or ₹85,500, which lifts monthly operating profit to ₹4,41,900. The total of 36,900 meals sits inside the kitchen's 40,000. She would keep the consumer line, because it earns ₹36 not ₹33.

Next, study the Business Model and Lean Canvas, which lays out all nine boxes; revenue models; cost structure and operating leverage, which explains why a ₹6 cost rise cut profit by more than half; and changing a business model, which is the trade Pranoti faced.

Fifty-one minutes later it ended where it began. Was Vyavahar a software company that had learned to sell credit, or a credit business that had bought its borrowers with free software?

2. The company, and the decision that still holds

Vyavahar was founded in Pune in February 2016 by Mulgaonkar and Ghanashree Mhaskar, who had audited chemists' books for eleven years. Their first product was a billing book for small pharma distributors in Pune and Nashik; the GST rollout of July 2017 did their selling. A ₹86 crore Series A followed in March 2019, raised on the proposition that the paid plan would carry the company. The free tier was added in 2020 to survive a year nobody could sell in, and never removed. Vyavahar Connect, routing retailers' orders to distributors, launched in November 2021 at 1.5 per cent commission, raised to 2.0 per cent in April 2024.

The decision that constrains tonight was signed on 12 February 2023: Vyavahar became exclusive sourcing and servicing partner to Arunoday Credit, a Mumbai NBFC, at 3.1 per cent of disbursed principal, and would place no retailer loan through any other lender until 31 March 2028. The board minute called credit "a retention feature". Nobody wrote down what would happen if it became the business.

3. The industry

Vyavahar sells into roughly thirteen million kirana, chemist and hardware counters, a market crossed from four directions. Tally and Vyapar sell billing software outright; Khatabook and OkCredit built free ledgers at scale and then looked for monetisation; Udaan and Jumbotail went at the order flow; and Reliance Retail's distribution arm, Zepto and Swiggy Instamart supply the same counters directly. UPI and the NPCI rails made collection trivial, and ONDC made order interoperability a live question for anyone charging a take rate on routing.

Three regulatory facts bear on revenue. The Reserve Bank's digital lending framework makes Vyavahar a lending service provider: fees come from the lender, and credit risk stays with Arunoday, which holds the lending licence. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 governs onward use of outlet-level data, and GST e-invoicing thresholds decide how many counters need software at all. Tuljai Kitchens: What Kind of Business Is This?

A decision case on business models, Pune, November 2026

1. Opening

At 7.15 on the morning of Tuesday 3 November 2026, Ekanshi Lawande stood at the dispatch counter of Tuljai Kitchens' Baner kitchen in Pune, watching lunch cartons being sealed for office towers a few kilometres away. As head of product she owed the board a paper by Friday 13 November, ahead of the board meeting on Friday 20 November. The paper had to recommend what kind of business Tuljai should be for the next eighteen months. Three colleagues each held a different answer, and each was backed by numbers that were honest as far as they went. Diwali falls on Sunday 8 November, and she knew that once the festival break began, the argument would be settled mostly by whoever had spoken last, unless she gave the board a clear way to think about it.

2. Company background

Tuljai Kitchens Private Limited was founded in March 2022 in Kothrud by Evaan Lolayekar, a hospitality manager from Goa, who began with about 40 subscribers recruited through a Kothrud housing society's WhatsApp group. It sells home-style Maharashtrian and Konkani lunches, such as varan-bhat, bharli vangi and solkadhi, on monthly subscription to office workers in Pune. Meals are cooked in three central kitchens, at Kothrud, Baner (opened January 2024) and Wakad (opened April 2025), and delivered by Tuljai's own riders. Growth came from office referrals rather than advertising, and each new kitchen was opened once its predecessor ran close to full.

In the second quarter of FY27 (July to September 2026) the company averaged about 3,000 active subscribers, each taking around 20 meals a month. That is 60,000 meals a month at a realised price of ₹140 before GST, against kitchen capacity of 90,000. Its rivals sit on every side: Swiggy and Zomato for on-demand delivery, EatSure and other Rebel Foods brands for packaged meals, and neighbourhood tiffin services, whose punctuality is judged against the Mumbai dabbawalas. ONDC is beginning to list food sellers. Prepared meals attract 5 per cent GST, and every kitchen, including any home kitchen that sells through Tuljai, needs FSSAI registration or a licence.

3. The situation

Tuljai is losing money. Exhibit 1 shows where the month's result comes from: each meal leaves ₹28 after variable cost, but the three kitchens, the technology team and management cost ₹21.0 lakh a month whatever the volume. Cash stood at ₹3.10 crore on 30 September 2026. A Mumbai fund that has met Evaan twice has told him that investors in December will want an "asset-light" story, and the board expects the paper to say how a recommendation would be explained to them.

The team sees the problem from several cities. The Berlin designer, who rebuilt the subscription app in the spring, suspects that users open it mainly to pause or resume a plan, not to browse, though no one has measured this. Tuljai's customer-success lead in Singapore, who handles support across time zones, reports that subscribers write about taste far more than about price. Exhibit 3 gives the survey behind that impression.

Three pieces of evidence have arrived in the last two months. A survey of 412 subscribers was run between 14 and 25 September. A six-week pilot with home cooks in Kothrud ran from 7 September to 18 October. And two employers, one in Hinjewadi and one in Magarpatta, have each sent a non-binding term sheet that lapses on 30 November, so the board's date leaves ten days to negotiate before the offers expire. Exhibit 2 prices the three directions these point to, in steady state and before GST.

4. The people

Evaan Lolayekar, co-founder and chief executive, Pune, favours turning Tuljai into a marketplace of home cooks. He believes the December raise depends on it and wants the company to stop owning kitchens.

Edwina Lotlekar, vice-president of operations, Pune, runs the 61 cooks and packers in the three kitchens. She started as a kitchen supervisor in Kothrud in 2022. She wants the kitchens fuller, not closed, and believes a dinner slot is the cheapest way to get there.

Eshal Lembhe, data scientist, Toronto, designed the pilot analysis and the survey. She joins the weekly review at 9.00 pm IST, which is 10.30 am in Toronto since the clocks changed on 1 November. She wants the choice made on measured quality, not on a story.

Ekavya Lokurkar, partnerships lead, Pune, brought in the two employer term sheets. He spent four years selling cafeteria services before joining and knows how employers buy. He argues that a company whose product is reliable lunch should sell it to those who already pay for reliable lunch.

Exhibit 3 holds the survey and the pilot. In the pilot, Tuljai's own Kothrud kitchen served the same zone during the same six weeks, which gives a comparison.

5. The options

Option A: deepen the consumer subscription. Tuljai adds a dinner slot and a fourth delivery zone in Hinjewadi, and aims for 75,000 meals a month, filling its kitchens to 83 per cent. It keeps the ₹140 price and one-time spending of ₹24 lakh. It continues to cook, deliver and sell directly, so it still owns every kitchen and still wins each customer one subscription at a time.

Option B: become a marketplace. Tuljai recruits home cooks under its menu and hygiene standard, keeps 30 per cent of the ₹140, and continues to run delivery and payments. It exits the three leases at a one-time cost of ₹38 lakh and fixed costs fall to ₹10.0 lakh a month, the technology team and management alone. The 61 kitchen staff would be offered cook-partner onboarding rather than jobs. The brand and the app remain.

Option C: sell to employers. Tuljai stops individual subscriptions and supplies the two campuses, 45,000 meals a month in Hinjewadi and 35,000 in Magarpatta, at ₹125 a meal on twelve-month contracts with 45-day payment terms. It spends ₹15 lakh on a bulk-packing line and keeps its kitchens, at 89 per cent of capacity. Diners see the employer's cafeteria, not the Tuljai brand.

6. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibits 1 and 3, describe how Tuljai creates, delivers and captures value today. Which part of the model are customers actually paying for?
  2. The options in Exhibit 2 differ in volume and in what counts as revenue. Restate them on one comparable basis and say what you learn.
  3. For each option, which single assumption would most damage it if wrong, and which can Ekanshi test before 20 November?
  4. Which model should she recommend to the board, and what condition would you attach?

7. A note for the learner

A business model is unit economics plus the way value is captured. It asks who creates the value, who delivers it, and who pays. The same ₹140 meal gives Tuljai ₹140 of revenue and ₹28 of contribution when it cooks and delivers, and ₹42 of revenue and ₹17 of contribution when it only brokers, so the model changes what a figure means before it changes the figure.

One defensible path is Option C. The survey places the value in the kitchen: taste and trust in a known kitchen together account for 242 of 412 answers, about 59 per cent. The pilot's complaint rate was 6.4 per cent against 2.1 in the kitchen, though 14 cooks over six weeks is a small trial, so it points in a direction rather than proving one. Option C keeps the kitchen that creates the value and sells it to a payer who values reliability and settles in volume. Its weakness is concentration in two clients and 45-day receivables. A sound recommendation would therefore be conditional: seek minimum-volume clauses, shorter payment terms, and a review after three months, and sign only if both employers accept. If either employer refuses, the recommendation should return to the board rather than proceed.
exp40v2-bm.canvas:
Business Model and Lean Canvas

Nine boxes as a diagnostic, not a pitch: what the canvas measures, the one identity that binds it, and how two companies used it in October 2026 to find out which box was carrying the error.

1Two decisions, two weeks apart

On Wednesday 30 September 2026 Bhoominathan Innasimuthu closed the books on Pudhumai Learning's second full year. The Chennai company sells state-board exam preparation for classes 9 to 12 in Tamil and Telugu, at ₹1,999 a year or ₹299 a month. It held 18,40,000 registered accounts, 4,60,000 active in September, and 58,000 paying. Trailing revenue was ₹1,133.78 lakh against ₹1,408 lakh of cost: a loss of ₹274.22 lakh. At the board meeting on Thursday 22 October his lead investor would ask for a path to ₹60 crore of revenue by the year to 31 March 2029 — reached, he suspected, by compounding two years and rounding up.

On Thursday 8 October, roughly 600 kilometres away, Bedabrata Indukuri faced a narrower question. Pantham Systems sells cold-chain telemetry to pharmaceutical distributors from Hyderabad: a sensor unit per vehicle at ₹18,500 on delivery, then ₹1,450 per monitored vehicle per month on a 36-month contract. Across 34 accounts it monitored 4,120 vehicles, plus 68 cold rooms at no charge under the same contracts — so the whole ₹7.1688 crore software run-rate is 4,120 × ₹1,450 × 12 — and earned ₹2.4790 crore on 1,340 hardware units. Three of his five largest prospects wanted the device at zero upfront, and Bishnupriya Ilamvazhuthi, who ran commercial, had drafted a bundled ₹1,780 and called it margin-neutral.

Both had a filled-in canvas on the wall and neither had told them anything for a year. A canvas is usually read as a pitch — nine individually defensible assertions — when its value is as a diagnostic: a layout that makes one identity visible, and a particular box answerable for a shortfall.

2The idea, and the four schools that disagree about it

A business model is the architecture by which a firm creates value, delivers it to a defined customer and captures part of it for itself. Peter Drucker's 1994 "theory of the business" put the point first: every enterprise runs on assumptions about environment, mission and core competence, and those assumptions decay. Joan Magretta's 2002 Harvard Business Review essay narrowed it — a model is a story about how the business works, and it must pass a narrative test and a numbers test. In practice the first test gets run and the second does not.

The canvas answered a different problem: the words had no shared referent. Alexander Osterwalder's 2004 doctoral work at Lausanne, published with Yves Pigneur as Business Model Generation in 2010, fixed a finite layout — nine blocks, one sheet — so two people arguing about a model at least pointed at the same box. Ash Maurya's 2010 Lean Canvas, which his own account dates to 2010, kept five of those blocks and replaced four, on the ground that a company with no product has no activities, resources, partners or relationships worth describing, but does have a problem, a solution, a metric and a defensibility question.

Four schools read those boxes differently, and the disagreement is not cosmetic. The grouping is this page's, not a taxonomy its authors use. The design school — Osterwalder, with Raphael Amit and Christoph Zott on design themes — signs that a model is a composable choice set, not that it is derivable from industry structure. The positioning school, from Michael Porter's 2001 attack on loose business-model talk through Ramon Casadesus-Masanell and Joan Enric Ricart, signs that a model must be judged against rivals' likely responses, not that a complete canvas is a strategy. The capability school — David Teece's 2010 treatment, alongside Henry Chesbrough's work on the same question — signs that one technology monetises differently under different appropriability regimes, not that a model can be chosen before you know what you can defend. The discovery school — Steve Blank, Maurya, and Rita McGrath and Ian MacMillan's 1995 discovery-driven planning — signs that the canvas ranks what to falsify first, not that it should be finished before contact with customers.

3Mechanics: eight scalars, one identity, eight degrees of freedom

An expert fills each box with a measured quantity carrying a stated denominator and window. Segments gives S, the reachable base; Value Proposition gives c, the share of it that pays, price being the operationalisation practitioners trust; Channels gives a, the cost of one new paying customer still paying at the close; Relationships gives r, annual retention; Revenue Streams gives R, revenue per paying customer per year; Key Activities gives v, the variable cost of serving one for a year; Key Resources gives F, the annual cost of what does not scale; Key Partners gives m, the revenue share leaving as partner margin. Eight boxes, eight scalars. Cost Structure yields no ninth: it holds v, F, a and m re-sorted into fixed and variable, a cut and not a new fact.

π = S·c·[ R(1−m) − v − (1−r)a ] − F

Add π, the annual operating result, and nine quantities are bound by that one identity. Eight can be set independently; the ninth is arithmetic. Fix the margin you need and seven of the eight operating quantities are yours, the eighth determined. A pitch gets this wrong in both directions: nine independent facts overstates the freedom, and "the model turns on pricing and churn" understates it, leaving six quantities unexamined.

Read the identity on Pudhumai, holding September volumes still. S·c is 18,40,000 × 3.1522% = 58,000 payers; the bracket is ₹1,723.10 a payer-year as Figure 1 derives it; contribution is ₹999.40 lakh and π = ₹999.40 − ₹914.32 = +₹85.08 lakh. Yet the closed year lost ₹274.22 lakh, and the ₹359.30 lakh gap is growth. It decomposes exactly. Revenue was earned over an average base of (34,000 + 58,000) ÷ 2 = 46,000, not 58,000 — realised revenue 46,000 × ₹2,464.74 = ₹1,133.78 lakh — costing 12,000 payer-years at ₹2,464.74 − ₹381.91 = ₹2,082.83, or ₹249.94 lakh. Acquisition ran at ₹318 lakh against the ₹208.64 lakh a settled 58,000-payer base would spend replacing its 44.1 per cent annual lapse (58,000 × 0.441176 = 25,588 payers at ₹815.38), a further ₹109.36 lakh; the two sum to ₹359.30 lakh. Pudhumai is a profitable business buying growth, which points at a different box.

4When the canvas works, and when it misleads

Three conditions, each testable. First, Segments must hold a countable base, and every other box's denominator must be traceable to it. That is weaker than it sounds: only c divides by Pudhumai's 18,40,000. Revenue divides by the 58,000 payers, v by the 46,000 average payers, a by the 39,000 new payers still paying at the close, r by the 34,000 opening payers. Each is S·c at a stated date or a stated flow into or out of it, and the condition is that the page says which. Pantham passes on another unit — 4,120 vehicles across 34 accounts, 121.2 an account — and the vehicle, not the account, is what its price and unit cost use.

Second, the eight quantities must sit on one window. Pudhumai's end on 30 September 2026, with S and c at the close and r across the year. Pantham fails this: its stocks are dated, its 1,340 units a twelve-month flow, and its retention a 36-month contract term inside which r is 1 by contract — so (1−r)a is zero and the identity flatters it for three years. What it has to produce is r at month 37, which no box holds. Third, the identity assumes separability, and that is where it fails.

It becomes actively misleading where one box's level drives another's. If c rises with S through word of mouth, the bracket is not constant and multiplying it by S·c understates the return to scale. Pudhumai has a mild version; a two-sided marketplace a severe one, since liquidity makes c a function of S on both sides at once, so a canvas printing one c a side mis-prices what it compares. For Pantham, R per account is not independent of r: tenure is how a 34-account book reaches 4,120 vehicles. An expert who notices states the dependence and stops treating the bracket as constant.

5Hard edge cases

Multi-product firms break the single-base assumption first. A second product has its own c on a base overlapping the first by an unknown amount; the usual fudge is two canvases with the revenue lines added, which double-counts F. Two-sided businesses break separability, as above. Regulated businesses break Key Partners: a supervised partner has m set by rule, so the box holds no choice. Hardware-plus-software breaks Key Resources, because working capital appears nowhere on the canvas: under a zero-upfront bundle, 1,340 units at ₹13,600 of unit cost would tie up ₹1.82 crore, which a sheet of annual costs cannot show.

AI-native products break Key Activities. Inference cost is variable in a unit the customer does not buy — tokens, not seats — so v and R are denominated differently, and a canvas saying "per seat" in Revenue and "per million tokens" in Activities has hidden the quantity that decides the business. At the organisational seam the canvas is owned by nobody: Segments belongs to marketing, Revenue to finance, Activities to engineering, the identity to no one. Which is why mature companies say they run canvases annually and in fact run them when a new line of business needs one sheet.

6Eight things an expert sees that a competent practitioner does not

Cost Structure is a view, not a fact. Its content already sits in four other boxes, re-sorted. The tell-tale sign is a Cost Structure listing categories — "platform", "operations" — appearing nowhere else: the boxes were filled in qualitatively and the costs from the ledger, so the two cannot be reconciled.

A flow cost takes the average base, not the closing one. Pudhumai's ₹175.68 lakh of payer-attributable service cost arose across a base growing from 34,000 to 58,000. Divided by the closing 58,000 it gives ₹302.90; by the average 46,000, ₹381.91 — the first is 20.7 per cent low, and the unit-economics conclusions inherit it. The sign is a cost per customer improving in the quarters the base grows fastest.

A blended CAC is not a channel CAC, and a retained CAC is not a gross one. Pudhumai's ₹815.38 is ₹318 lakh of paid spend over the 39,000 new payers who survived to the close, organic arrivals included. Per retained payer is the right basis for (1−r)a and not what a channel buys: if new payers lapsed at the opening cohort's rate over half a year of average exposure, √0.5588 = 0.7475 survival implies about 52,170 gross acquisitions and a gross CAC of ₹318 lakh ÷ 52,170 = ₹610. The sign is a CAC falling while paid spend rises.

Key Partners is a claim on somebody else's canvas. If m is 22 per cent, that margin is a revenue line in a partner's model and must clear their costs. The sign is a Channels box naming a partner that Revenue and Cost ignore: a channel with no share and no commission is a hope. Section 8's third example is that error, priced.

Retention sits inside the bracket, not above it. Because the acquisition term is (1−r)a, retention changes the per-customer economics, not merely the count. Lifting Pudhumai's r from 55.88 to 65 per cent cuts (1−r)a from ₹359.73 to 0.35 × ₹815.38 = ₹285.38, worth ₹74.35 a payer-year, or ₹43.12 lakh at 58,000 payers — about half the settled result. The sign is a retention target with no change to the unit-economics page.

Value Proposition has no natural unit. Its content is adjectival, which is why experts grade c and the price Revenue can hold instead. The sign is a Value Proposition rich in claims beside a Revenue box holding a model but no price: the proposition was asserted, not tested.

Eight degrees of freedom, not nine and not two. Nine quantities bound by one identity leave eight free, so naming "price and churn" as the levers hides six. The sign is a sensitivity analysis with two rows. Pudhumai's three paths to ₹60 crore each move a different quantity, and one is shut by the company's own market sizing.

A cost line an option claims to retire is often pinned by another box. Bishnupriya's margin-neutral bundle assumed the ₹2,400 install fell away with a self-calibrating device, leaving ₹11,200 to recover: ₹11,200 ÷ ₹330 = 33.94 months, inside the 36-month term. But Pantham's pharmaceutical customers require a named technician's signature on installation qualification, so the line stays and recovery is 41.21 months. That 7.27-month swing is the decision; the sign is a saving booked against a constraint in another box.

7How it differs by product type and by stage

The real differences sit in which quantity is hardest to measure, not in the layout. In consumer subscription the base is large and c tiny, so a canvas lives or dies on the denominator: Pudhumai's c is 3.1522 per cent of registered accounts and 12.61 per cent of active ones, and the two support different plans. In B2B software the base can be enumerated and r dominates, since a 36-month contract makes (1−r)a small and lets F decide. In enterprise sales a is so lumpy it behaves like F for years. On platforms c is not independent of S. In hardware the hidden quantity is working capital, which appears nowhere on the sheet. In AI products v is in a unit the customer does not buy.

By stage, what changes is which box is answerable. Before product-market fit S and c are guesses and on Maurya's view the Lean Canvas is the better sheet, because it replaces four boxes a pre-product company can only guess at. After fit, F has grown and the canvas's job becomes arithmetic rather than hypothesis-ranking. At scale the binding box is usually Partners or Channels, because m and a are what a growing firm concedes to others. The identity itself does not change by stage.

8Three worked examples

Pudhumai's board asked for ₹60 crore. At ₹2,464.74 a payer-year that is 2,43,433 payers. Path i holds the base and needs c of 2,43,433 ÷ 18,40,000 = 13.23 per cent, 4.20 times today's. Path ii holds c and needs 2,43,433 ÷ 0.031522 = 77.23 lakh registered accounts against a company sizing of 62 lakh students in the boards it serves. Path iii holds c, grows the base to 50 lakh for 1,57,609 payers, and needs R of ₹60 crore ÷ 1,57,609 = ₹3,806.90, up 54.5 per cent. The canvas did not produce the target; it produced three paths, each naming a box.

Pantham's bundle is the second. Figure 4 prices it: the ₹330 uplift recovers ₹11,880 of a ₹13,600 unit cost over the term, ₹1,720 short, and the claim rested on retiring an install line the customers' qualification protocol pins. Margin-neutral is also the wrong name. Pantham earns ₹18,500 − ₹13,600 = ₹4,900 a unit today, so neutrality needs ₹18,500 ÷ 36 = ₹513.89 of uplift and a price of ₹1,963.89, or ₹2,071.81 with carry at (₹18,500 + ₹3,885) ÷ 36 = ₹621.81. Figure 4's ₹1,907.11 is cost-recovering, not neutral.

The third is a failure. Paasarai Agritech, founded in Guntur by Bitopan Immaneni, sold soil-test and advisory subscriptions through farmer producer organisations. Its canvas named FPOs in Channels, gave them no share in Revenue and no line in Cost, and assumed 25 per cent of 4,62,000 reachable members would pay ₹600 — ₹693 lakh. Over the eighteen months that followed it gave the channel an m — 22 per cent commission, farmer price ₹750, net ₹585 — which addressed recruitment but left conversion at 11.6 per cent against the planned 25.

9Failure modes and their early warnings

None of the failures below is a failure of any single box in isolation. Each is a canvas read as a pitch when the identity binding it was never closed. The common diagnostic is to insist that one number in one box be derivable from the others.

10Where experts genuinely disagree

The first disagreement is whether the canvas is a strategy instrument at all. The design school's strongest form is empirical: Zott and Amit found novelty-centred model design associated with the performance of entrepreneurial firms, and treated the model as a locus of choice distinct from product-market strategy. For that to be wrong, the association would have to be the shadow of an unmeasured capability — novel composers being firms that could already execute. The positioning school's strongest form is that a canvas is silent on rivalry, and the identity prices the point. If a rival halved the ₹1,999 plan and Pudhumai matched, R falls to ₹1,232.37, the bracket to ₹1,232.37 − ₹381.91 − ₹359.73 = ₹490.73, contribution to ₹284.62 lakh, and the settled +₹85.08 lakh becomes ₹284.62 − ₹914.32 = −₹629.70 lakh: no box heading moved and the result moved ₹714.77 lakh. For that to be wrong, competitive response would have to be slower than the cycle on which the identity is re-measured, which in Indian consumer subscription it sometimes is.

The second concerns the nine boxes. Maurya's claim is that four are unfillable before product-market fit and that filling them anyway manufactures false confidence; his evidence is the behaviour of pre-revenue teams, who write aspirations into Key Partners. For that to be wrong, writing the aspiration would have to be informative — and for someone who later measures it, it is. The third is sharper: whether the canvas should be scored at all. Teece holds that a model's worth is inseparable from the appropriability regime, so two firms with identical canvases can be excellent and worthless. For that to be wrong, imitability would have to be legible from the boxes, which no version of the canvas claims.

11What mastery looks like

Someone who has studied the canvas fills nine boxes and presents them. Someone who has internalised it does three things differently. They write the denominator and window beside each quantity before the quantity itself, so 18,40,000 and 30 September 2026 travel together. They close the identity out loud and treat a residual as a finding rather than a rounding — Pudhumai's ₹359.30 lakh gap is one such finding, and it is 12,000 payer-years at ₹2,082.83 plus ₹109.36 lakh of growth acquisition, not a plug. And they name the answerable box before proposing an action, and they say which box it is before they say what to do about it.

12What they decided

On Thursday 22 October Bhoominathan took the board neither a plan nor a refusal. He took Figure 3 and asked them to restate ₹60 crore as a pair — a base and a conversion rate — because the single figure admits a path the company's own sizing shuts. He proposed path iii: hold c near 3.15 per cent, grow the base to 50 lakh, and lift R to ₹3,806.90 through a second priced product rather than a 54.5 per cent rise on a ₹1,999 plan sold to state-board families. Binodini Irrinki, his VP of product, noted that this moves the risk into a box the canvas had carried as settled.

Bedabrata kept the ₹18,500 on delivery for the 34 accounts already on contract and offered the bundle only on new business — starting with the three prospects that had asked — at ₹1,910 a vehicle-month over 36 months, clearing by ₹2.89 the ₹1,907.11 that recovers ₹13,600 plus ₹2,856 of carry. He also said what it is not: at ₹1,910 Pantham gives up the ₹4,900 device margin it earns today, ₹65.66 lakh across a 1,340-unit year, so the bundle is cost-recovering, not margin-neutral. The ₹1.82 crore that full-volume adoption would tie up was, he told the board, the number the canvas never held.

  1. Bhoominathan asked his board to replace one revenue number with a base-and-conversion pair. What does a board lose by agreeing, and what does a single number give it that a pair does not?
  2. Where among the nine boxes would you record the capital a zero-upfront bundle ties up for 36 months, and what does a tenth box cost a tool whose discipline is fitting one sheet?
  3. Exhibit 3 splits Paasarai's shortfall into recruitment, FPO size and conversion. Which would you have tested in the first ninety days, and what would the test have had to show?

13Going deeper

What a business model is
The prior topic: nine boxes laying out what this defines in a sentence.
Revenue models
Unlocks R: transaction, subscription, licence and usage set price against periods differently.
Subscription economics
Where r and (1−r)a get cohorts, not the two-point 19,000/34,000 — Pudhumai's next correction.
Advertising business models
The payer is not the user, so the identity needs two bases.
Marketplace economics
Section 4's separability failure: liquidity, take rate, two-sided conversion.
Freemium as a business model
Where the free tier's cost belongs — Pudhumai's ₹112.32 lakh sits in F, and whether it should is the argument.
Hardware business models
Working capital, attach rates, and the ₹1,907.11-against-₹1,963.89 gap between recovering a cost and holding a margin.
case20v1-bm.canvas:
Chaibagan Direct: Nine Boxes Before the Board

A Lean Canvas decision case, Kolkata, November 2026

1. Opening

On Monday 2 November 2026, Koyena Sarkhel sat in the Chaibagan Direct office in Kolkata's Salt Lake and looked at the one slide that would not come right. The board was to meet on Friday 13 November. Diwali fell on Sunday 8 November, a heavy week for gifting tea, and the directors expected her plan for the ₹4.8 crore growth reserve left from the 2025 funding round, for November to April.

For three years the plan had been to acquire subscribers faster, and most board meetings had ended with a request for more. At the end of September 21,000 subscribers were active, and two messages from her team did not fit the plan. So Koyena decided to lay the business out on a Lean Canvas, nine boxes, and test each box against evidence instead of describing it. She needed one recommendation.

2. Company background

Koyena founded Chaibagan Direct in 2019 after eight years in tea packing. The company buys whole-leaf tea from estates in Assam and Darjeeling, packs it in Howrah, and sells a monthly box of three estate teas, 250 grams in all, at a list price of ₹899. Its customers are urban professionals in the eight largest metros. Payments run on UPI through Razorpay, and parcels travel with Delhivery.

The shelf is crowded. In supermarkets, Tata Tea and Tetley set the price expectation; online, Teabox and Vahdam sell premium loose-leaf, and Amazon and Flipkart carry them. Chaibagan's own claim is traceability: each box names its estates, and exclusive buying agreements with six estates covered 54 per cent of the kilograms bought in FY26, the year from April 2025 to March 2026. The Tea Board of India and FSSAI govern its quality.

3. The situation

Growth had been bought with advertising. In September 2026 Chaibagan spent ₹62.57 lakh to bring in 4,700 subscribers, 4,100 of them through paid social. Monthly subscription revenue stood near ₹1.60 crore. Subscribers and revenue were the numbers the board watched.

Two other findings arrived. A data scientist in Toronto built a cohort table from the 8,400 subscribers who started between January and March 2026, and found that of every 100 who began, 40 were still billed in month six. Kasturika Sadhukhan's team in Singapore read the 1,260 cancellation tickets from July to September, and 693 of them, 55 per cent, said the customer still had unopened boxes at home. Board packs through August had shown only subscribers, revenue and gross margin; from September they added CAC, six-month retention and contribution per subscriber.

On Thursday 29 October the team met at 8:30 pm in Kolkata, which was 11:00 am in Toronto, 7:00 pm in Dubai and 11:00 pm in Singapore. They agreed one test for each canvas box and a threshold for passing it. Exhibit 1 records the results, and Figure 1 shows the canvas they filled. Eight boxes met their thresholds. Channels did not, because paid social, which took 4,100 of 4,700 starts, did not: on the pooled cohort curve, an acquired subscriber would return about ₹1,160 of contribution within six months, against a paid-social acquisition cost of ₹1,450. Exhibit 2 shows the first figure, and Exhibit 3 splits acquisition cost by channel.

4. The people

Koyena Sarkhel, founder and chief executive, Kolkata. She wants a plan the board will not read as a retreat from growth: the company hopes to raise again in 2027, and the lead investor in Mumbai watches subscriber counts.

Kishalay Samaddar, head of estate partnerships, Jorhat. He negotiated the six exclusive agreements, which carry annual minimum purchases, and he needs volume to honour them. A Dubai gift retailer has given him a letter of intent for 5,000 gift boxes at ₹1,500 each, for delivery before Diwali 2027.

Kasturika Sadhukhan, customer-success lead, Singapore. She reads the cancellation tickets and wants subscribers to skip, pause and swap teas. A designer in Berlin has drawn the screens and engineers in Bengaluru and Pune estimate four weeks to build them, but the finance team counts a skipped box as lost revenue.

5. Exhibits

Read Exhibit 1 one row at a time; each box has its own base.

6. The options

Option A: scale paid social. Spend the whole ₹4.8 crore reserve on paid social at ₹80 lakh a month for six months. At today's CAC of ₹1,450 this brings in about 33,100 subscribers. On Exhibit 2's curve they return 80 per cent of the spend, ₹3.84 crore, within six months of joining, which leaves ₹96 lakh unrecovered in that window, a floor if CAC rises as monthly spend goes from ₹59.45 lakh to ₹80 lakh. The plan leaves cancellation behaviour and the gifting letter untouched.

Option B: open a gifting channel. Keep paid social at September's ₹59.45 lakh a month, ₹3.57 crore over six months, and spend ₹1.2 crore on two gifting salespeople, samples and travel to build corporate and diaspora sales, beginning with the Dubai retailer. The 5,000 boxes at ₹1,500 are ₹75 lakh of revenue, and Kishalay's costing puts contribution at 30 per cent, ₹22.5 lakh. The plan adds a customer segment and a lumpy revenue stream, and leaves retention untouched.

Option C: fewer paid subscribers, referrals and a flexible plan. Cut paid social to ₹30 lakh a month and put ₹10 lakh a month into referral credits, ₹2.4 crore in all over six months, and spend ₹1.0 crore on the skip, pause and swap plan, holding ₹1.4 crore in reserve. At ₹1,450, ₹30 lakh buys about 2,100 paid subscribers a month, roughly 2,000 fewer than September, and ₹10 lakh at ₹520 buys about 1,900 referrals against 600 in September. The plan leaves the Dubai letter unanswered until the new year.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. Restate the test for each box in Exhibit 1 in your own words. Which test would you trust least as evidence about its box, and why?
  2. Exhibit 3 shows a six-month contribution percentage for each channel, but both come from one pooled curve. What does that figure assume, and what could change it?
  3. Name the box or boxes each option is meant to change, and the evidence in the case that the box needs changing.
  4. Which option would you take to the board on 13 November? What would you measure by the end of March, and what result would make you reverse?

8. A note for the learner

A canvas is a diagnostic when every box is made to answer a question that evidence can settle. Koyena's nine tests were not a pitch: one box failed, and the lens then asks what feeds the failing box. A well-reasoned answer works on the cause rather than the symptom, states what it will measure, and says in advance what would reverse it.

One defensible path is Option C. The Channels test fails because projected six-month contribution is ₹1,160 against ₹1,450 of acquisition cost. Three inputs set that gap: the cost of acquiring a subscriber, the months she stays, and the contribution each month earns. Option C works on the first two: referral credits cost ₹520 a subscriber, and the flexible plan responds to the 693 cancellation tickets that mention unopened boxes. Paying back ₹1,450 inside six months would take 4.46 subscriber-months of ₹325, 25 per cent above today's 3.57, or a CAC 20 per cent lower.

The checkpoint is the share still billed in month four among starters between the mid-December launch and 31 December, the only starters reaching a fourth billing by March's end, against the 48 per cent in Exhibit 2, with paused subscribers reported separately. If the billed share is no higher and pauses do not explain it, the board has no evidence the plan works and can reopen the choice with the ₹1.4 crore still held. The Dubai letter concerns Diwali 2027, so Option B can wait for that review.
exp20v2-bm.canvas:
Business Model and Lean Canvas

Strategy & Business: nine boxes as a diagnostic, not a pitch

1. Two cities or one

On Tuesday 14 April 2026, Arulmozhi Hemanathan sat in a rented office in Mylapore, Chennai, rewriting a funding deck. She had founded Neythal Catch in August 2024 with Amarnath Harinathan, who ran sourcing. The company sold cleaned and cut fresh fish by subscription: two boxes a month at ₹900 a box, bought from fishing co-operatives at Kasimedu and Pulicat and delivered to households in fourteen Chennai pin codes. On 31 March it had 2,400 active subscribers.

Her draft asked a Chennai angel syndicate, meeting on Tuesday 21 April, for ₹6 crore to open Bengaluru. It promised an annualised revenue run rate (monthly revenue multiplied by twelve) of ₹30 crore by September 2027. Abinaya Hanumantharao, the part-time finance adviser, read it on Sunday and replied with one line: draw the nine boxes, and mark the one you would bet against.

Arulmozhi had filled in canvases at workshops and remembered coloured sticky notes, not decisions. But the stakes were concrete. A syndicate that funded a plan whose arithmetic failed would be funding a second city on top of a first city that was leaking subscribers, and ₹6 crore does not come back easily. This page follows her through the nine boxes.

2. The idea

A business model is the logic by which a firm creates value for a customer and keeps part of it as revenue. A canvas is a one-page template that forces that logic into nine labelled boxes, so that it can be read at a glance, argued over and marked up. Alexander Osterwalder developed the Business Model Canvas in doctoral work at the University of Lausanne in the early 2000s and published it with Yves Pigneur in Business Model Generation (2010). It was invented because forty-page business plans buried the assumptions on which everything rested; few could say which sentence, if wrong, sank the plan.

In 2010 Ash Maurya adapted it for start-ups as the Lean Canvas. He judged that a new venture's main risk is whether the problem is real, not who the partners are, and swapped four boxes accordingly.

Table 1. What the Lean Canvas swaps (approximate pairings)
Business Model Canvas box removedLean Canvas box added
Key PartnersProblem
Key ActivitiesSolution
Key ResourcesUnfair Advantage
Customer RelationshipsKey Metrics

The five boxes both versions share are Customer Segments, Value Proposition, Channels, Revenue Streams and Cost Structure. The sentence Arulmozhi could repeat in a meeting without sounding glib was this: every box is a guess, and the canvas shows which guess the other eight lean on.

3. How it actually works

Maurya suggests, roughly, filling the boxes in a deliberate order, which Arulmozhi followed. Choose a customer segment, a group that shares a problem and would pay to solve it. Write the problem and the existing alternatives customers use today. State the unique value proposition, the reason a customer would switch. Describe the solution, the channels that reach the segment, the revenue and cost structures, the key metrics that would tell her it is working, and last, the unfair advantage that a competitor cannot easily copy or buy.

Three steps are usually left implicit. First, every box should hold numbers or observable facts; "premium customers" is a mood, "1,240 planners" is a claim. Second, each box should carry an evidence grade: measured, estimated or guessed. Neythal measured the subscriber count and the per-box costs, estimated the reachable households, and guessed the Bengaluru figures. Third, the boxes must be checked against each other, since revenue equals customers times price times periods, and the customer count in Segments must be the count that Revenue and Cost use. Figure 1 uses 2,400 in all three places: Segments, Revenue (2,400 × ₹1,800) and Cost (₹1,100 × 2,400 = ₹26.4 lakh to have won them).

4. A worked example

Abinaya's challenge was to price one subscriber. Table 2 builds the contribution per box, which is price less the costs that vary with each delivery.

At two boxes a month a live subscriber contributes ₹144 a month. Acquiring one costs ₹1,100, the Q4 2025 advertising spend and referral credits divided by sign-ups. If monthly churn (the share of subscribers who cancel each month) is constant, a subscriber lives on average one divided by churn months. The team's first view was a single pooled figure, but Abinaya asked for the October to December 2025 sign-ups split by an onboarding question: do you cook fish four or more times a week? Those who said yes are planners; the rest are occasional buyers.

Implied churn is one minus the cube root of survival (7.95 and 20.03 per cent, rounded). The Mix column weights the two lifetimes by the 30/70 sign-up split. The canvas shows planners as 52 per cent of today's 2,400 (1,240); that is a stock of survivors, whereas the 30/70 split describes new sign-ups, and planners' longer lives lift their share of the stock. Neythal's average sign-up costs the same ₹1,100 in both segments, an assumption.

The mixed subscriber returns ₹1,044 against ₹1,100 spent to win them, a ratio of 0.95. Figure 2 shows the same fact over time: the 30/70 line flattens below the dashed acquisition-cost line and never crosses it.

The second pass. Change one input: write the Customer Segments box as planners only. Lifetime contribution becomes ₹1,800, a ratio of 1.64; if narrower targeting lifts acquisition cost to ₹1,500, the ratio is still 1.20. One box changed, and Revenue, Cost and Key Metrics moved with it. The same edit shrinks the revenue the canvas can honestly claim, which Table 4 tests against the deck's ₹30 crore. At ₹1,800 a subscriber a month, or ₹21,600 a year, ₹30 crore needs 13,889 subscribers.

Table 4. Does the revenue line fit the segment line?
