Households are Neythal's own estimates. Today's 2,400 is 5.5 per cent of Chennai's 43,524. The 30 per cent planner share is the sign-up mix applied to the whole reachable base, an assumption.

Capturing 15 per cent of the planners in both cities, a working assumption rather than a measurement, gives 3,917 subscribers and ₹8.46 crore a year. The canvas had found its weak box, and the deck's headline was nowhere near it.

5. Nuances a learner must absorb

A canvas is a set of hypotheses, not a plan

Each box records what the team currently believes, with a date. A canvas without a date cannot be checked, which makes it useless.

One canvas per segment

Neythal's single Segments box hid two customers with churn of 8 and 20 per cent. When two segments have different problems, value propositions or economics, draw two canvases; averaging them produces a business that does not exist.

Lean Canvas and Business Model Canvas answer different questions

The Lean version suits uncertainty about whether anyone wants the product. The original suits a firm whose offer is proven and whose question is how to organise partners, activities and resources around it. Using the wrong one hides the real risk.

The boxes constrain each other

A canvas is not nine independent lists. Revenue must equal customers times price times periods; costs must scale with the same customers. Most of the diagnostic value lies in the links between boxes, which is why Section 4 changed one box and traced the results.

Unfair advantage is rarely present at the start

The test is whether a rival could copy or buy it. Neythal's co-operative agreements are renewed yearly, so they are a head start, not a moat. An honest blank is better than a flattering entry.

What a canvas cannot tell you

It cannot say whether a guess is true, how large a market is, or how a competitor will respond. The 8 per cent planner churn is a measurement from 300 people over three months; it is evidence, and thin evidence at that.

Questions to ask before relying on one

Who filled it in, and when? Which boxes rest on measurement? Do the numbers in different boxes describe the same customers? Is any box a competitor's description of the market rather than the team's own?

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace; early and large

Table 5. Where the canvas bends
ProductBox carrying the weightWhat changes
ConsumerChannels, Cost StructureAcquisition cost and churn dominate
B2BCustomer Segments, RevenueA few large buyers; one buyer can distort the average
MarketplaceSegments, twiceTwo canvases, one per side

Neythal is a consumer subscription, so the weight sat on retention and acquisition cost. In B2B the same discipline applies to account counts: a dozen enterprise customers make a revenue line fragile, and the buyer who signs is rarely the person who uses the product. A marketplace needs a canvas for each side, because suppliers and buyers have different problems, and the revenue box must say which side pays.

Scale changes the use. An early-stage team redraws the canvas monthly because boxes are guesses. A large company draws one per business unit and uses it as a map of dependencies, since its question is rarely whether anyone wants the product.

7. Common mistakes

Adjectives instead of numbers. From outside, most boxes could belong to any company in the sector. The misunderstanding is that the canvas is a pitch. The cheapest diagnostic is to replace the company's name with a rival's and see whether anything needs editing.

One canvas for several customers. From outside, retention is quoted as one blended figure and few can say who leaves. The misunderstanding is that a segment is a market category rather than a group with shared behaviour. The diagnostic is to split the main metric by an onboarding answer, as Abinaya did.

A revenue line that does not fit the customer line. The deck's market-size slide and revenue slide quote different customers. The misunderstanding is that boxes can be filled independently. The diagnostic is division: revenue over price over periods gives a customer count, and that count is compared with Segments.

Filing it. From outside, the canvas is older than a quarter and has no crossed-out entry. The diagnostic is to count how many boxes changed since the last review; zero suggests nobody tested anything.

8. What good looks like

A well-handled version of Arulmozhi's decision has a dated canvas for each segment. Every box carries an evidence grade. The riskiest box is marked, with a stated test, a threshold and a date. The Revenue box reconciles to the Segments box in one visible line of arithmetic, and the deck's headline is the figure that survives that line. Someone who has never met the team can say within a minute what the team is least sure of.

9. The decision, and what comes next

On Monday 20 April Arulmozhi redrew the canvas for planners alone and dropped the ₹30 crore claim. She kept the Bengaluru plan but made it conditional: before any money goes to a second city, a Chennai cohort of planners must show at least 82 per cent survival at month two, which implies monthly churn near 9.5 per cent and a lifetime contribution of about ₹1,524, just above a ₹1,500 acquisition cost. She told the syndicate the weak box was Customer Segments, and showed it the arithmetic.

Next, study pricing and unit economics, because the canvas flags the weak box but contribution, payback and lifetime value say how weak it is.

Two questions to sit with. Which box on a canvas you have drawn would you bet against, and what evidence would change your mind? If two of your segments had churn of 8 and 20 per cent, which decisions on your canvas would differ for each?

Dibru Commerce Technologies: The Model on the Whiteboard

Bengaluru · November 2026

Four revenue lines, a term sheet with two tests in it, and a founder spending the weekend working out which part of her business is load-bearing.

1. Sunday night

The rain had stopped over Indiranagar by eleven, and Luitika Teron had run out of reasons to leave the flat. On the wall of the second bedroom, where the whiteboard had lived since before the company had an office, she had drawn nine rectangles on Saturday morning and been adding to them since. Seven across the top, two underneath. Most now carried something in her handwriting. Two carried a question mark.

It was Sunday 15 November 2026, a week after Diwali. The board of Dibru Commerce Technologies met at half past nine next morning above the Hosur Road office, and the only substantive item was headed Revenue model: direction. Behind it sat a term sheet from a Singapore growth fund — ₹310 crore of primary capital at a pre-money valuation of ₹1,240 crore — lapsing on 15 December if unsigned. It carried two conditions, both tested on the audited accounts for the year ending 31 March 2028, and both about the shape of the revenue rather than its size.

Luitika had founded Dibru in 2017 to sell software to the fast-moving consumer goods distributors of tier-two and tier-three India. It now had four revenue lines, 1,689 live distributors at the end of September (Exhibit 2), offices in six cities on three continents, and no agreement about which of the four lines the others were paying for.

2. How Dibru got here

Dibru was registered in May 2017 and named for the river that runs past the town Luitika grew up in. The first product was unglamorous: a distributor management system replacing the ledger book and the WhatsApp order, sold as an annual licence. It went to a Nashik distributor in August 2018 at ₹96,000 a year.

In January 2021 Dibru put an ordering app in the hands of the distributor's retailers, and with it a second line: a platform fee charged to the distributor on the value of orders placed through the app. For three years nobody had cause to separate them.

The decision that still shapes 2026 was taken in March 2023. To win the co-selling support of Dhenu Consumer Brands Limited, a listed foods and household-care company whose field force reaches distributors Dibru's staff could not afford to visit, Luitika signed a five-year agreement to 31 March 2028. Dhenu receives 22 per cent of the subscription revenue from every distributor introduced through its field force, for as long as that distributor stays live, and holds category exclusivity on any insights product Dibru sells in Dhenu's categories. Both clauses survive a change of control.

3. The industry around it

Indian FMCG distribution is being rebuilt in public. ONDC has made the question of who owns the retailer relationship a live one; UPI and the NPCI rails made collection from a kirana counter routine; GST e-invoicing pushed small distributors into structured data. Udaan and Jumbotail sell inventory to the retailers Dibru's distributors sell to, Reliance Retail's cash-and-carry network reaches them directly, and the goods moving over Dibru's platform carry the labels of Dabur, Marico, Parle, Britannia and Amul. None is a software competitor exactly, and each changes what software is worth.

Two regulatory frames bear on Dibru's revenue. The Reserve Bank's digital lending directions govern how a platform may be paid for sourcing credit: the fee comes from the lender, not the borrower, and Dibru carries no default loss guarantee on the book it refers. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act governs the retailer order data the insights line rests on; the consent notices Dibru collects it under were drafted in 2024 for one named lender.

Dibru's exposure beyond India is one contract. Dhow Gate Trading LLC, a Dubai grocery and wholesale group, licensed the platform on 1 July 2025 for 36 months at ₹9.60 crore, deployed as a dedicated instance inside the UAE under a data residency clause.

4. What was believed, and what has since turned out wrong

In January 2021 the platform fee was introduced on the belief that it would carry the model as order value grew, because its cost would not grow with it. The FY26 audited accounts (Exhibit 1) put the fee line at ₹17.30 crore of revenue against ₹11.90 crore of direct cost, almost all of it the field reconciliation team, which Lohajit Timung's zonal managers say scales with disputed orders rather than with their value.

In March 2023 the Dhenu channel was taken on the belief that it was a cheaper way to add a distributor than Dibru's own field sales, and on the acquisition numbers Dibru keeps (Exhibit 3) it is. The 22 per cent share is not in those numbers; since 2023 it has been recorded as a cost of revenue inside the subscription line, and appears in Exhibit 5.

In May 2024 the credit referral line was launched on the belief that it stood apart from the rest — a fee from a lender, no capital at risk, no field cost. The fee is 0.875 per cent of disbursed value, which on ₹1,120 crore disbursed across 1,75,000 originations in FY26 is ₹9.80 crore. On 9 November 2026 the lender, Dighal Finance Limited, proposed a flat ₹400 an origination instead.

And since 2017 the model had been drawn with one customer segment. By November 2026 the subscription line holds a licence sold to a retail group outside India, the insights line is paid for by seven brands, the credit line by a lender, and the 84,600 retailers who placed an order in March 2026 pay nothing.

5. The people

Luitika Teron, 38, founder and chief executive, Bengaluru. Holds that the weak box is Revenue Streams and that Dibru must pick one line before the board picks for her. Her incentive is the term sheet: she is diluted far less at ₹1,240 crore than at anything she expects she could raise in March. She has not told the board she first drew the nine boxes this weekend.
Lonika Tikadar, 44, chief financial officer, Bengaluru. Argues the problem is Cost Structure: the 196-person field organisation is charged across lines by a convention untouched since 2023. Her 4 November note models the subscription option and states that it clears both investor tests. She has not circulated the working behind the ₹7.60 crore of field cost she assumes persists.
Lohajit Timung, 41, vice-president, field operations, Pune. Says the weak box is Channels: Dibru treats the distributor as customer and as route to the retailer at once, and prices only the first. He is measured on live accounts, on which Finance's price rise falls. He has not said that four of his eleven zonal managers have been approached by a competitor.
Luhita Taid, 35, head of product design, Berlin. Says the weak box is Value Propositions: the app's value to the retailer has never been measured, nor the retailer asked to pay. Her 2027 roadmap is almost all retailer-side. Her only willingness-to-pay study, whose size she has not mentioned, covered eleven retailers in one Pune ward.
Lubdhak Tisso, 39, principal data scientist, Toronto. Says the weak box is Key Resources: the order data is not unambiguously Dibru's to sell, between the Dhenu exclusivity and consent notices written for one lender. He has an offer from a Canadian analytics firm, and has not said his own 2024 memo recommended the language he calls thin.
Lekhasri Tezpuria, 36, customer success lead for Asia, Singapore. Says the weak box is Customer Segments: Dhow Gate is not a distributor, buys nothing the Indian accounts buy, and runs on a separate instance with four assigned engineers. She carries the regional renewal number. Dhow Gate has twice asked her what becomes of the UAE instance if Dibru is acquired; she has not passed this on.
Lavendra Tiladar, 50, head of enterprise sales, New Jersey. Says the weak box is Key Partnerships and the answer more Dhenu-style agreements; he reads first-half FY27 as evidence the model works at scale. His variable pay is written on new contract value. Two of three brands in his late-stage pipeline compete in Dhenu's exclusive categories, which he has not said.

Lonika Tikadar, note to the board pack, Wednesday 4 November“Holding FY26 volumes and losing no account, a 77.9 per cent uplift on the average licence replaces the platform fee exactly, and on that basis the subscription option clears both of the investor's tests.”
Lohajit Timung, zonal call, Thursday 12 November“You want me to tell a Solapur distributor his bill goes from ₹1.56 lakh to ₹2.78 lakh and that he should be pleased because something else went away. Which of my eleven managers makes that call?”
Lavendra Tiladar, email to Luitika, Friday 13 November, 09:12 EST“Order value in the first half was ₹2,310 crore. Double it and we are over ₹4,600 crore against ₹3,840 crore last year. We need two more Dhenus, not a theory.”
Lohajit Timung, reply, Friday 13 November, 20:04 IST“You cannot double a half that already has September stocking in it, nor assume the Diwali half repeats it. Ask me in April.”
Lubdhak Tisso, chat thread, Friday 13 November, 11:20 EST“Before we sell insights as the main line, which clause lets us sell a Dhenu competitor a view of Dhenu's own categories? I have asked three times since June.”
Luhita Taid, message to Luitika, Saturday 14 November, 21:10 CET“Every box on that board is about the distributor. Eighty-four thousand shops open our app monthly and we have never asked one of them for money.”
Lekhasri Tezpuria, Monday 9 November, 09:00 SGT“Dhow Gate's finance director asked again whether the UAE instance travels if we are sold. Twice now.”

8. The options as Luitika sees them

A. Consolidate on the licence. Withdraw the platform fee and raise the distributor licence by 77.9 per cent — ₹17.30 crore over the ₹22.20 crore of FY26 licences billed in India — from an average of ₹1.56 lakh a year per closing account to ₹2.78 lakh, which at FY26 volumes and with no account lost leaves distributor-paid revenue where it was. Finance's 4 November working assumes ₹7.60 crore of the ₹11.90 crore now on the platform fee line persists, the reconciliation team serving the same accounts either way. The Dhow Gate instance is untouched; the Dhenu share, computed on subscription revenue, rises with the licence.

B. Consolidate on the transaction. Withdraw the licence and raise the platform fee from 0.4505 per cent of order value to 1.0286 per cent, which on FY26 order value of ₹3,840 crore is the ₹39.50 crore the distributors paid across both lines, about 2.28 times the present rate. The Dhenu share is computed on subscription revenue, so it goes with the licence.

C. Make credit the engine. Accept Dighal's flat ₹400 an origination, which on FY26 volumes of 1,75,000 originations is ₹7.00 crore against the ₹9.80 crore booked, and seek the ₹2.80 crore difference in volume from a second lender. That requires the consent notices to be re-issued across the retailer base under the DPDP Act.

D. Make insights the engine. Sell order-level category insights to brands as the principal line. At the FY26 average of ₹44.29 lakh across seven brands, and holding that price, ₹30 crore of insights revenue, above half of FY26 revenue, is 68 brands. Dhenu's exclusivity runs to 31 March 2028; Dibru has not priced releasing it early.

Each of the four is written as a change to the revenue line. In Figure 2 the Dhow Gate contract, a licence sold to a group that is not a distributor, and the seven brands appear only as counts in the Customer Segments box; neither has a line of its own elsewhere.

9. The deadline and what cannot move

Cash at 31 October 2026 was ₹38.40 crore and net burn in that month ₹2.65 crore, which at that rate is 14.5 months, to mid-January 2028. The term sheet lapses on 15 December 2026; its two conditions, tested on the FY28 audited accounts, are subscription of at least 60 per cent of revenue and blended gross margin of at least 70 per cent. In FY26 subscription was ₹24.60 crore of ₹54.80 crore, 44.9 per cent, at a blended margin of 59.7 per cent.

The Dhenu agreement runs to 31 March 2028 and the share follows the account, not the contract date. The Dhow Gate contract runs to 30 June 2028, its data residency clause forbids serving it from the Mumbai region, and the instance took nine engineer-months to build and keeps four engineers assigned. Headcount is 318, of whom 196 are field, across Bengaluru, Pune, Berlin, Toronto, Singapore and New Jersey; hiring has been frozen since 1 September 2026.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Figure 2 and Exhibit 5 lay the model out in nine boxes. Working down Exhibit 5, which figures are measured on a base that matches the box they sit in, and which are not? What follows for the box with no figure?
  2. Exhibit 4 gives three readings of revenue per distributor account. Which, if any, is the right input to a licence-price decision, and what would you need to know to choose?
  3. Take Lonika Tikadar's 4 November note with Option A. Using Exhibit 1 and the ₹7.60 crore she assumes persists, work out the subscription share and blended gross margin Option A produces against the term sheet's two tests. What does each test turn on?
  4. Exhibit 3 puts co-sell at ₹1.10 lakh an account and direct sales at ₹1.87 lakh; Exhibit 5 puts an estimated ₹1.43 crore a year with the same partner. Over how many years of an account's life would the Dhenu share close that gap, and what must you assume to work it out?
  5. Luhita Taid and Lubdhak Tisso locate the weakness in different boxes. What single measurement would most change your view of each claim, and what would it cost Dibru to obtain?
  6. What should Luitika Teron do on Monday morning, and what would she say to the board about the term sheet, the Dighal proposal and the Dhow Gate contract?

At a quarter to midnight she wrote a figure into the Key Resources box, looked at it, and rubbed it out. The board met in ten hours, the whiteboard still had two question marks on it, and she was no longer sure the nine were the right nine.

Cost structure and operating leverage

Strategy & Business, Business Models: which costs are fixed, which are variable, and how scale changes the model.

1. The August offer

On Thursday 13 August 2026, Charukesi Jeevanandam, general manager of Rupakam, a Chennai software company, received a message from her cloud provider. Its account manager would lock Rupakam's server capacity at a discount if Rupakam signed a 36-month commitment by Monday 31 August. The commitment was a fixed monthly charge, payable whether or not the capacity was used.

Rupakam sells a monthly subscription that reconciles GST invoices for small garment manufacturers in Tiruppur and Coimbatore. Her finance head, Chandrahasan Janarthanan, had put the company's position on one page, summarised in Table 1. The business was profitable, but only just: ₹6 lakh on ₹108 lakh of monthly revenue.

Table 1. Rupakam at 31 July 2026 (monthly, current pay-as-you-go cloud)
ItemFigure
Paying accounts1,200
Price per account per month₹9,000
Team size, and loaded cost per person per month30 people, ₹2.0 lakh each
Monthly operating profit₹6 lakh

The stakes were uneven. If accounts kept growing, the commitment would add profit quickly. If a competitor or a regulatory change shrank the base by a third, Rupakam would owe the same fixed charge on a smaller business. Jeevanandam had to decide which kind of company she wanted to run, and the decision turned on one question: which of her costs move with the number of customers, and which do not?

2. The idea

A variable cost rises and falls with volume; each extra account at Rupakam brings its own cloud usage, payment-gateway fee and text-message charges. A fixed cost stays the same across a range of volume, such as salaries and office rent. Operating leverage is the degree to which a business's costs are fixed rather than variable, and therefore how violently operating profit moves when volume moves.

The problem it was invented to solve was a manager's, not an accountant's: how much must be sold before the business stops losing money? The break-even chart, usually credited to the engineer Walter Rautenstrauch around 1930, drew the answer as two lines crossing. The vocabulary of contribution and of a "degree" of leverage was developed by cost accountants and corporate-finance teachers over the following decades; the attributions here are approximate.

Jeevanandam could repeat the idea in a meeting without sounding glib: each extra customer adds only the margin left after variable cost, while fixed cost does not care, so profit moves much faster than revenue in both directions.

3. How it works

Begin with the unit. Rupakam's unit is a paying account for a month. Its price is ₹9,000. Chandrahasan Janarthanan listed the costs that arrive with each account: ₹1,800 of cloud usage, ₹180 of gateway fee (2 per cent of the price) and ₹520 of messaging and document-reading charges, a total of ₹2,500. That is the variable cost per unit.

The step practitioners leave implicit comes next. Price minus variable cost is the contribution: ₹6,500 per account, or 72.2 per cent of price (6,500 ÷ 9,000), called the contribution margin. Contribution is not profit; it is what each account contributes toward fixed costs, and it becomes profit only after those are covered.

Fixed costs were the second list. Thirty people, sales team included, at ₹2.0 lakh each per month, a rate per person, come to ₹60 lakh for the whole team, or ₹7.2 crore a year. Offices, software tools and administration added ₹12 lakh. Fixed costs total ₹72 lakh a month. Profit is therefore contribution times accounts, less fixed cost: four inputs (price, variable cost per account, accounts, fixed cost), all free to vary. Contribution margin, break-even and leverage are derived from them and add no degrees of freedom.

Break-even is the volume at which total contribution equals fixed cost: ₹72 lakh ÷ ₹6,500 = 1,108 accounts, rounded up because a fraction of an account does not pay. Rupakam stood at 1,200, a margin of safety of 92 accounts, 7.7 per cent of its base. The degree of operating leverage is contribution divided by operating profit: ₹78 lakh ÷ ₹6 lakh = 13.0. A 1 per cent change in accounts moves profit by about 13 per cent.

4. A worked example, and a second pass

Option A is the status quo. Option B is the commitment: ₹9.6 lakh a month of fixed charge buys capacity for up to 1,600 accounts, and the cloud charge per account falls from ₹1,800 to ₹600. Table 2 sets the two side by side at today's 1,200 accounts.

Table 2. The two options at 1,200 accounts (monthly; ₹ per account unless stated)
LineA: pay as you goB: commit
Variable cost per account (cloud + 180 + 520)2,5001,300
Contribution per account (9,000 minus variable)6,5007,700
Contribution margin72.2%85.6%
Contribution, all accounts, ₹ lakh (× 1,200)78.092.4
Fixed cost, ₹ lakh (72, then 72 + 9.6)72.081.6
Operating profit, ₹ lakh6.010.8

Degree of operating leverage (contribution ÷ profit)13.08.6

Break-even: 81.6 lakh ÷ 7,700 = 1,059.7, rounded up. Leverage B: 92.4 ÷ 10.8 = 8.56.

The commitment raised fixed cost by ₹9.6 lakh and cut variable cost by ₹1,200 an account, so it paid back at once: 1,200 × ₹1,200 = ₹14.4 lakh saved against ₹9.6 lakh committed, a gain of ₹4.8 lakh. The two options cost the same where ₹1,200 × accounts = ₹9.6 lakh, which is 800 accounts. Above 800, B is cheaper; below it, A is.

The second pass changes one input, the account count, in Table 3. At 900 accounts, a 25 per cent fall, A's profit moves from +₹6 lakh to −₹13.5 lakh, exactly what leverage of 13.0 predicts (6 − 13.0 × 25% × 6 = −13.5). B falls from +₹10.8 lakh to −₹12.3 lakh. B suffers a larger absolute loss in the fall (₹23.1 lakh against ₹19.5 lakh) yet is still ahead at 900. Below 800 it loses.

Table 3. Monthly operating profit by account count (₹ lakh)
Accounts7008009001,2001,500
A: pay as you go−26.5−20.0−13.56.025.5
B: commit−27.7−20.0−12.310.833.9

The figure shows why a commitment is a bet on volume. B's steeper line pays for its higher fixed cost only while volume stays to the right of the crossing.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

Fixed over what range, and for how long

A fixed cost is fixed across a range and a horizon. Option B's capacity covers 1,600 accounts; beyond that, a further block must be bought, so the cost steps up. Support staff behave the same way: hired in ones, they look fixed month to month and variable over a year. Ask "fixed up to what, and until when?"

Fixed is not the same as unavoidable

A salary can be cut by redundancy; the 36-month commitment cannot be cut without penalty. Both are called fixed; their exit costs differ greatly. The useful question is who can undo the cost, and at what price.

Contribution margin is not gross margin

Contribution deducts only costs that move with volume. Gross margin, as most companies report it, also deducts some fixed items such as support salaries or hosting reserved in advance. Quote a margin without naming which, and two people will argue over one number.

Operating leverage is not financial leverage

Financial leverage comes from borrowing; operating leverage comes from fixed costs. A company can have one without the other, and they compound when held together.

Leverage is a reading at one volume, not a property of the firm

Rupakam's 13.0 is true at 1,200 accounts. At 1,320 accounts (10 per cent more) A's contribution is ₹85.8 lakh, profit ₹13.8 lakh and leverage 6.2. The measure falls as profit grows. A business near break-even is highly levered; one far above it is not.

The average unit hides the distribution

The ₹1,800 cloud cost is an average. If a few large accounts use most of the capacity, the real variable cost for a new account of that type is higher, and the formula is blind to this unless the unit is redefined.

Price is an input, not a given

A 10 per cent price cut to ₹8,100 leaves contribution of ₹5,600 under A. To hold the ₹6 lakh profit, Rupakam needs (72 + 6) ÷ 0.056 = 1,393 accounts, 16.1 per cent more. The model cannot say whether that many extra customers exist; it turns a guess about demand into a number to test, and cannot supply the forecast.

6. How it looks in different products and at different stages

Table 4. Where the cost sits, by product type
ProductMostly fixedMostly variable
Consumer appEngineering, brandPayment fees, support, acquisition spend per user
B2B software (Rupakam)Engineering, sales teamHosting, third-party services
MarketplaceTechnology, trust-and-safety teamPayment fees, incentives, delivery or insurance per transaction

In consumer products, acquisition spend behaves like a variable cost: each new user is bought, which blunts leverage. B2B software tends to carry a high fixed share, but annual contracts, where used, also fix the revenue, so leverage is partly tamed. In a marketplace the supply side must exist before demand, a fixed burden carried while volume is thin; thereafter each extra transaction is cheap, so leverage is large once both sides are active.

Stage changes the picture too. An early-stage company, with few customers, is far below break-even; leverage in the formal sense is undefined or negative, and the question is how far to the right break-even lies. A large firm sits well above it, so its leverage figure is low, and its real exposure is the size of its commitments.

7. Common mistakes

Pricing a project off the whole team's cost. The symptom is a business case whose cost is several times what the people involved are paid. The misunderstanding is mixing a rate per person with a rate for the team. At ₹2.0 lakh per person per month, one person-week costs ₹46,154 (2.0 lakh × 12 ÷ 52). A four-person squad working six weeks is 24 person-weeks, ₹11.1 lakh. Priced off the whole team's ₹7.2 crore annual cost (₹83.1 lakh for six weeks), the same project looks 7.5 times dearer, which is 30 ÷ 4. The cheapest diagnostic is to divide any labour cost by headcount and ask whether the answer is a salary.

Treating a fixed cost as free at the margin. The symptom is discounting to win accounts below ₹2,500 under A, where each one loses money. The diagnostic is to compare any quoted price with variable cost per unit before approving it.

Quoting a margin without its definition. The symptom is two reports disagreeing on "margin". The diagnostic is to ask which costs sit above the line.

Reading leverage from one point. The symptom is a forecast that applies 13.0 to a 40 per cent volume change. The diagnostic is to recompute profit at the new volume from contribution and fixed cost.

8. What good looks like

A well-handled version of the August decision starts with a one-page split of cost into fixed and variable, with each rate stated per person or per team, per account or per month. It shows both options' profit at five volumes, including one that hurts. It names the crossing volume, 800 accounts, and expresses it as a distance from today, a third below 1,200. And it records who can undo each commitment and at what price.

9. The decision, and what to learn next

Jeevanandam signed on 28 August. Her reasoning was arithmetic first: B was ahead of A anywhere above 800 accounts, and the largest single-month net fall in accounts in the previous 24 months had been 31, or 2.6 per cent of the base. A fall of 400 accounts inside 36 months means an average net loss of 11 accounts every month (400 ÷ 36 = 11.1), about a third of the worst month observed, with no offsetting growth. Growth also favoured B: accounts had risen from 960 to 1,200 in a year, 25 per cent, and at compound growth of 25 per cent a year the 1,600-account ceiling lay roughly fifteen months away (20 months if growth is a flat 240 accounts a year). Beyond it a further capacity block must be bought, at a price the offer does not quote, so Table 3 stops at 1,500. She added a review trigger: if accounts fell below 1,000, she would reopen the cost plan.

The next topics are unit economics, which restates the same split per customer and adds lifetime and acquisition cost, and pricing, where the break-even volume for a price change is computed as above.

Two questions to sit with. What in your own product is called fixed but could be undone in a quarter, and what is called variable but is in fact committed? And if Rupakam's account count had been falling 2 per cent a month instead of rising, would the same arithmetic have pointed to the other option?

Strategy & Business · Business Models

Cost structure and operating leverage

Which costs are fixed, which are variable, and how scale changes the model — two companies, one fortnight, one trade.

Section 1Two decisions, one question

On Tuesday 14 April 2026, at a converted spinning shed in Coimbatore, Dhanavel Kannabiran had a one-page note in front of him and a board call at four. Sahasrara Instruments Private Limited makes a bench-top haematology analyser for small NABL-accredited laboratories and sells the cartridge it consumes. In the year to 31 March 2026 it sold 1,250 analysers at ₹1.80 lakh each, billed 37.80 lakh cartridges at ₹46 and collected ₹18,000 of subscription per analyser-year on an average active base of 3,500 machines: ₹4,618.80 lakh of revenue, ₹475.10 lakh of operating profit. The note proposed placing 900 of next year's analysers free against a 36-month commitment to buy 1,500 cartridges a year rather than selling them. His chief financial officer, Dhayanithi Karuppiah, had written three words in the margin: who funds this?

Four days earlier, on Friday 10 April, Devahuti Kambhampati took a similar question to the board of Sthiti Labs Private Limited in Hyderabad. Sthiti reads secured credit files of a hundred and eighty pages for thirty-eight non-banking financial companies, at ₹2,350 a file plus ₹24.00 lakh of platform fee per lender-year. A file consumes about 9,000 accelerator-seconds, or 2.50 accelerator-hours. Sthiti holds a laddered three-year reservation, renewed in blocks, on 22 accelerators at ₹20.25 lakh per accelerator-year and buys peaks on demand at ₹418 per accelerator-hour. Deenadayalan Kuchimanchi, who runs the platform, wanted six more. Devaprabhu Kondaveeti, the growth investor on the board, wanted to know why a company losing ₹468.38 lakh a year would volunteer more fixed cost.

Neither decision is about cost reduction. Both ask how much of the cost base to make fixed, and what that does to profit's shape.

Section 2The idea, and who disagrees about it

A cost is variable only with respect to a named driver, over a named range of that driver, and over a named horizon. Drop any of the three and the classification stops meaning anything. Sahasrara's cartridge material is variable with cartridges, between roughly 20 and 48 lakh units, over any horizon beyond the eight-week purchase-order cycle. Its ₹186.00 lakh of regulatory and quality spending is fixed with respect to cartridges and analysers alike but variable with respect to licences held, a driver that moves once in several years. Fixed and variable are properties of a cost paired with a driver, a range and a horizon, not of the cost alone.

Idle capacity forced the distinction on accounting. John Maurice Clark's Studies in the Economics of Overhead Costs (1923) argued that overhead has no single correct figure, leaving the dictum that there are different costs for different purposes; break-even charts spread the idea. Two schools later attacked that apparatus from opposite sides. Robin Cooper and Robert Kaplan's activity-based costing, in the Harvard Business Review in 1988, held that apparently fixed overhead is driven by transactions, batches and variety rather than units, so spreading it on volume mis-prices small orders. The throughput tradition that grew out of Eliyahu Goldratt's theory of constraints went the other way: in the short run nothing but material is variable, and the only questions are throughput and the constraint.

Each school signs propositions the others refuse. The contribution school signs below capacity, a price above variable cost improves profit and refuses fully absorbed unit cost is decision-relevant. The activity-based school signs overhead is caused, and the cause is rarely volume and refuses period costs should be spread on units. The throughput school signs only the constraint's hour has a cost and will not allocate at all. A fourth position, visible in the cloud-cost argument following Sarah Wang and Martin Casado's 2021 essay, treats the choice as buying flexibility, a premium per unit purchasing the option to stop; it signs the right structure depends on forecast variance.

Section 3Mechanics: the recut, and what it yields

Expert practice recuts the profit and loss account by behaviour rather than function, each rate per unit of its own driver: Sahasrara's ₹23.00 lakh of engineering cost is per person-year across 26 people, not per team.

Exhibit 1. Sahasrara Instruments, year to 31 March 2026, recut by behaviour. Cartridge volume is 1,080 per active analyser-year on average × 3,500.

Distributor commission sits inside the analyser and cartridge rates. One split governs every Sahasrara figure here.

The decision-relevant quantities then follow. Contribution is 4,618.80 − 2,288.70 = ₹2,330.10 lakh, 2,330.10 / 4,618.80 = 50.4482 per cent of revenue, so the variable-cost ratio is 49.5518 per cent. Operating profit is 2,330.10 − 1,855.00 = ₹475.10 lakh. Break-even revenue is 1,855.00 / 0.504482 = ₹3,677.04 lakh, 79.61 per cent of actual, a margin of safety of 20.39 per cent. The degree of operating leverage, contribution over operating profit, is 2,330.10 / 475.10 = 4.9044 — the margin of safety restated, since 1 / 0.2039 = 4.9044. Ten per cent more volume at constant mix lifts profit to ₹708.11 lakh, up 49.04 per cent.

Two second-order points get skipped. Operating leverage is local: a derivative at one volume, collapsing as you move from break-even. Sahasrara's 4.9044 becomes 2,912.62 / 1,057.62 = 2.7539 at a volume 25 per cent higher, 47.25 lakh cartridges, still inside the sealing line. And the identity behind all of it — profit = (price − unit variable cost) × volume − fixed cost — binds five quantities with one equation, so four are free and the fifth follows; those who object that "these are not free parameters" mean the five are estimated from overlapping data, a precision problem, not a counting one.

Section 4When the frame applies, and when it misleads

Three conditions can be stated as tests, and each has to be run on both companies. Does the named driver actually drive the line? At Sahasrara it does for cartridge material, one cartridge per test; not for selling cost, since 34 salaried people cost ₹391.00 lakh whether they sell 900 analysers or 1,600, so a percentage-of-revenue treatment is wrong by construction. At Sthiti it does for human adjudication, bought per file, not for its 41 engineers. Does the range contain the plan? The sealing line is fixed at ₹412.00 lakh only to its 48-lakh design throughput; a plan that doubles volume needs a second line. Sthiti's range ends at 60,544 reserved files; its plan is already outside it. Is the horizon shorter than the commitment? Sthiti's reservation has 26 months left in April 2026, so inside that window the ₹445.50 lakh is fixed in the strict sense that no decision removes it.

The frame actively misleads in three situations: a step cost whose step lies inside the planning range, which is Sthiti's position; an accept-or-reject decision taken on absorbed unit cost, which Saptarang Fresh will demonstrate by getting wrong; and a driver that is a proxy for the real one. Sahasrara books service at ₹3,600 per active analyser, but field visits are driven by cartridge-handling errors clustered in the ninety days after installation, so in a year of heavy installation that rate under-recovers. The range test is live here too: Exhibit 3 prices the choice between the contract filler and an in-house line.

Section 5Hard edge cases, and what mature firms really do

Sthiti is the instructive case, because its principal cost is neither fixed nor variable but step-fixed with a visible step. Its 22 reserved accelerators offer 8,600 usable hours each after maintenance, 1,89,200 in all; peak shape fills only 80.0 per cent of them, so the fleet delivers 1,51,360 hours, which at 2.50 hours a file is 60,544 files. FY26 volume was 76,000, so 15,456 files — 38,640 hours — ran on demand at ₹418, ₹161.52 lakh. Sthiti therefore has two marginal costs: below 60,544 files a marginal file adds only ₹414.95 of non-compute variable cost, its accelerator hour being paid for already; above it, 2.50 × 418 = ₹1,045 of compute too, ₹1,459.95.

Exhibit 5. Sthiti Labs, year to 31 March 2026. Reserved capacity is fixed — the reservation is non-cancellable, 26 months to run; overflow is variable. This split governs every Sthiti figure here.
LineDriver and rate₹ lakh
File processing revenue76,000 files at ₹2,3501,786.00
Platform revenue38 lenders at ₹24.00 lakh each912.00
Total revenue2,698.00
On-demand accelerator overflow38,640 hours at ₹418161.52

Engineering, research41 people at ₹34.00 lakh each1,394.00

Contribution ₹2,221.12 lakh, 82.3248 per cent of revenue; operating loss ₹468.38 lakh. That ratio flatters per-file economics, because the ₹912.00 lakh platform line carries no variable cost: variable cost per file is 476.88 lakh / 76,000 = ₹627.47, so file-level contribution is (2,350 − 627.47) / 2,350 = 73.30 per cent. Hours reconcile with Exhibit 4.

Other seams bend the same way. Where two products share one constrained resource — Sahasrara's sealing line runs two cartridge formats — the fixed cost is joint and any per-product unit cost rests on an indefensible allocation. In a marketplace the driver question comes first: fulfilment scales with orders, trust-and-safety with listings, and one cost per order mis-reads leverage whenever the listings-to-orders ratio moves. Regulated costs are fixed per entity and per licence; Sahasrara's ₹186.00 lakh does not halve when volume halves. At the organisational seam a reservation is signed by finance and consumed by engineering, which is why mature firms buy commitments as a ladder of staggered expiries rather than one block, and charge teams a dual rate: low inside committed capacity, the on-demand rate above it. Exhibit 6 prices that threshold.

Section 6Eight things experts see that competent practitioners miss

One. "Fixed" is a claim about a horizon, and the horizon sits in a contract. The tell is that an expert asks the notice period before the number. Sthiti's ₹445.50 lakh is fixed for 26 months and variable at month 27; its 41 engineers are fixed over a quarter, variable over a year. Fixedness does not belong to the cost category: two lines in one category can have opposite horizons.

Two. Step costs hide inside the word "variable". The tell is a unit cost suspiciously stable across volumes: real variable costs wobble with purchase lots and wage drift, so a flat rate usually means a block divided by a volume. Sahasrara's ₹412.00 lakh sealing line is ₹10.90 a cartridge at FY26 volume and ₹7.49 at 55 lakh, past its 48-lakh capacity anyway.

Three. Average variable cost is not marginal cost, and with a step it matches neither zone. Sthiti's exhibit shows ₹627.47 of variable cost a file; the marginal file in slack costs ₹414.95 and above the step ₹1,459.95. The average is an artefact of the mix; the tell is that it drifts month to month while the product does not.

Four. Operating leverage is a local derivative, not a company attribute. Sahasrara's leverage falls 43.85 per cent for a quarter more volume, the same ₹1,855.00 lakh being a smaller share of a larger contribution. The tell is one leverage figure across a three-year plan; it confuses the structure with the operating point.

Five. Every labour rate is per person or per team, and the gap is the team size. The tell is a cost per engineer-week got by dividing a squad's annual cost by 52. Sahasrara's engineering is 26 people at ₹23.00 lakh each, so a person-week is 23,00,000 / 52 = ₹44,231, while a squad-week for nine is nine times that, ₹3.98 lakh.

Six. The annualisation factor comes from the window's own days. Sahasrara metered 240 analysers whose laboratories had signed minimum-pull cartridge contracts, from Thursday 1 January to Wednesday 4 March 2026 inclusive — 63 days, not two months — recording 54,600 cartridges, 227.5 each. The factor is 365 / 63 = 5.7937, giving 1,318 a year, above the base-wide average of 1,080 because a committed lab stops rationing. The first pass multiplied by six, got 1,365 and overstated pull by 3.56 per cent; the sibling error treats 30 trading days as a twelfth of a year when, against roughly 250, it is 12.0 per cent — a factor of 8.33.

Seven. Contribution-positive and full-cost-negative are not a contradiction. They answer different questions: whether to take the next order with capacity idle, and whether the capacity should exist. The tell is a sales team and a controller arguing over one price with two unnamed cost figures. Saptarang Fresh loses money on a contract contribution-positive by ₹275 a crate.

Eight. Concentration bites less in profit than in revenue when the customer sits above a capacity step. Sthiti's largest lender is 21 per cent of files, 15,960 files and 39,900 accelerator-hours. Losing it removes ₹399.06 lakh of revenue but also ₹161.52 lakh of overflow and ₹66.23 lakh of per-file cost, so profit falls ₹171.31 lakh — 42.93 per cent of the revenue it removes. The tell is a risk register ranking customers by revenue share alone.

Section 7How this differs by product type and stage

What mostly differs is which driver carries the cost, not whether the framework applies. The table below sets out where each type's variable cost sits; three consequences follow. Enterprise software's support cost is variable with respect to customers rather than usage, so moving upmarket can cut gross margin while raising it per account. Hardware recovers its ₹1.08 lakh of variable cost at the moment of sale, which is why Sahasrara's placement proposal is a financing decision in a pricing costume. And in AI-native products the reserved-versus-on-demand choice sets the step, making cost structure partly a procurement decision.

Exhibit 7. Where the cost actually sits, by product type.
TypeDriver of variable costCommon mis-reading
Consumer subscriptionpayment fees, licence per streamminimums called variable
B2B, enterprise softwareimplementation, support per customerone margin across tiers
Marketplaceorders for fulfilment, listings for trusta single cost per order
Hardware plus softwarebill of materials, service per active unitplacements read as sales
AI-nativeaccelerator-hours, human reviewreservation called variable

Stage changes the question, not the answer. A seed-stage company's fixed cost is almost all payroll, genuinely variable over six months, so its break-even is a hiring plan. At growth stage commitments appear — reservations, leases, minimum volumes — and break-even becomes a contract calendar. At scale fixed cost is lumpy capacity, and leverage becomes a question of when to buy the next step.

Section 8Three worked cases, one of them a failure

Sahasrara's placement proposal. The commitment is take-or-pay: the 182 cartridges billed and not pulled are never shipped, a placed analyser earns yearly 1,500 billed cartridges at ₹46 less 1,318 consumed at ₹21.50 — ₹69,000 − ₹28,337 = ₹40,663 — plus ₹18,000 of subscription less ₹3,600 of service: ₹55,063. Over 36 months 900 placements return 900 × ₹1,65,189 = ₹1,486.70 lakh against ₹972.00 lakh of build cost carrying no revenue, a net ₹514.70 lakh. The alternative is selling to whichever laboratories would have bought anyway: ₹1.80 lakh less ₹1.08 lakh = ₹72,000 at once, then ₹40,860 a year, ₹1,94,580 over 36 months. The paths are equal at 5,14,70,100 / 1,94,580 = 264.5 laboratories. Dhanavel's field estimate was 420, so placement gives up ₹302.54 lakh across the commitment and overtakes only in month 47.21.

Sthiti's reservation step. Six more reserved accelerators add ₹121.50 lakh of fixed cost and 51,600 usable hours, of which 80.0 per cent — 41,280 — can be filled, covering the whole 38,640-hour overflow and removing ₹161.52 lakh of on-demand spending: operating profit improves ₹40.02 lakh, to a loss of ₹428.36 lakh. The new units would run at 38,640 / 51,600 = 74.88 per cent of usable hours, above the 56.33 per cent indifference point. The risk is computable: if the largest lender leaves, demand falls to 1,50,100 hours, below the existing fleet's 1,51,360, so the six run at nothing — ₹121.50 lakh of newly fixed cost with no work. The step also rewrites the growth plan. At the all-in margin of 82.3248 per cent, break-even looks like 2,689.50 / 0.823248 = ₹3,266.94 lakh, 21.09 per cent above FY26; but growth above capacity earns ₹890.05 a file, so closing the ₹468.38 lakh loss needs 52,624 extra files, 69.24 per cent more volume — where the slack margin of ₹1,935.05 would have suggested 24,205 files, 31.85 per cent — understating by 54.00 per cent.

Where it failed: Saptarang Fresh. The Nashik table-grape brand costed its pack-house and chilling block at a design capacity of 5,22,000 crates and an assumed 92 per cent utilisation, 4,80,240 crates: ₹1,152 lakh / 4,80,240 = ₹239.88 a crate, which the commercial team rounded to ₹240 and used as a cost per crate. When FY26 volume fell 23 per cent from 4,80,000 to 3,69,600 crates, ₹240 was still in every quote. The error was not the number; it was the unit.

Exhibit 9. Saptarang Fresh: one contract, 1,44,000 crates at ₹795, costed two ways (₹ per crate).
ComponentAs quotedAt FY26 volume
Fruit, packaging, last mile (variable)520.00520.00
Plant cost absorbed per crate240.00311.69
Total cost per crate760.00831.69
Margin against the ₹795 price35.00−36.69

Plant cost ₹1,152 lakh a year over crates: 4,80,240 gives ₹239.88, rounded to ₹240; 3,69,600 gives ₹311.69. The ₹36.69 shortfall over 1,44,000 crates is ₹52.83 lakh. Contribution per crate at that price is 795 − 520 = ₹275.

Dhanyatha Kanakasabai, chief executive since November 2025, found the recovery in three moves rather than cancelling a contract that, at ₹275 of contribution a crate, was paying for a third of the plant. She repriced on renewal to ₹868, recut every quote to show contribution and absorption separately, and sold 1,60,000 crate-equivalents of third-party cold storage at ₹95 of contribution each, ₹152.00 lakh, cutting net plant cost to ₹1,000 lakh and absorption to ₹270.56. The fixed cost did not fall; the revenue on it rose.

Section 9Failure modes and their early warnings

Pricing off absorbed unit cost. Early sign: a quote carrying a cost per unit with no volume beside it. Diagnostic: at what volume was this rate computed? Caught late it reads as Saptarang's ₹52.83 lakh, or as contracts refused on an inflated rate. Committing capacity to a forecast rather than a floor. Early sign: a reservation sized to the plan, not the worst recent quarter. Diagnostic: if our largest customer left tomorrow, what utilisation would this commitment run at? For Sthiti, zero on the six incremental units. Mistaking a cost conversion for a cost reduction. Early sign: a business case claiming lower unit cost while omitting the new fixed line. Diagnostic: what is the indifference volume, and is the plan above it? Sahasrara's in-house line would cost ₹64.06 lakh a year at FY26 volume. Letting the driver drift from the cost. Early sign: a per-unit rate not re-derived in four quarters while the mix moved. Diagnostic: regress the line on its claimed driver and read the intercept; a large intercept is a fixed cost wearing a variable label, and every unit cost quoted off it is wrong by the intercept over volume.

Section 10Where experts genuinely disagree

The first disagreement is about what fixed cost is for. One camp holds that a high-fixed, low-variable structure is the only durable source of margin, because variable-heavy structures hand their gains to suppliers; the evidence is the margin profile of software and asset-light models' tendency to price down toward variable cost. It would be wrong if demand variance made the option value of stopping exceed that premium — the cloud-repatriation contention, which Sthiti's stranded capacity prices at ₹121.50 lakh.

The second is about allocation. The activity-based position is that refusing to allocate leaves managers blind to the cost they cause, and that a firm pricing on contribution long enough acquires a portfolio of contribution-positive, capacity-negative business — Saptarang's position exactly. The throughput position is that every allocation base is arbitrary and allocation produces the worse error, refusing profitable orders. Both can point to real wreckage; settling it needs evidence on which error is commoner in an industry, and that is absent.

The third is specific to AI products: whether inference behaves like a variable cost at all over three years. One side argues unit inference cost has fallen fast enough that pricing on today's cost destroys value, so capacity should be committed aggressively. The other argues capability expands to consume whatever compute exists, so cost per useful task is flat and commitments are bets on a price curve. The first is wrong if per-task compute rises faster than per-unit price falls; the second is wrong if a task's compute requirement is capped by the task. Sthiti sits between them.

Section 11What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this behaves differently in three visible ways. They ask the driver and the notice period before the number, because those fix what it means. They quote two margins rather than one — Sthiti's ₹1,935.05 on the next file in slack, and the ₹2,689.50 lakh of fixed cost that has to be absorbed — and say which question each answers. On finding idle capacity they look for revenue to put into it before cost to take out, the cost being committed already. The studied practitioner computes a break-even; the expert asks which of its five quantities is under decision this quarter.

Section 12What each of them decided

Dhanavel declined the blanket proposal on 14 April and approved placement only for laboratories that had twice refused a quote, about 140 machines, where the would-have-bought share is observably near zero; at the proposed scale placement buys volume he already has, at ₹1.80 lakh of forgone revenue a machine. Devahuti recommended four reserved accelerators rather than six, staggered to expire six months apart, taking some overflow in exchange for a commitment that strands ₹81.00 lakh rather than ₹121.50 lakh if the largest lender leaves.

  1. Sahasrara's arithmetic turns on one unobservable: how many of the 900 laboratories would have bought anyway. What evidence would move your estimate, and what would make the 264.5 threshold itself wrong?
  2. Sthiti's marginal contribution is ₹1,935.05 a file in slack and ₹890.05 above it. What price and contract terms would you set, knowing the cost of the next file depends on the order in which files arrive?
  3. Saptarang's contract was contribution-positive and full-cost-negative at once. Which figure should a sales incentive use, and what does that commit you to about capacity?

Section 13Going deeper

  • What a business model is — the revenue half decides which driver the cost is matched against.
  • Reading a P&L — the recut starts there; where a line is reported makes it auditable.
  • Business Model and Lean Canvas — the canvas names drivers; this prices them.
  • Revenue models — placement versus sale acts through cost behaviour.
  • Subscription economics — the lines with no variable cost drive the leverage.
  • Advertising business models — fill rate is Exhibit 6 again.
  • Marketplace economics — the two-sided driver problem.
  • Freemium as a business model — free users are a variable cost with a step.
