Gaatha Voice Technologies: the November term sheet

A Bengaluru voice-AI company must decide, by 30 November 2026, whether to convert part of a variable line in its cost base into a thirty-six-month fixed commitment — while its biggest customer decides whether to stay.

1. Sunday evening, Indiranagar

On the evening of Sunday 15 November 2026 the Gaatha Voice Technologies office in Indiranagar, Bengaluru, held a whiteboard nobody had wiped since Diwali the week before. Nayantika Yantradhar, who co-founded the company in 2019 and has run it since, had come in for a board meeting at eleven the next morning.

The whiteboard carried three dates. 30 November, when the reserved-capacity term sheet from Gaatha's cloud provider lapsed at the vendor's quarter end. 31 December, the last day on which Ghantoot Retail Group of Dubai, the largest account, could serve or receive notice on a contract running to 31 March 2027. And “FY28”, under which somebody had written 60% and circled it twice.

Gaatha sells conversational voice agents in eleven Indian languages and in Gulf Arabic to lenders, insurers, brokers and retailers, and bills by the minute of connected call. In the year ended 31 March 2026 it handled 16.00 crore minutes, billed ₹96.40 crore and lost ₹2.40 crore at the EBITDA line (Exhibit 1). The question on the agenda was narrow: sign thirty-six months of reserved GPU capacity in the provider's Mumbai region, or let the paper expire. Nayantika had spent the week finding out how much else moved when she touched it.

2. How Gaatha came to be shaped this way

Nayantika and Nabajyoti Yogbasak, now chief technology officer, started the company in March 2019 with speech recognition for Indian-accented English and Hindi, sold to one Mumbai non-banking financial company. Volume arrived before the model did, and by 2021 the product was a hybrid: a model that handled the conversation and a bench of analysts in Coimbatore who reviewed every escalated call.

The decision that still shapes the firm came in November 2022, when Ghantoot Retail Group, a Dubai chain of supermarkets and electronics stores, agreed to a contract running to 31 March 2027, well below Gaatha's Indian list price, on two conditions. All Ghantoot conversations would be processed and stored in a UAE region, and the account would be served by a named pod of forty-six analysts in Coimbatore that could not be reduced while the contract ran. Gaatha signed; Ghantoot took it from twenty-one customers to credibility in the Gulf, and the pod clause looked like an administrative detail.

Two consequences followed: Gaatha's largest single block of volume cannot run on Indian infrastructure, and forty-six of its delivery analysts cannot be released before 31 March 2027. Figure 1 places both against the later commitments.

3. The industry

Indian conversational-AI vendors sell into a market that is large, price-transparent and regulated at both ends. Gupshup, Haptik, Exotel, Ozonetel and Yellow.ai chase the same banking, insurance and retail budgets. Buyers compare quotes per minute, and a rate cut published by one vendor is quoted back by procurement within a fortnight.

Regulation sets the shape of the working day. The Reserve Bank of India's directions on recovery agents confine collections calling to between eight in the morning and seven in the evening, concentrating Gaatha's Indian collections minutes into an eleven-hour window and making peak concurrency, rather than annual minutes, the quantity that sizes infrastructure. RBI outsourcing guidance requires regulated entities' data to stay in India, and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 adds consent and retention duties the insurer client reads strictly.

Scale economics sit on the other side. Telephony is bought per minute from Indian carriers and resold, and has not moved in two years. Inference comes from a hyperscaler whose Mumbai and UAE regions bill at the same published rate, which has fallen since 2023. Dubai revenue is invoiced in dirhams under a letter of undertaking for GST.

4. What happened, and what has turned out to be wrong

In January 2023 finance adopted a written policy classifying inference, telephony and delivery staff as variable and engineering, sales and administration as fixed, on the belief that the bench flexed with volume. The same policy put FY26 break-even at ₹101.07 crore of revenue, being ₹51.90 crore of fixed cost over a 51.3 per cent contribution margin. The Coimbatore floor was then leased in June 2023 to 31 March 2029, analysts moved to permanent contracts with ninety days' notice in April 2024, and forty-six were pledged to Ghantoot (Exhibit 3).

In August 2024 Gaatha drew ₹14 crore of venture debt for the Coimbatore build-out. The covenants were read as liquidity protection; one requires the lender's written consent for new contracted spend above ₹10 crore in aggregate, which nobody connected to a cloud contract until October 2026.

In April 2025 the provider cut its published rate from ₹1.15 to ₹1.05 a minute. Gaatha's FY26 inference bill of ₹16.80 crore is that rate across 16.00 crore minutes, 5.44 crore of them in the UAE region (Exhibit 4). The cut was read as evidence that inference would keep getting cheaper, which is one reason nobody pushed for a commitment in 2025.

In September 2026 the provider offered a thirty-six-month reserved-capacity agreement, and Niharranjan Yajnaguha, the chief financial officer, asked at what volume it paid for itself. The answer in the board pack was 12.00 crore minutes a year (Exhibit 2). The term sheet places the cluster in the provider's Mumbai region; the pack's volume column was headed simply “minutes a year”.

On 1 July 2026 a sixty-two-day pilot began on Ghantoot's order-status queue with a model version that hands off less often (Exhibit 5). On 2 October 2026 the provider wrote indicating an intention to publish ₹0.95 a minute from 1 April 2027, without binding itself to it. On 8 November 2026, the Sunday of Diwali week, India-region telemetry recorded a peak of 486 concurrent sessions against the term sheet's rated sustained 420.

5. The people

Nayantika Yantradhar, 41, co-founder and chief executive, Bengaluru. Has not declared a position. Her incentive is a Series C conversation opening in February 2027, where the gross-margin trajectory is the number investors want. Not saying: on 29 October she told the prospective lead investor, informally, that FY28 gross margin would be “north of 60 per cent”.

Niharranjan Yajnaguha, 56, chief financial officer, Bengaluru, eleven years at a listed IT services firm before joining in 2023. Argues for the rate card until the Ghantoot renewal is settled; owns the covenant tests and the Series C model. Not saying: the ₹4.67 crore of analyst cost he has quoted to the board comes from applying the pilot's fall in escalation to the whole book.

Nabajyoti Yogbasak, 38, co-founder and chief technology officer, Pune. Argues for the full reservation: dedicated hardware carries a fourteen-month training roadmap that burst capacity cannot support, and he is recruiting against it. Not saying: the term sheet's rated sustained concurrency of 420 was measured on an older model version, and his own telemetry showed 486 on 8 November.

Nilabanti Yatikundu, 44, vice-president, delivery operations, Coimbatore. Has told Nayantika that cutting the bench is being discussed without her. Her variable pay is set on delivery cost per thousand conversations, which falls if analysts leave. Not saying: bench attrition is running at 31 per cent annualised and she carries twenty-two unfilled posts against a sanctioned 202.

Narottam Yugasanyal, 49, president, North America, Edison, New Jersey. Wants a price cut funded from somewhere to close two logos by March 2027; his accelerators begin above quota. Not saying: one prospect has told him it will not sign a per-minute contract at all, and wants billing per resolved case.

Niyor Yatrapalit, 33, principal data scientist, Toronto, ten and a half hours behind Bengaluru since 1 November. Ran the pilot; says the result is real and the queue the most templated in the book, and wants a second pilot on collections first. Not saying: the lower escalation came partly from raising the hand-off threshold, and the account's satisfaction score fell 0.3 points in August.

Nabaranjan Yojanmedhi, 36, head of customer success, Singapore, two and a half hours ahead. Believes Ghantoot renews at a 6 per cent cut, which from ₹5.31 a minute is ₹4.99; his bonus is set on gross renewal rate. Not saying: Ghantoot's procurement team holds a competing quote at ₹4.80 a minute and has shown him its cover page.

6. Exhibits

7. Voices

“Twelve crore minutes. We did 10.56 in the region last year and the plan says 15.20. It pays for itself inside the plan, and the plan is the plan.”

Nabajyoti Yogbasak, management meeting, Pune, 11 November 2026

“It also pays for itself on these numbers if we miss the plan by a fifth. And it does not change if Ghantoot goes, because Ghantoot was never going to be on that cluster. Two different anxieties, and we keep merging them.”

Niyor Yatrapalit, reply on the #commit channel, 11 November, 11:04 Toronto time

“Run the pilot number across the book. Escalation at 7.2 less the pilot's 2.8 points, so 4.4 per cent, gives 28.16 lakh reviews, 97.78 analyst-equivalents against 160 today. The 62.22 we stop needing, at ₹7.50 lakh each, is ₹4.67 crore a year — three times the ₹1.51 crore that separates the two GPU options at last year's India-region volume.”

Niharranjan Yajnaguha, board pre-read circulated 13 November 2026

“Forty-six of those posts are promised to Ghantoot by name until March, and I carry twenty-two sanctioned posts I have never filled. The 2.8 points came off one queue in one account over sixty-two days with the threshold moved. I am not saying it will not travel. I am saying nobody has asked whether it travels to a collections call in Bhojpuri.”

Nilabanti Yatikundu, email to Nayantika Yantradhar, 14 November 2026

“We are not buying minutes, we are buying a shelf that answers the phone. If your price is per minute and a competitor's is per resolved case, procurement will call you the expensive one even when you are not.”

Nourah Yaqoubi, group chief operating officer, Ghantoot Retail Group, renewal call, 12 November 2026, 20:00 Gulf time, with Narottam Yugasanyal listening from Edison at 11:00

8. The options as Nayantika sees them

She has written four, in the order the term sheet forced them; the first three are the shapes drawn in Exhibit 6.

A. Sign the full reservation. Thirty-six months from 1 January 2027 at ₹1.05 crore a month, rated at 1.60 crore minutes a month and 420 sustained sessions, overage ₹0.78 a minute. Aggregate commitment ₹37.80 crore, requiring the lender's consent, plus ₹2.80 crore of migration in the cutover quarter. Ghantoot volume stays on the rate card in the UAE region; the bench is untouched.

B. Let the term sheet lapse. Stay on the rate card at ₹1.05 a minute in both regions, with no commitment and no consent to obtain. The letter of 2 October indicates an intention to publish ₹0.95 from 1 April 2027.

C. Reserve half. Twenty-four months at ₹0.80 crore a month covering 9.60 crore India-region minutes a year, the balance at rate card. Aggregate commitment ₹19.20 crore, also above the consent threshold. Migration is the same ₹2.80 crore, the cross-connect being the same.

D. Leave the contract alone and take the review layer down. Roll the pilot model across the book from 1 February 2027, freeze analyst hiring and serve notice on part of the non-pod bench. Ninety days' notice applies, the forty-six pledged posts stay to 31 March 2027, and the lease runs to 2029 whatever the headcount does.

She has not written a fifth: what Gaatha would charge for, if it did not charge for minutes.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

Dates. The term sheet lapses 30 November 2026; Ghantoot notice falls due 31 December 2026 and that contract ends 31 March 2027. Cutover under A or C is 1 January 2027.

Money. Unrestricted cash was ₹41.20 crore at 30 September 2026, against a covenant floor of ₹15 crore tested each quarter end, and ₹7.80 crore of the 2024 venture debt is outstanding. New contracted spend above ₹10 crore in aggregate needs the lender's written consent, which it has said takes four to six weeks.

People. 223 delivery staff, 46 pledged to Ghantoot by name; ninety days' notice; 22 unfilled posts against a sanctioned 202 analysts; the lease to 31 March 2029.

Regulation and contract. RBI outsourcing guidance keeps the regulated Indian clients' processing in India; clause 7.2 keeps Ghantoot's in the UAE; collections calling is confined to 08:00–19:00.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Classify each FY26 line in Exhibit 1 as fixed or variable over one quarter, then over three years. Which, if any, change, and what in Exhibit 3 bears on your answer?
  2. Exhibit 2 reports a volume at which A and B cost the same. List every cost and volume it leaves out, and for each say which way it moves that volume.
  3. Exhibit 5 reports two sixty-two-day windows with different volumes. What annual saving does it support, over what population, and what would you measure before applying it elsewhere?
  4. Gaatha bills per minute, meters inference per minute and sizes its bench by reviews. What happens to each option if a large customer insists on being billed per resolved case?
  5. Nayantika has described FY28 gross margin as “north of 60 per cent”. From the figures here, what combination of volume, price and cost structure would have to hold, and what must be true of the Ghantoot renewal in each?
  6. It is Monday morning, 16 November 2026. What do you do, in what order, and what do you say to the board about the risk you are taking on and the risk you are declining?

Sunday, late

At a quarter to eleven Nayantika put the three dates in a column and wrote beside each what she would not know by then. By 30 November, whether Ghantoot was renewing. By 31 December, whether the pilot travelled past one queue. By the time FY28 began she would have signed, or not signed, thirty-six months of something.

Nabajyoti's message arrived from Pune at 22:52: “Either we believe the plan or we do not. Pick one by eleven.” She looked at the whiteboard a while, rubbed out the circle around 60%, then drew it again.
case20v1-bm.cost.structure:
Elavar Technologies and the Volume Commitment

A case on cost structure and operating leverage

1. Opening

At 8.30 pm on Thursday 22 October 2026, Mainak Vidyaghosh closed his laptop in Elavar Technologies' Bengaluru office and then opened it again. The vendor's contract was still on the screen. Elavar, the identity-verification company he had co-founded seven years earlier, had until Saturday 31 October to accept a twelve-month commitment from the licensed aggregator behind its Aadhaar and DigiLocker checks: ₹40 lakh a month, flat, for up to nine lakh checks, in place of the ₹6 a check Elavar paid today. After that date the offer would lapse.

Mahasweta Varthakur, his CFO, wanted one answer before the board call on Friday 30 October: did the commitment make Elavar's cost base safer or riskier? His machine-learning lead in Toronto had been urging a different route since August. Mainak had nine days to choose.

2. Company background

Elavar sells verification to lenders. A lending app or NBFC sends a customer's Aadhaar, PAN or selfie to Elavar's API, which routes it to the aggregator and to DigiLocker, runs liveness detection and returns a pass or fail in seconds, supporting the lender's obligations under the RBI's KYC Master Direction. Each completed verification is one check, billed at a blended ₹14. About 60 clients, mostly NBFCs, fintech lenders and insurers, use it. IDfy, Digio and Signzy compete for the same lenders.

Revenue follows lending, and lending follows festivals. Checks rose from 3.6 lakh in April to 6.0 lakh in September (Exhibit 1), and Diwali on 8 November was expected to lift October and November further. Fourteen engineers in Bengaluru and Pune run the API and routing. Support sits in Bengaluru and Singapore, and compliance covers audits, CERT-In reporting and DPDP Act data handling. Those costs barely move when one more check arrives.

3. The situation

Exhibit 2 gives September. Every check carried ₹7.20 of cost that rose with volume, so each added check contributed ₹6.80. The remaining ₹34.0 lakh a month did not move with volume at the range under discussion. At 6.0 lakh checks Elavar earned ₹6.8 lakh, and the break-even for that cost base is 5.0 lakh checks, which July's 4.9 lakh would have fallen just short of at September's costs. The aggregator's fee was ₹36.0 lakh of ₹77.2 lakh in total cost, nearly half of everything Elavar spent.

October looked stronger. Through 21 October Elavar had completed 4.41 lakh checks, 0.21 lakh a day, a pace of 6.51 lakh for the 31-day month, ahead of Diwali. Mahasweta's board paper priced each route at the same prices and the same volumes (Exhibit 3), and she had circulated it to the team ahead of a 7.00 pm IST call, which was 9.30 am in Toronto and 9.30 pm in Singapore. Nobody on the call disputed her arithmetic. They disputed what volume to believe.

The view differed by city. In Bengaluru and Pune the engineers saw a vendor dependency they had long resented. In Toronto, Monalisa saw a team that could own the capability. In Singapore, Minoti saw two clients whose renewal decisions Elavar could not control, and in Mumbai Mahasweta saw twelve months of payments that would continue whatever those clients decided.

4. The people

Mainak Vidyaghosh, co-founder and CEO, Bengaluru, forecasts 10 lakh checks a month by March 2027 and wants a lower unit cost to bid against IDfy and Digio for larger NBFC mandates. He regards the commitment as the price of growth.

Mahasweta Varthakur, CFO, Mumbai, forecasts 7.5 lakh by March. She dislikes any cost that continues when revenue does not, and calls the commitment "a volume discount with a bill attached". Mainak calls it "a fixed cost we can still outgrow".

Minoti Vanbaruah, head of customer success, Singapore, reports that Elavar's two largest clients, together 2.28 lakh checks a month or 38 per cent of September volume, are piloting a second vendor. Both contracts renew in January 2027.

Monalisa Vasubhuyan, machine-learning lead, Toronto, has a prototype liveness model that matched the aggregator's accuracy on a 5,000-image test set. She wants to build, with two engineers from Pune writing the integration, and treats the ₹28 lakh a month as an investment Elavar owns.

5. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 shows volume above the current break-even since August, rising by two-thirds in five months. Exhibit 2 shows a cost base in which the aggregator's fee is the largest variable line and engineering the largest fixed one. Exhibit 3 puts the routes side by side at one price and the same four volumes, so any gap between columns comes from cost design (C at steady state), not from a different forecast.

6. The options

Option A: stay on per-check pricing. Elavar keeps paying ₹6 a check. Variable cost stays ₹7.20 a check at every volume, fixed cost stays ₹34.0 lakh within the 5 to 10 lakh range, and nothing is committed beyond today's contracts. Profit moves by ₹6.80 lakh for each additional lakh checks.

Option B: sign the commitment. Elavar pays ₹40 lakh a month for twelve months, ₹4.80 crore in all, for up to 9 lakh checks, and ₹5 a check beyond. Variable cost falls to ₹1.20 a check; total fixed cost rises to ₹74.0 lakh. The fee is owed whether or not the checks arrive, and the team and tooling are untouched.

Option C: build in-house. Monalisa's team of eight, ₹16 lakh a month at ₹2 lakh each, plus ₹12 lakh of infrastructure, audit and certification, takes five months to reach production. A residual ₹1.60 a check still goes to the aggregator for the authentication that cannot be replaced, so variable cost is ₹2.80. Total fixed cost becomes ₹62.0 lakh. If the team is hired in full from month one, the five build months add ₹140 lakh to Option A's spend while the aggregator's fee continues at ₹6.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibit 2, which of Elavar's lines are fixed and which variable, and over what range of volume would you defend each classification?
  2. For each route in Exhibit 3, at what monthly volume does its profit equal Option A's, and how does that volume compare with Exhibit 1 and the October pace?
  3. Mahasweta asks which route is riskier. Recompute each route's profit if the two pilot clients leave, at Mahasweta's March forecast and at Mainak's. What changes?
  4. What would you recommend to the board on 30 October, and what evidence would make you change that recommendation?

8. A note for the learner

A cost structure describes which costs wait for volume and which do not. Option A carries the lowest fixed cost and, of the three, the lowest operating leverage at 6.0 lakh checks. B and C swap variable cost for fixed cost: each added check earns more, and more checks are needed to cover the base. The lens therefore asks not "which route is cheapest?" but "which range of volume do we believe, and how costly is being wrong?"

One defensible path is to sign B. B's profit exceeds A's whenever volume sits above 40 ÷ 6 = 6.67 lakh checks, up to the 9 lakh cap and beyond it, even after the ₹5 overage. That is 11 per cent above September and about 2.4 per cent above October's pace of 6.51 lakh (6.667 ÷ 6.51). At Mahasweta's 7.5 lakh forecast B earns ₹5.0 lakh a month more than A. At Mainak's 10 lakh it earns ₹15.0 lakh more. B's shortfall against A is capped at the ₹40 lakh monthly fee, the extreme in which no checks arrive, not the forecast.

The risk is real. If both pilot clients left and the 2.28 lakh checks a month they send today simply disappeared, volume at 7.5 lakh would fall to 5.22 lakh and B would trail A by ₹8.7 lakh a month. Treating the outcomes as either both clients stay or both leave, B is ahead of A in expectation in March so long as the chance they both leave is below 36.5 per cent (5.0 ÷ (5.0 + 8.68)). Minoti's pilot evidence is what the board should test that chance against. C is held for March, when volumes and renewals are known, since its ₹28 lakh a month starts before it saves anything.

Elavar Technologies and all individuals are fictional. Real organisations are named for market context only.
exp40v2-bm.freemium.model:
Strategy & Business · Business Models

Freemium as a business model

Free users are leads and costs at the same time. The craft lies in naming the denominator, pricing the cost curve, and knowing which of the two a given cohort actually is.

1Two decisions, three days apart

On 6 October 2026, in a converted godown in Chennai, Govardhini Muthuvel opened a memo from her finance director. Muthuvel is VP Product at Velicham Studio, whose mobile tool lets small online sellers shoot, cut and publish product videos. In September the product had 18,40,000 free monthly active users and 2,76,000 paying subscribers at ₹249 a month — monthly recurring revenue of ₹6.87 crore. The memo, from Girivardhan Munuswamy, said the free tier cost ₹1.93 crore a month to serve, 28.11 per cent of that revenue, and proposed closing free accounts past two years that had not paid. Her instinct was that it was aimed at the wrong people.

On 9 October, in Gachibowli, Gurunandan Meduri faced the mirror image. Meduri runs self-serve at Vidiyal Systems, which sells workspace analytics to Indian mid-market firms at ₹480 per seat per month. Vidiyal's free tier is capped at three seats; at 30 September it held 38,400 free workspaces and 2,640 paying ones. His growth team wanted the cap raised to five, arguing that free workspaces which grow convert far better than those which do not. The proposal carried one number: conversion improves by 67 per cent. Meduri asked: a percentage of what? Nobody could answer.

Shrinking a free tier and enlarging one look like opposite decisions and are the same decision. Both ask whether a free user is a lead or a cost, and both were about to be settled with a conversion rate whose denominator had never been written down. Most costly freemium mistakes are denominator mistakes in the clothes of a strategy debate.

2The idea, and the three schools that disagree about it

Freemium is a subscription business in which a permanently free tier is operated as a marketing and sorting instrument. Two conditions make it a model rather than a promotion. The free tier must be indefinite, not a trial with an expiry; and the fence between free and paid must be a deliberate choice of which dimension of value to meter — seats, volume, time, support, retention or a capability.

The problem it solves is older than software. Where the marginal cost of a copy approaches zero but the buyer's cost of evaluating it does not, price screens badly: it keeps out people who would have paid had they known. The screening economics is older still, but Shapiro and Varian's Information Rules (1999) brought it to information goods as versioning: degrading a product deliberately to sort willingness to pay. The word entered circulation in 2006, in a comment on Fred Wilson's blog attributed to Jarid Lukin, and spread through Wilson and Chris Anderson's Free (2009).

Three schools read the same tier differently and sign different propositions. The channel school treats it as a line in the acquisition budget and signs: review a free tier like a paid channel, and cut it when its cost per conversion exceeds paid CAC. It will not sign that unpriceable network value justifies a loss. The distribution school treats it as an asset returning through referral, habit and category default, and signs: a tier converting at 0.5 per cent can beat one at 4 per cent if it is ten times larger — 5,000 conversions from 10,00,000 against 4,000 from 1,00,000. It will not sign that cost per conversion is a sufficient test. The versioning school treats it as price discrimination and signs: the only legitimate design question is which fence separates the segments. It will not sign that a tier should be sized for reach. All three agree on the arithmetic and disagree about what it is for.

3Mechanics: the denominator, the cost curve, the hazard

Velicham's June 2026 install cohort — 4,20,000 installs — produced 5,040 paid conversions in the ninety days to 28 September, the most recent cohort whose window had closed when Munuswamy wrote. Figure 1 divides that undisputed numerator by five denominators with a claim to the phrase “conversion rate”. Installs in July, August and September averaged about 2.8 times June's, which is why Table 1's 0–3 month band holds 5,52,000 free actives where three June-sized cohorts would stand at 1,94,880.

Twelve and a half times. A board told “two per cent” and then “five per cent” has learnt nothing unless both name their base and its date.

The cost side has an equivalent trap. Munuswamy's memo quoted “₹10.50 per free monthly active per month”, a mean over a distribution with a slope. Velicham's free-tier cost is well approximated by a ₹2.40 account overhead — storage, authentication, a share of support — plus ₹1.20 per export rendered. Exports run from 0.8 a month in the lightest quartile to 17.2 in the heaviest, so cost per user runs from ₹3.36 to ₹23.04 and the heaviest quartile carries 54.86 per cent of free-tier cost.

Now join the two sides, on the whole standing free base rather than one cohort. In September 14,720 free monthly actives began paying. The honest unit is not a conversion rate but a monthly hazard on a stated base: 14,720 / 18,40,000 = 0.800 per cent per free-monthly-active-month. On the paid side ₹249 of revenue carries ₹34 of serving cost, so gross profit is ₹215 a month; at 3.6 per cent monthly churn the expected life is 1/0.036 = 27.78 months and lifetime gross profit ₹215 / 0.036 = ₹5,972.22.

Two routes then agree, which is the test that the model is coherent. As a channel, ₹1,93,20,000 bought 14,720 conversions — ₹1,312.50 each, against ₹2,480 through performance marketing, so lifetime gross profit covers the free route 5,972.22/1,312.50 = 4.55 times and the paid route 2.41 times. Per free-user-month, expected gross profit is 0.00800 × ₹5,972.22 = ₹47.78 against ₹10.50 of cost: net ₹37.28, the same 4.55. Break-even follows: h* = ₹10.50 / ₹5,972.22 = 0.176 per cent per free-user-month.

Note what h* is denominated in: a cost recovered across free-user-months, not across converters. Dividing ₹1,312.50 over all free users is a category error, since it already contains every rupee spent on users who never pay.

4When the model applies, and when it misleads

The conditions are testable. (a) The blended hazard exceeds cost divided by lifetime gross profit. Velicham: 0.800 per cent against h* of 0.176 — passes with room. Vidiyal: 1.10 per cent a quarter on workspaces, about 0.37 a month, against a workspace h* of ₹96 / ₹2,96,125 = 0.032 per cent — passes widely, because B2B lifetime value is large. (b) Marginal cost per unit of engagement is small relative to the signal that engagement sends. Velicham passes at ₹1.20 an export against ₹84.81 of expected gross profit a month from its heaviest quartile; Vidiyal passes more easily, at ₹40 a free seat-month against ₹2,96,125 of workspace lifetime. (c) A fence exists that a determined free user cannot cheaply work around. Vidiyal's cap fails this in part: two three-seat workspaces substitute for one six-seat workspace, and 1,840 of its free workspaces share a billing-email domain with another. Velicham's export meter holds, because splitting the work across two free accounts means doing it twice.

The model misleads in three situations. Where the free side is a different population from the paying side — a marketplace's buyers and sellers — free usage is a subsidy, and a rate between two populations means nothing. Where free usage substitutes for a purchase that would have happened anyway, measured conversions overstate incremental ones. And where free-tier cost is cash rather than allocated capacity, negative contribution is not a marketing accrual.

5Hard edges

Five situations bend the model, and mature firms handle them differently from the way they describe it. Multi-product: a free tier in product A feeds paid demand in B, so cost sits in A's profit and loss while revenue lands in B's, and the ratio that matters sits in no single statement. Firms that cope move the cost to a shared line rather than asking A to defend it. Two-sided: free for sellers to buy buyer liquidity is a transfer price, and the test is whether the subsidised side lifts the monetised side's take, not whether sellers convert. Regulated: in lending, insurance and diagnostics a free account can trigger identity verification, consent capture and retention duties; in two of Velicham's planned markets a free account holding uploaded customer photographs carries a five-year retention duty, committing 60 × ₹0.90 = ₹54 of cold storage per account before any conversion. Hardware plus software: a free terminal has a bill of materials, and recovery runs on the asset's life rather than the subscription's. AI-native: here the cost curve is the business model — marginal cost rises with engagement, so the heaviest free users are at once the strongest buying signal and the largest bill.

At the organisational seam the pattern repeats. Free-tier infrastructure sits with platform engineering, conversion with growth, free-user support with customer operations, and each can hit its target while the ratio between them worsens. Firms that run freemium well put one person on that ratio, with authority over the fence.

6Eight nuances that separate the expert

1. The denominator is a choice, and the choice is political

Every funnel offers four or five defensible bases, and a team reaches for the one that flatters its own work. Tell-tale: the rate in the quarterly pack improves while new paying accounts fall — usually a denominator narrowing, not a product improving. The obvious reading, that the rate measures the product, is wrong: it measures product and base jointly, and the base moves faster.

2. The free tier's cost is a curve, not a rate

A blended cost hides a distribution whose top quartile is several times the bottom: Velicham's Q4 costs ₹23.04 against Q1's ₹3.36. Tell-tale: an engineer can say what a ninety-ninth percentile free user costs while finance quotes one average. Where those figures come from different people, nobody has looked at the curve.

3. The heaviest free users are often leads, not freeloaders

The intuitive move is to cap the top of the distribution. At Velicham the heaviest quartile converts at a 1.42 per cent monthly hazard: expected gross profit 0.0142 × ₹5,972.22 = ₹84.81 per user-month against ₹23.04 of cost, net ₹61.77, earned by the quartile with the highest cost per user in Figure 2. Tell-tale: whoever proposes a usage cap cannot state the capped segment's hazard.

4. Break-even lives per free-user-month, not per converter

The break-even that generalises is h* = cost per free-user-month over lifetime gross profit per converter: ₹10.50 / ₹5,972.22 = 0.176 per cent. A segment carries its weight when its own hazard clears it. Tell-tale: somebody divides a cost per acquisition across the free base, or recovers free-tier cost from converters alone — both out by roughly the reciprocal of the hazard.

5. The discount rate decides which segments are in

Undiscounted lifetime value flatters long-lived cohorts. At a 14 per cent cost of capital the monthly rate is 1.141/12 − 1 = 1.0979 per cent, so Velicham's lifetime gross profit falls to ₹215 / (0.036 + 0.010979) = ₹4,577 from ₹5,972.22, and h* rises from 0.176 to 0.229 per cent. Tell-tale: a 62.5-month B2B lifetime quoted undiscounted; that choice alone cuts Vidiyal's per-workspace figure from ₹2.96 lakh to ₹1.76 lakh, a fall of 40.7 per cent.

6. Tenure is a weak proxy for freeloading

Munuswamy's memo targeted accounts past two years. Table 1 shows that band losing ₹3.1 lakh a month — small, and, because its hazard is a residual of three modelled bands, 0.44 standard errors from zero rather than the 2.74 its own sampling alone suggests. Cut tenure against the cost curve and the loss concentrates, and becomes measurable: free users both past two years and in the heaviest quartile number 71,760, carry 8.56 per cent of free-tier cost on 3.90 per cent of the base, convert at 151/71,760 = 0.2104 per cent and lose ₹7.52 lakh a month. Tell-tale: a cohort chart with tenure on one axis and nothing cut against it.

7. The lift that matters is usually smaller than the lift you can measure

Vidiyal's five-seat cap needs conversion to rise from 1.1000 to 1.1365 per cent to pay for itself — 0.0365 of a point, against a standard error on one quarter's rate of √(0.0110 × 0.9890 / 36,000) = 0.0550 of a point, so 0.66 standard errors. Tell-tale: a team proposing an experiment for a decision whose break-even sits inside its own noise.

8. Measured conversions are not incremental conversions

Some share of converting free users would have bought on first contact. A funnel cannot reveal that share; a holdout can. Tell-tale: a firm comparing free-tier cost per conversion with paid CAC having never withheld the tier from a region or cohort. Velicham has not run that test, so its ₹1,312.50 is a floor on incremental cost per conversion: the bias has a known direction and an unknown size.

7What changes across product types and stages

Four of the five differences commonly asserted are real; the fifth, platforms, is not a free-tier difference at all. In consumer products hazards are low and the cost curve binds: a 0.42 per cent monthly hazard is a fine business at ₹1.85 a user-month and ruinous at ₹25. In B2B and enterprise the unit is the account, not the person, and the fence that holds is usually administrative — audit logs, provisioning, support response — because a buying committee cannot work those around. Platforms and marketplaces are where the word is most often misapplied: what looks like a free tier is a subsidy to one side, and the diagnostics are take rate and liquidity. In hardware the free item consumes working capital, so the question is payback in months on a physical asset. In AI products the slope of the cost curve replaces the intercept as the thing to manage.

By stage the honest statement is narrower than the usual one. Before product-market fit a free tier is a research instrument and its cost a research budget; hazards on a base of a few thousand carry standard errors too wide to act on. At growth stage it is a channel, and cost per conversion against paid CAC is the comparison. At scale it is a balance-sheet item: a large free base is an option on future pricing and a liability in serving cost at once, inseparably. What does not change is the discipline of naming the denominator.

8Three worked examples, one of them a failure

Vinmeen, a Pune language-learning app, ran 96,00,000 free monthly actives at ₹1.85 each — ₹1.78 crore a month — with a 0.42 per cent monthly hazard and ₹1,180 of lifetime gross profit per subscriber. That is 40,320 conversions a month, ₹1,77,60,000 / 40,320 = ₹440.48 each, and 2.68 times cover. Its hazard is just over half Velicham's; it works because its cost per free user-month is ₹1.85 against ₹10.50. A hazard is uninterpretable without the cost it sits against.

Vaarthai, a Bengaluru document-extraction company, is the failure. In January 2026 its 11,200 free workspaces cost ₹410 each a month against a 0.41 per cent monthly hazard and ₹2.14 lakh of lifetime gross profit per converted workspace — net ₹467.40 a workspace-month. Through the year it shipped a stronger model, free usage rose, and by September cost had reached ₹1,340. Lifetime gross profit had not moved, so h* rose from 0.1916 to 0.6262 per cent while the hazard stayed at 0.41 and net turned to −₹462.60 a workspace-month — ₹51.81 lakh a month on a tier still described as a marketing line. Nobody had re-derived h*, because the conversion rate had not changed. The recovery was not a shutdown: metering free extraction at 300 pages a month cut free workspaces to 7,900 and cost to ₹505 and lifted the hazard to 0.63 per cent, taking monthly conversions from 45.9 to 49.8 and contribution to +₹66.61 lakh. Two cautions were recorded: the hazard rise is confounded with composition, and the 3,300 workspaces that left may have held buyers.

Virundhu, a Coimbatore restaurant-systems firm, placed 14,600 billing terminals free at ₹4,150 each in bill of materials and logistics — ₹6.06 crore of cash — to sell software at a 1.35 per cent monthly hazard and ₹58,400 of lifetime gross profit. Expected gross profit is 0.0135 × ₹58,400 = ₹788.40 a terminal-month, so a terminal repays its cash cost in ln(1 − 4,150/58,400) / ln(1 − 0.0135) = 5.42 months of being held; the simpler 4,150 / 788.40 = 5.26 ignores the terminal's own survival as an unconverted asset. What kept it solvent was recovering idle terminals: the asset, unlike a software account, can be redeployed.

9Failure modes and their early diagnostics

The free tier that is good enough
Warning: free-tier satisfaction runs above paid, and hazard decays with tenure while retention holds. Diagnostic: what does paid do that a determined free user cannot work around? Caught late, the fix is repricing an installed base.
The flattering denominator
Warning: the rate rises while absolute conversions fall. Diagnostic: name the denominator and the date it was struck. Caught late, a year of planning rests on a trend that never existed.
The cost curve outrunning the hazard
Warning: cost per free user-month grows faster than conversions, usually just after a capability ships. Diagnostic: re-derive h* every time the free experience changes. Vaarthai's cost of catching this eight months late was ₹51.81 lakh a month.
The fence placed before the value
Warning: activation falls when the paywall moves. Diagnostic: does the free tier still deliver one complete unit of the core outcome? Caught late, the hazard it suppressed is indistinguishable from a product that nobody wanted.
Attribution capture
Warning: paid marketing and the free tier both report improving cost per acquisition while blended CAC worsens. Diagnostic: do the two channels' claimed conversions exceed the total? At Velicham that total is 14,720 a month, so claims summing above it are arithmetic, not analysis. Caught late, budget has moved to the channel taking credit.

10Where experts genuinely disagree

Is the free tier a channel or an asset? The channel position rests on accountability: a cost per conversion can be compared, budgeted and cut — Velicham's test gives 4.55 times cover, Vaarthai's September one 0.0041 × ₹2,14,000 / ₹1,340 = 0.65. The asset position rests on referral and default effects no funnel attributes, and on the option value of an installed base when prices change. The channel view fails if holdouts show most conversions arriving by paths the funnel cannot see; the asset view fails if removal costs little paid volume. Few firms have run either.

Should the habit-forming action ever be metered? One camp holds that whatever creates the habit must stay free indefinitely, and that reverse trials — full capability for a fortnight, then a downgrade — convert better because they show what is lost. The other holds that the habit is the product's durable asset and metering it trades compounding reach for a quarter's revenue. Metering is wrong if a cohort moved behind the paywall loses lifetime value against one left in front of it, and free-forever is wrong if it does not; Velicham's heaviest quartile converting at 1.42 per cent against a 0.800 blended is read by each camp as its own evidence.

Does a free tier raise or lower willingness to pay? The zero-price literature in behavioural economics finds that free is not a low price but a different category, which can anchor expectations downward and make a later charge feel like a loss. The evaluation-cost argument runs the other way: use reveals value and raises what a buyer will pay. The zero-price position is wrong if free users and cold traffic return the same willingness to pay in one price test, which Velicham cannot run, because all 18,40,000 of its free actives have already seen a price. Both effects are real and the sign of the sum is empirical, product by product.

11What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied freemium recites conversion benchmarks. Someone who has internalised it asks three questions before looking at any rate: what is the numerator, what is the denominator, and when was each measured. They quote hazards per user-month rather than conversion rates, because hazards compare across products and rates do not. They re-derive break-even whenever the free experience changes, knowing a discounting choice alone moves h* from 0.176 to 0.229 per cent. They cut the free base by cost and by hazard jointly, size the lift a decision requires before designing the test — 0.0365 of a point for Meduri — and say so when the test cannot see it. And they can name which school they argue from, which makes a disagreement about freemium resolvable rather than recurring.

12What the two protagonists decided

Muthuvel declined the tenure cap. Table 1 is the reason.

Closing the whole 25+ band would save ₹25.1 lakh of cost at the blended ₹10.50 and forfeit ₹22.0 lakh of expected gross profit, netting ₹3.1 lakh — which sits 0.44 standard errors from zero. Muthuvel instead metered exports past twenty-four months, targeting the 71,760-user cell that loses ₹7.52 lakh a month, ₹90.19 lakh a year, at its own measured ₹23.04 rather than the blended rate. The smaller population shows the larger loss because the bases differ.

Meduri's slide was wrong, and his decision rested on something the slide never gave him. The 67 per cent was a ratio of two rates on different bases: the same 396 conversions in the September quarter give 396/36,000 = 1.1000 per cent on the free workspaces that existed at 1 July and, because converting workspaces averaged 4.0 seats against the base's 2.4, 1,584 seats over 86,400 free seats, or 1.8333 per cent. The ratio 4.0/2.4 = 1.6667, as Figure 4 shows, is a statement about workspace size and not about conversion.

Priced that way, the cap needs between 14.0 and 40.3 extra conversions a quarter to pay for itself, depending on whether a converted workspace is credited with the 11.5 seats a paying one eventually averages or the 4.0 it has on the day it converts. On 422.4 conversions that is a required lift of 3.3 to 9.5 per cent, and nothing Meduri had could show one. Detecting even the smaller figure, 0.0365 of a point at 80 per cent power and five per cent two-sided significance, needs (1.9600 + 0.8416)2 × 2 × 0.0110 × 0.9890 / 0.000364712 = 12,83,914 workspaces per arm against a free base of 38,400; split in two, that base's minimum detectable effect is 0.2982 of a point, 8.2 times the 0.0365 and 2.8 times the 0.1049. He raised the cap and instrumented cost instead: average seats per free workspace, read monthly, cap reverting above 3.6.

Discussion questions.

1. What would have to be true of Velicham's referral and substitution effects for ₹1,312.50 to be the right input to a comparison against ₹2,480 of paid CAC, and what test would settle it?

2. Meduri's cap needs a lift of 3.3 to 9.5 per cent to pay for itself, and his free base cannot detect one below 0.30 of a point. What would have to be true of the seat-growth mechanism to justify ₹13,82,400 a month, and which of Section 2's three schools is he arguing from?

3. The 25+ band's shortfall sits 0.44 standard errors from zero on modelled hazards; the 25+ / Q4 cell's sits 10.2 on a counted one. What does that asymmetry say about which cuts of a free base are worth instrumenting first?

13Going deeper

Subscription economics — churn, expansion and discounting set the lifetime value every figure here divides by — the step from ₹5,972.22 to ₹4,577 is one discounting choice. What a business model is — places the free tier among a model's other choices, so it stops being a growth tactic. Business Model and Lean Canvas — the one-page frame where the free tier's cost and revenue sides sit together. Revenue models — the alternatives to metering seats or volume, where fence design happens. Advertising business models — the other way to monetise a free base, by revenue that needs no conversion. Marketplace economics — the frame for the two-sided case where the word misleads. Hardware business models — what changes when the free thing costs cash, as at Virundhu.
case20v1-bm.freemium.model:
Hoolock Bills: Free Users, Leads or Costs?

A decision case on freemium as a business model

1. Opening

On Wednesday 7 October 2026, at half past eight in the evening, Prosenjit Akhaury sat in Hoolock's Guwahati office with three proposals and a deadline. On Friday 6 November the board would meet, two days before Diwali, and expect a decision on the free plan of Hoolock Bills, the GST invoicing app that had drawn 4,00,000 sign-ups in twelve months and turned 8,400 of them into paying customers.

Every one of those paying accounts had begun as a free account. Yet free accounts that did not pay used servers, support hours and SMS credits every month, and the investor who had put ₹40 crore into Hoolock in 2024 had asked, in writing, whether the free plan was a marketing channel or a charity. The board pack closed on Friday 30 October. Traders across eastern India buy new billing software when they open fresh account books after Diwali, so whatever the board approved had to be live as soon after the festival as it could be built.

2. Company background

Hoolock was founded in Guwahati in 2021 by Prosenjit and a college friend, and named after the hoolock gibbon of Assam's forests. Hoolock Bills lets a small trader issue a GST-compliant invoice from a phone, record the UPI payment and send the invoice to the customer on WhatsApp. Its users are kirana owners, pharmacists, tailors, electricians and small wholesalers in Assam, West Bengal, Bihar and Odisha, nearly all below the turnover at which GST e-invoicing is mandatory.

The market is crowded. Vyapar and Zoho Books sell to the same traders, Tally holds the accountant's desktop, and Khatabook and OkCredit give ledger apps away. Hoolock chose to give invoicing away too. The free plan has no time limit and, so far, no limit on invoices. Each free invoice carries a footer, "Made with Hoolock Bills", and a link. The paid plan, launched in October 2023, costs ₹3,000 a year plus 18 per cent GST and removes the footer, adds staff logins and gives priority support. Figure 1 shows the milestones.

3. The situation

Exhibit 1 shows where the year's sign-ups came from. The largest source, 1,60,000, was the footer: a free user sends an invoice, the customer taps the link, and some customers open accounts of their own. Those sign-ups activated (five invoices within 30 days) at 40.0 per cent, against 35.0 per cent from search and app stores and 27.0 per cent from partners and ads. Of 1,40,000 activated accounts, 8,400 paid within 90 days of activation: 6.0 per cent of activated accounts, and 2.1 per cent of sign-ups. The other 1,31,600 stayed free.

Exhibit 2 prices the same cohort for a year, treating every account as present for all twelve months. Serving cost was ₹128.16 lakh against ₹252.00 lakh of plan revenue, before marketing and salaries. Accounts that had not paid within 90 days accounted for ₹94.56 lakh of the serving cost.

Hoolock's people read this from different places. Pubali Ambastha in Bengaluru sees a cost line. Pulok Agasti in Singapore, where the 8.30 pm India call falls at 11 pm, hears "I tried it because it was free". The Berlin contract designer thinks the footer looks cheap. In Toronto, where the same call falls at 11 am, Purbasha Asaduzzaman spent September building one template that prices every option on the same cohort, and her estimates are assumptions, not measurements.

4. The people

Prosenjit Akhaury, co-founder and chief executive, Guwahati. He presents to the board and instinctively protects the free plan, which built the company, but has a runway to defend.

Pubali Ambastha, head of product, Bengaluru. She wants the free plan to stop carrying heavy users and proposes a usage limit.

Pulok Agasti, customer-success lead, Singapore. He wants traders to pay for what they plainly value, the GST work, and proposes gating it.

Purbasha Asaduzzaman, data scientist, Toronto. She wants Hoolock to stop paying for users who were never going to buy, and proposes replacing the free plan with a trial. She is also the author of every estimate in this case.

5. Exhibits

6. The options

Exhibit 3 shows who a limit would touch. Options A and B are priced on the same 4,00,000-sign-up cohort as Exhibit 2; Option C changes that base by design. Each take-up and leaving rate is Purbasha's assumption, and all margins are revenue less serving cost.

Option A: cap free plans at 50 invoices a month. Pubali's proposal reaches the 26,320 free accounts above the cap. Assume 10 per cent pay (2,632), 40 per cent leave (10,528) and 50 per cent stay under the cap. Plan revenue rises ₹78.96 lakh and serving falls ₹6.32 lakh for those who leave, but the new payers cost ₹340 a year more each to serve, ₹8.95 lakh. The margin gain is ₹76.33 lakh a year. Build cost is ₹6 lakh, one month of Pune work. The footer, sign-up flow and 1,05,280 other free accounts are untouched; the leavers take their footers with them.

Option B: move GST return exports to the paid plan. Pulok's proposal reaches the 32,900 free accounts that use them. Assume 6 per cent pay (1,974) and 20 per cent leave (6,580). Revenue rises ₹59.22 lakh, serving falls ₹3.95 lakh, and new payers add ₹6.71 lakh of serving: a gain of ₹56.46 lakh a year. Build cost is ₹18 lakh, three months of the Pune team re-plumbing exports into the paid-plan entitlements. The footer stays on the invoices of the 24,346 who remain free; the 6,580 who leave take theirs, and the 1,974 who pay lose it. Option B's figures assume it is run alone.

Option C: close the free plan to new sign-ups and offer a 30-day trial. Purbasha's proposal removes free invoices and therefore the footer, so the 1,60,000 referral sign-ups go and the cohort falls to 2,40,000, with 76,000 activated (49,000 plus 27,000) at unchanged rates. Assume sign-ups from search, app stores, partners and ads, and their activation, are unchanged by the switch. Activated trial accounts that do not pay are assumed to cost ₹15 a year, not ₹60. At 10 per cent of activated paying (7,600), the margin is ₹177.50 lakh, ₹53.66 lakh above today's, net of the lost referral channel; if the trial converts at today's 6.0 per cent (4,560), it is ₹98.00 lakh, ₹25.84 lakh below. Build and migration cost ₹10 lakh, plus unpriced work closing existing free accounts under the DPDP Act's erasure rules.

7. Questions for discussion

1. Looking at Exhibits 1 and 2, in what sense are Hoolock's free accounts leads, and in what sense costs? Do your answers differ by account group?

2. Using Exhibit 3, which free accounts would Options A and B each change, and what does each estimate assume about how those users behave?

3. For Option C, what conversion of activated accounts would leave the margin where it is today, and how confident could the board be that a 30-day trial would reach it, given that only 6.0 per cent within 90 days under the free plan has been measured?

4. What would you put to the board, what would you ask Purbasha to measure first, and what would make you reverse course?

8. A note for the learner

Freemium asks one question of every free user: is this account a lead, a cost, or a distributor? Hoolock's activated free accounts are plausibly all three; Exhibit 1 does not show what the never-activated accounts do. The serving cost of accounts that had not paid within 90 days was ₹94.56 lakh (Exhibit 2, first two rows), or ₹1,126 for each of the 8,400 payers, against ₹3,000 of first-year revenue (₹2,600 after their own serving cost). That figure covers serving cost only, not marketing, and it is a price worth paying only while the free plan keeps supplying what Exhibit 1 shows: 1,60,000 sign-ups at the highest activation rate, brought by the footer.

One defensible path is Option A, which needs one month of Pune work after approval and so goes live in the weeks after Diwali. It touches the 20.0 per cent of free accounts with the heaviest invoice volume, so the footer goes from half of them (13,160 who pay or leave) but stays on the other 1,05,280 and on the 13,160 who remain under the cap, and it has the smallest build. Its 10 per cent conversion is a guess, so Prosenjit would say that a 90-day readout on the first cohort decides whether to follow with Option B. Option C is not rejected: on serving margin alone, and assuming the ₹15 serving cost for unpaid trial accounts, it matches today's ₹123.84 lakh at about 5,550 paying accounts, 7.3 per cent of 76,000 activated (at ₹60 it would need about 6,740, or 8.9 per cent). That is 1.3 points above the 6.0 per cent paid within 90 days under the free plan, a different clock from a 30-day trial. Hoolock has no evidence yet of that lift, and it would be bought with a channel it cannot easily reopen.
exp20v2-bm.freemium.model:
Freemium as a Business Model

Are free users leads or costs, and what converts them?

1. The email on 6 October

On Tuesday 6 October 2026, Elamathi Lakkamsetty, head of product at Thoranam Software in Coimbatore, opened a message from Enbarasan Lingutla, the finance lead. Thoranam's app, Thoranam Bills, lets small traders raise invoices under the goods and services tax (GST) from a phone. The message proposed ending its free plan on 1 November, for approval at the board meeting of 13 October. His reasoning was a number: the September 2025 cohort, everyone who signed up that month, had cost ₹3.8 lakh to serve for free, and her own team was about to add a free GST-return reminder that would lengthen the bill.

Elamathi's instinct was that free users were Thoranam's marketing. Enbarasan's was that they were a line in the hosting bill. Neither had said what the share was a share of. If the free plan went, Thoranam would be discarding the funnel that a ₹6 lakh acquisition spend had filled. If it stayed and was wrong, the damage would surface a year later. This page follows her arithmetic, and it argues one thing: a free user is a cost that buys an option, and the honest question is what the option is worth.

Table 1. The September 2025 cohort, twelve months to 30 September 2026 (rounded)
ItemValue
Signups10,000
Acquisition spend, ₹60 per signup₹6,00,000
Activated (sent at least one invoice within 30 days of signup)6,000
Paying within twelve months of signup240

2. The idea

Freemium is a pricing model in which a product offers a free tier to everyone, with no time limit, and charges for a paid tier, so the free tier works as marketing for the paid one. It builds directly on subscription economics, the logic of a recurring fee: freemium is a subscription with a free entry level that pays for distribution. In 2006 the venture investor Fred Wilson described the pattern on his blog and asked readers to name it; freemium, usually credited to Jarid Lukin, stuck. Its ancestor was 1980s shareware.

The problem it solved was distribution. Software costs almost nothing to copy, but a buyer cannot judge it before using it, and advertising to strangers is expensive. A free tier removes the buyer's risk and lets the product make the sale. The sentence Elamathi could repeat in a meeting without sounding glib: the free plan is a marketing budget we spend per active user per month, and we keep it only while the users it converts repay it.

3. How it works, step by step

Elamathi walked the September cohort through six steps. First, acquisition: 10,000 people signed up after Thoranam spent ₹60 on each. Second, activation, the point at which a signup becomes a real user. Thoranam defines it as sending an invoice within 30 days, and 6,000 did, so 60 per cent of signups. This step is routinely left implicit, yet it fixes the base of the conversion rate. Third, free use, where cost accrues. Each activated user costs ₹12 per active month, from hosting, invoices sent by message and support, and the cohort stayed active on average five months before lapsing.

Fourth, the upgrade trigger: the limit or feature a user comes to need, which pricing specialists call the value metric. Fifth, conversion: 240 of the 6,000 began paying. Sixth, retention as payers, because payers must stay long enough to repay the many free users who never convert. Conversion also ends a user's free-plan cost, a detail the arithmetic below ignores, which overstates cost a little.

The figure shows why the denominator must be named. The same 240 payers are 4.0 per cent of activated users (240 ÷ 6,000) and 2.4 per cent of signups (240 ÷ 10,000). A third base is the standing stock of active free users. If every month looked like September, 6,000 users would activate monthly and each would stay five months, so the stock would hold 6,000 × 5 = 30,000 active free users, and 240 monthly conversions would be 0.8 per cent of that stock a month.

4. A worked example, and what happens when one input moves

Enbarasan's ₹12 breaks down as hosting ₹3, messaging ₹6 and support ₹3. A paying user costs ₹41 a month (hosting ₹3, messaging ₹12, payment gateway about ₹6, support ₹20), so each payer contributes (revenue less variable cost) ₹299 − ₹41 = ₹258 a month. Pro payers leave at 5 per cent a month (churn, the share of payers lost each month), so the expected life is 1 ÷ 0.05 = 20 months, and contribution lifetime value, the total contribution one payer is expected to deliver, undiscounted, is ₹258 × 20 = ₹5,160. Each signup also costs ₹2 in verification messages.

Netreturn − outlay+2,58,400−29,600
Payers needed to break evenoutlay ÷ 5,160189.9, so 190245.7, so 246
Break-even as % of activatedpayers needed ÷ 6,0003.17%4.10%

Conversion held at 240 payers (4.0% of activated) in both columns. Break-even is a threshold, not a forecast: it is the payer count whose lifetime contribution repays everything spent on the cohort. The overstated free cost and the undiscounted lifetime value pull in opposite directions; neither is adjusted.

The baseline clears break-even: 4.0 per cent against a required 3.17, a return of 12,38,400 ÷ 9,80,000 = 1.26 times. The free plan alone is repaid by 3,80,000 ÷ 5,160 = 73.6 payers, so 74, against 240 observed. For the second pass Elamathi changed one input. The reminder feature, in the team's own estimate, would lengthen average free life from five months to nine, with conversion unchanged. The free-plan cost rises to 6,68,000, the break-even rises to 246 payers, and the cohort loses ₹29,600.

5. Six nuances that separate users of the vocabulary from users of the idea

One programme, three denominators

Three rates are all true of the same 240 payers: 0.8 per cent a month of the free stock, 4.0 per cent of activated users and 2.4 per cent of signups. A conversion rate means nothing until its base and period are named, and it must keep that base throughout a memo.

Free is not zero

Marginal cost near zero is true of copying software, not of serving a user. Messaging, support and payment handling scale with activity, so ₹12 an active month is a real unit cost.

Freemium is not a trial

A free trial has a clock: users must decide when it runs out. Freemium has none, so cost accrues until the user lapses, which is why free months is an input at all. Advertising-funded products differ again, earning from the free user directly.

The limit and the conversion rate move together

Letting users stay free longer changes who meets the upgrade prompt. Holding conversion at 4.0 per cent in the second pass is therefore an assumption, and Table 2 is a test of tolerance rather than a prediction.

Figure 4 draws that tolerance. Each added free month costs 6,000 × ₹12 = ₹72,000 and raises the required conversion by 0.23 points. The line meets 4.0 per cent where (240 × 5,160 − 6,20,000, the acquisition and verification costs) ÷ 72,000 = 8.59 months. Past that, the cohort no longer repays itself.

A cohort must be old enough, and its lifetime value is an estimate

Conversions keep arriving across the twelve months, so a cohort read at month four understates its conversion; compare cohorts at equal age. The 5 per cent churn is also an estimate. At 7 per cent, lifetime value falls to ₹258 ÷ 0.07 = ₹3,686, break-even in the baseline rises to 266 payers (4.43 per cent of activated), and the same 240 payers return ₹8.85 lakh against a ₹9.80 lakh outlay.

What the model cannot tell you

It says whether payers repay the outlay. It cannot say how many of the 240 would have paid had Thoranam offered a trial or no free plan; a holdout, in which some new signups are denied the free tier, is the direct way to find out. Before relying on any freemium figure, ask: which denominator, which period, what cost per active user, how old the cohort is, and what the counterfactual is.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace; early and large

Table 3. Where the free user sits
SettingWhat the free user isWhat converts themCost risk
ConsumerAn audience, often very largeRemoving friction or ads, extra capacityHeavy use by people who will never pay
B2BA small account, a possible future teamTeam features, admin controls, supportSupport time on accounts that stay small
MarketplaceOne side of the market, usually supplyA commission on transactions, not a planListings that never transact

Thoranam sits in B2B at micro scale: each user is a trader, and the upgrade trigger is business growth. In a marketplace the free side is often the product itself, so the question is whether free supply attracts demand. Between stages, a company with 10,000 signups a month can read a cohort on one page, and its free plan costs ₹3.8 lakh a cohort. At a hundred times that volume the same plan is a multi-crore line (₹3.8 crore a cohort if unit costs held, which at that scale they rarely do), and caps tend to tighten.

7. Three mistakes, how they look from outside, and the cheap check

Quoting conversion on the wrong base. From outside, the product team and the board report different conversion rates for the same quarter and each is annoyed at the other. The misunderstanding is treating "conversion" as one number. The cheapest diagnostic is to ask for the numerator, the denominator and the period behind every rate, in one line each.

Pricing the free tier at zero. From outside, signups grow while gross margin falls, and the messaging bill rises faster than revenue. The misunderstanding is the belief that software has no marginal cost. The diagnostic: divide the actual monthly bill by active free users and compare the result with the plan's ₹12 estimate.

Declaring success on an unaged cohort. From outside, a launch is celebrated at week six, then the numbers sag as later cohorts arrive. The misunderstanding is that early converters are representative. The diagnostic is a chart of conversion by cohort age, which takes one query.

8. What good looks like

Handled well, the board memo would be a single page. It states three conversion rates with their bases, a cost per active free month taken from invoices, and a cohort table by age. It shows the break-even payer count beside the observed count and the number of free months at which they cross. It names one input the team can move, and the figure at which it would act.

9. What Elamathi decided

On 13 October she asked the board to keep the free plan, release the GST-return reminder on Pro only, and set a tripwire. The reasoning rested on Table 2. The baseline returns 1.26 times its whole outlay, and 74 payers repay the free plan against 240 observed. Free in the proposed form would have put the cohort ₹29,600 under water with no margin left, and her own 4.0 per cent was an assumption she could not test in advance. The tripwire: review if average free months per activated user pass 7, where break-even conversion is 3.63 per cent (218 payers), ahead of the 8.59-month crossover. Enbarasan accepted the design, with one condition, that a holdout be run on part of the next cohort.

The next topic to study is pricing and unit economics, where lifetime value, acquisition cost and cohort retention are built carefully, followed by experiment design, because the counterfactual question needs it. Two questions to sit with. If Thoranam doubled Pro to ₹598 with churn and variable cost unchanged, what would the break-even payer count become, and what would you need to believe about conversion to leave the free plan as it is? And in a product you know, which free users would you stop serving first, and what would you have to measure to be sure?

Imarat Systems: What Is the Free Tier For?

Imarat Systems Private Limited is fictional; the market and institutions around it are real.

Strategy & Business · Business Models · Pune, March 2026

1. Sunday night, 15 March 2026

The Baner office had been dark since eight, and Rumela Bhuyan was working by the glow of an undimmed monitor. On it sat the board pre-read due by morning: eleven slides, of which she had written ten. The eleventh, titled Free tier: recommendation, was empty.

At four the next afternoon, in Lower Parel, the board would be asked to approve a plan for the thing that had made Imarat: a free tier holding 31,80,000 registered accounts, 2,96,000 of which had opened the product in February. The board had not asked whether the free tier worked. It had asked what it cost, and whether the company could reach cash-flow break-even without changing it.

Her co-founder had messaged at eleven: Cap it. We can argue about the rest in June. Her head of enterprise sales, nine and a half hours behind in New Jersey, had sent nine hundred words the other way. Both were reading the same six exhibits.

2. The company, and a clause from 2022

Imarat was founded in Pune in 2017 by Rumela Bhuyan and Raktim Buragohain, who had tired of watching engineers test APIs with pasted shell scripts. Imarat Workbench let a developer design, run, mock and document an API in one place, and for three years it was free because nobody would have paid for it. Paid tiers arrived in 2020, priced per seat. By February 2026 the company employed 214 people across seven offices on three continents, on annual recurring revenue of ₹91.14 crore, against ₹68.20 crore a year earlier.

Two earlier decisions shape what is possible now. In August 2022, to win Iqraar Logistics Group of Dubai — then Imarat's largest contract, at ₹1.84 crore a year — Rumela agreed a clause giving every Iqraar employee a free personal workspace, uncapped, for the life of the agreement. It went into the standard enterprise template and survives in 26 of the 41 agreements live today, covering ₹16.42 crore of enterprise revenue and 47,000 free accounts, 16,000 of them monthly active in February 2026.

The second decision was technical: in August 2024, facing a more generous competitor, Imarat raised free-workspace storage from 500 MB to 2 GB. Nobody modelled the bill.

3. The industry

Indian software companies have made a durable business of giving the first unit away: Zoho sells a suite in which several products have free entry tiers, and Freshworks and Postman grew bottom-up out of developer adoption before enterprise contracts followed. Imarat's board had never questioned having a free tier; the live question was what it was for.

Three forces press on it. The first is cost: a free workspace holds request histories, mock definitions and response payloads in AWS Mumbai and Frankfurt, and runs scheduled collections that consume compute whether or not anyone pays.

The second is Indian payment regulation: the Reserve Bank of India's framework for recurring card mandates requires registration and a pre-debit notification before each charge, and a lapsed mandate has to be set up again.

The third is data protection: counsel's note of 2 March 2026 reads the Digital Personal Data Protection Act's notified rules as applying to free workspaces exactly as to paid ones, because a free workspace holds the same customer payloads.

India supplies 13,03,800 of the 31,80,000 registered free accounts, 41.00 per cent, and ₹26.43 crore of the ₹91.14 crore book, 29.00 per cent. Renewal differs too: of the Team seats that fell due for renewal in the year to February 2026, 8,094 of 11,400 in India renewed, 71.00 per cent, against 26,400 of 30,000 elsewhere, 88.00 per cent.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

The free funnel was believed stable. Through 2024 the growth team reported a signup-to-paid rate "between 1.8 and 2.1 per cent" and treated it as a constant; the 2025 plan was built on 2.00 per cent. Exhibit 1 shows what the cohorts did: signups grew 44.67 per cent from April to August 2025 while activation and day-90 survival both fell, and the April cohort's 2.00 per cent signup-to-paid rate became the August cohort's 1.60 per cent.

It was also believed that the free tier paid for itself in pipeline, because the CRM said so: at each deal close the account executive picked a lead source, and 27 of the 41 live agreements, 65.85 per cent, carry "free-tier user inside the account". In January 2026 Ritabrata Barbhuiya rebuilt the question from the identity log. Exhibit 5 sets the two readings side by side over the same 41 agreements and the same ₹22.95 crore.

The third belief was about cost, and it was revised once. Rupkatha Basak's memo of 3 March 2026 put the free tier at ₹28.00 per monthly active account, excluding support and the data-protection allocation; finance rebuilt it on 7 March with both pools in and reached ₹33.00 (Exhibit 2), ₹11.72 crore a year at February's run rate. Before either number existed, from 1 November 2025 to 12 January 2026, growth ran the storage-cap test now at the centre of the argument (Exhibit 4).

Figure 1. Imarat Systems, March 2024 to March 2026. Markers are month-level, each on the first day of the month it names, at 28 pixels to the month.

5. The people

Figure 2. Reporting lines, February 2026. Design reports to the CTO, data science to the VP, Self-Serve Growth.

Rumela Bhuyan, 41, co-founder and chief executive, Pune. She wants a decision defensible for three years; her incentive is a Series C term sheet conditional on a path to break-even. She has not told the board she agreed the 2022 clause herself, or that it sits in 26 contracts.

Raktim Buragohain, 44, co-founder and chief technology officer, Bengaluru. He wants the cap: the free tier, he says, is an engineering tax on paying customers. He has not circulated an analysis showing that 61 per cent of the free storage bill — ₹23.47 lakh of February's ₹38.48 lakh — comes from 12,432 accounts, 4.20 per cent of the monthly active base, mostly continuous-integration robots.

Rupkatha Basak, 36, VP, Self-Serve Growth, Bengaluru. She commissioned the November test and wants it shipped; her 2026 bonus is written on self-serve net new ARR. She has not said that her ₹28.00 figure left out two pools, or that the data scientist who sized and read the test reports to her.

Rathindra Bhunia, 49, chief financial officer, Mumbai. He calls ₹11.72 crore a year the easiest line to cut before a Series C. He has modelled a 6 per cent rise in the Team plan's realised price, worth ₹248.40 lakh a year before churn, and has not circulated it: he believes the last rise cost India renewals.

Ritabrata Barbhuiya, 33, principal data scientist, Toronto. He defends the uplift and attacks the annualisation; his credibility rests on a test he designed. He has not rerun it with the already-primed accounts excluded, because nobody asked and the request would go through Rupkatha.

Rwitika Borpujari, 38, customer-success lead, Singapore. She argues the cap lands hardest on free users inside paying accounts; her number is gross renewal. Three of her largest accounts have asked in writing for the clause at their next renewal, and she has not told sales.

Rudraprasad Basumatary, 46, head of enterprise sales, New Jersey. The free tier is the pipeline, and the Iqraar renewal lands on 31 March. He has his account executives record "free-tier user inside the account" whenever a free account exists on the customer's domain at any time, which is not the identity log's definition.

Rikhia Bairagi, 34, head of design, Berlin. A ninety-day clock, she says, reads as a trial, and the onboarding flow she built assumes permanence. The prompt shipped in November is one she argued against, and she believes the uplift measures the prompt, not the cap.

7. Voices

Raktim Buragohain, engineering channel, 6 March, 21:40 IST

"Twelve thousand accounts run scheduled collections against our mock servers every six hours and have never clicked upgrade. I am not asking the board for philosophy. I am asking them to stop paying for other people's CI."

Rathindra Bhunia, comment on the board pre-read, 9 March

"₹11.72 crore a year is 12.86 per cent of revenue, and it sits in the one place where a cut needs nobody's permission. If we are promising this board cash-flow positive before the cash runs out, why is this the line we defend?"

"Iqraar signs again on the 31st and their CTO has asked me twice to extend the free workspace clause to contractors — three thousand accounts that will never pay us a rupee, and I will give them away happily, because that clause is why we are in. Twenty-seven of our forty-one logos had somebody inside already using us for free."
