"The uplift is real — six tenths of a point on a hundred and thirty-five thousand accounts is not noise. What is not real is multiplying it by five. Two in five of the extra conversions were already past the soft warning on day one, and some were going to pay us in March anyway."

Rwitika Borpujari and Rikhia Bairagi, growth review, 12 March

Borpujari: "The accounts that hit a 500 MB cap first sit inside our paying customers. Their developers keep a personal workspace because the team one is governed. Those are the people who renew us."

Bairagi: "And we changed two things in that test. A cap and a prompt. I asked for the cap on its own and was told there wasn't time."

8. The options as Rumela sees them

Three options went into the pre-read, costed in Exhibit 6 on one base of 2,80,000 contract-eligible accounts.

Option A, leave the free tier as it is. No build, no contract exposure, no change to the upgrade surface. Exhibit 2's ₹11.72 crore a year continues and grows with the base, and the drift in Exhibit 1 goes untreated.

Option B, cap free workspaces at 500 MB and 100 saved requests. It costs ₹118.00 lakh and 46 engineer-weeks, touches the 2,80,000 accounts not covered by a clause, and leaves the 16,000 contract-protected accounts as they are. The November test arm combined a 500 MB cap with an upgrade prompt; it set no request limit. On the refreshed-pool reading it adds ₹840.00 lakh of ARR a year; on the fixed-stock reading the uplift happens once, ₹168.00 lakh. On both readings it saves ₹28.56 lakh of free-tier cost a year; on an assumed 1.60 per cent conversion among the accounts it removes, which the test did not measure, it forgoes ₹22.40 lakh once. Dividing the ₹118.00 lakh build cost by one year of the new ARR plus the cost saved, less the seats forgone, gives 1.67 months on the first reading and 8.13 months on the second, treating a full year's effect as arriving from the first day.

Option C, time-box the free tier at 90 days, after which a workspace becomes read-only. It costs ₹262.00 lakh and 104 engineer-weeks, applies to the same 2,80,000 accounts, and leaves the paid plans untouched.

Rumela had written the three herself, and reading them back she was not sure they were the whole set, or that "how much free" was the question the board would put to her.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board meets at 16:00 IST on Monday 16 March 2026 and expects a recommendation, not options. Four constraints bound it.

Money. Cash at 28 February was ₹38.40 crore against February's net burn of ₹1.92 crore, a runway of 20.0 months at that rate, and the Series C term sheet is conditional on a credible path to break-even inside it.

People. Between 16 March and 30 June there are 15 weeks, of which the quarter-end freeze takes 2. The platform squad is 11 engineers, so 13 clear weeks give 143 engineer-weeks, of which 92 are committed to the Iqraar integration and the data-protection work, leaving 51.

Contracts. The 2022 clause binds 26 agreements worth ₹16.42 crore and 47,000 free accounts; counsel's view of 4 March is that capping those accounts would breach it. Iqraar renews on 31 March and has asked to widen the clause to contractors.

Regulation. Data-protection obligations fall on free and paid workspaces alike, whatever the tier becomes.

At twenty to two Rumela opened the eleventh slide, typed a title — What the free tier is for — and deleted it, because she could not yet write the sentence that followed. Outside, the first auto-rickshaws of Monday were moving on Baner Road.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibit 1, describe what happened to the free funnel between April and August 2025. Which transition accounts for most of the fall in the signup-to-paid rate, and what denominator did you use at each step?
  2. Exhibit 2 puts a monthly active free account at ₹33.00. What does that figure include, what does it leave out, and what would you need to know before using it as a marginal rather than an average cost?
  3. Exhibits 3 and 5 are both evidence about whether free users are leads. What are the widest and the narrowest defensible claims about the share of enterprise revenue that began in a free account, and what does each one rest on?
  4. Exhibit 4 reports a 0.60 percentage-point conversion uplift and a 5.00 percentage-point inactivity increment over 73 days. Test Ritabrata Barbhuiya's "two in five" against the exhibit, and say what that share does to Exhibit 6's figures.
  5. Exhibit 6 prices Options B and C on one volume base and one realised seat price. Which choice does more work in the comparison, and what changes if converts from a capped free tier do not arrive on the Team plan?
  6. It is Monday morning, 16 March 2026. What does Rumela Bhuyan do, what does she say to the board that afternoon, and what evidence would she commit to having by September that she does not have now?

Bijuli: the Price of a Slot

A case for discussion. Bijuli Media Private Limited is fictional; the market, regulators and competitors around it are not.

1. Indiranagar, Sunday night

At twenty minutes to ten on the night of Sunday, 18 October 2026, Jonmoni Ramchiary sat on the floor of her flat in Indiranagar, Bengaluru, with four printed pages fanned out in front of her and the dhaak from a Puja pandal two streets away coming through the window. Diwali was twenty-one days off. In the Indian advertising year most of the money arrives in the second half, and the festive weeks open it.

The board of Bijuli Media Private Limited would meet at ten the next morning, with the investor director joining from Singapore. Ramchiary had co-founded Bijuli in Guwahati eight years earlier as an Assamese-language video feed her mother could use without typing. It now had 8.9 crore monthly active users and 2.21 crore daily, in eleven languages, and had never charged one of them a rupee.

Instead it sold their attention, and the question for the board was how much more of it to sell, to whom, and at what price. The four pages did not agree with one another. One was the quarter's inventory report from her own ad server. One was a billing statement from the Dubai partner that sells much of that inventory, counting the same impressions differently. One was an August experiment that said a heavier ad load would be worth a lot. The last was two estimates of how many of Bijuli's users were children, differing by about twenty-six lakh people.

2. How Bijuli got here

Bijuli was founded in March 2018 above a printing press in Guwahati, and for two years it was an Assamese and Bengali product with a staff of nineteen. A ₹46 crore Series A in November 2019 moved the headquarters to Bengaluru; language operations stayed in Guwahati, where 310 of the company's 1,090 employees still sit.

The decision that shapes everything on Ramchiary's floor was taken in June 2021. Bijuli had been requiring a phone number and an OTP before a user could scroll, and growth was flat. Jashojit Rajbarman, the co-founder who runs engineering, proposed making login optional: a user could watch, comment and follow on a device identifier alone. Daily actives rose 3.4 times in nine months. Five years on, 81 per cent of daily actives have never logged in, Bijuli cannot reliably say how old they are, and it cannot cap how often one person sees the same advertisement.

In February 2023 Bijuli signed an exclusive sales agreement with Bazm Media Networks FZ-LLC of Dubai, which brought international and programmatic demand when the direct sales team was four people. In January 2026 a ₹620 crore Series C valued the company at ₹4,100 crore and attached a revenue covenant to FY27. In April 2026 Bijuli launched a self-serve Ads Manager. Figure 1 sets these out.

3. The market Bijuli sells into

In Indian digital advertising the two global platforms take the largest share of spend and everybody else argues over the remainder. Bijuli competes for it with ShareChat and Moj, Josh, Dailyhunt, Kuku FM, Pratilipi and Stage, and with Jio's distribution. Brand money reaches them largely through a handful of Mumbai media agencies, which buy on CPM and settle in sixty to ninety days. Performance money — app installs, D2C, quick commerce — buys on CPC, settles faster and pays less per thousand.

Four regulatory facts bear directly on the business. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 restricts the processing of children's personal data and behaviourally targeted advertising directed at them; rules under the Act were notified in November 2025 with an eighteen-month transition, which Bijuli's counsel reads as a deadline in May 2027. The ASCI code and Ministry of Information and Broadcasting advisories govern what may be advertised and how it must be labelled. SEBI's rules on unregistered investment advice constrain a growing part of Bijuli's finance demand. GST at 18 per cent applies to advertising services, which matters to self-serve SMB advertisers who cannot always claim it back.

Bijuli's foreign exposure runs through Dubai: Bazm Media Networks sells Bijuli inventory to Gulf and South-East Asian buyers reaching the Indian diaspora, in dollars. That demand is seasonal and, as Exhibit 4 shows, measured by Bazm.

4. What happened, and what turned out to be wrong

In January 2026, closing the Series C, Bijuli's plan showed FY27 net revenue of ₹340 crore, and the covenant was written to it. The plan assumed fill rate would rise as the self-serve platform matured. What was believed was that unsold inventory was a demand problem. Exhibit 1 shows the quarter that followed: pooled fill of 73.1 per cent, with the highest-priced auctioned surface, pre-roll at ₹96, filling at just over half.

In April 2026 the Ads Manager launched, contributing by September the volume in Exhibit 1 and the advertiser mix in Exhibit 3. What was believed was that self-serve demand would lift the blended price. It added 945.0 crore impressions at an average of ₹14 per thousand, against a blended quarterly figure of ₹33.01.

Between Monday 10 and Sunday 23 August, Jaganmoy Rajbanik's team ran the ad-load experiment in Exhibit 2. On 1 September the result was circulated as an annual opportunity, and restated in October at ₹88.7 crore: eleven paise a day, 2.21 crore daily actives, 365 days. What has since turned out to be in dispute is the fortnight itself: Jurimoni Rajphukan's note of 6 October records feed-card fill across the test cells at 92 per cent in that window, against 74.4 per cent on the feed card for the quarter.

On 2 October 2025 the 180-day notice window on the Bazm agreement closed unremarked and the contract auto-renewed to 31 March 2028; what was believed in February 2023 was that the exclusive ran three years. On 6 October 2026 Jiteswar Ronghang, reconciling the quarter, found the impression discrepancy in Exhibit 4. On 9 October the metered panel returned the audience estimate in Exhibit 5, which does not match Bijuli's own.

5. The people

Figure 2 shows where they sit and who reports to whom.

Jonmoni Ramchiary, 36, co-founder and chief executive, Bengaluru. Wants a decision she can defend in three years, not three quarters. Her incentive is a secondary sale vesting on the FY27 covenant. She has not told the board she thinks that covenant was set on a plan she no longer believes.

Jashojit Rajbarman, 39, co-founder and chief technology officer, Bengaluru. Argues the 2021 login decision bought the company its scale, and unwinding it would cost more users than regulation will. He owns the roadmap the identity work would displace, and does not mention that his team's device-graph model, the left-hand column of Exhibit 5, was built in six weeks.

Juneli Rajgupta, 41, chief revenue officer, Mumbai. Carries the number. Wants the load raised on 1 November so the festive quarter catches it, and has written that the move covers the covenant gap. Her variable pay is set on gross billings, not net revenue. She has not mentioned that two large agency relationships have asked for frequency-capped buys Bijuli cannot deliver.

Jaganmoy Rajbanik, 34, vice-president, product, Pune. Ran the experiment and believes its retention finding more than its revenue finding. Wants the identity layer. His promotion case rests on the self-serve platform the identity work would slow.

Jaymoti Rongphar, 31, design lead, Berlin. Measures what she calls the user's bill: seconds of advertising per session, and the share of them a user cannot skip. Wants that number treated as a price. Reports to Rajbanik, three and a half hours behind Bengaluru. She has an offer from a Berlin company and has not said so.

Jurimoni Rajphukan, 37, senior data scientist, Toronto. Produced the fill-rate correction. Believes the panel in Exhibit 5 is closer to the truth than the internal model and cannot prove it. Reports to Rajbarman, whose model she is contradicting.

Jiteswar Ronghang, 44, head of partnerships and ad operations, Singapore. Manages Bazm day to day, found the discrepancy, raised it late. His relationship with Jadumoni Rajkakoti, Bazm's managing director in Dubai, is credited inside Bijuli with holding international demand through 2025. Rajgupta, revenue review, Mumbai, Tuesday 6 October "Eleven paise a day across 2.21 crore people for 151 days is ₹36.71 crore. That is the gap, and it is one configuration change. I will not explain to the board that we left it there because the design team is unhappy about seconds."

Rajkakoti, Bazm Media, Dubai, email of 13 October "We have billed on measured impressions since 2023 and you have invoiced against our statements every quarter since. If your server counts differently, that is a question about your server. Our rate card is set against measured impressions; re-base the count and the rate re-bases with it."
Rajbanik to Ramchiary, direct message, Friday 16 October, 11:12 p.m. IST "Ask them which number the covenant is written on. Then ask what we tell a fourteen-year-old's mother in May 2027. We keep holding only one of those meetings."

8. The options as Ramchiary sees them

Ramchiary wrote five lines on a sheet on Saturday morning, in the order the revenue team had raised them.

A. Raise the feed load to one in six from 1 November. A configuration change, no engineering. In Exhibit 2 the 1-in-6 cell ran 11 paise per user per day above control, on a gross basis, over fourteen days in August. It leaves the identity question, the Bazm agreement and the measurement dispute exactly where they are.

B. Terminate the Bazm exclusive. ₹24 crore now, and the 28 per cent partner share moves to Bijuli's own cost base — Rajgupta scopes a direct programmatic desk at eleven people. International demand would have to be rebuilt from buyers Bijuli does not contract with directly.

C. Build the identity layer. An optional phone login with a declared date of birth, consent capture, and frequency capping on logged-in users. Scoped at 96 engineer-weeks. Rajbanik's estimate is that a login prompt at the third session costs between 6 and 11 per cent of daily actives in the first month. It does nothing for users who decline it.

D. Launch a ₹59-a-month ad-free tier. At 1 per cent of monthly actives it bills ₹5.25 crore a month. Those users leave the inventory counted in Exhibit 1, and the billing and support stack has to be built in a company that has never taken money from a user.

E. Sell the audience as a commerce audience. A national quick-commerce platform has tabled an eighteen-month term sheet at a ₹40 crore annual minimum, conditional on device-level signal sharing. Counsel has not yet opined on it. The signals it asks for are device-level, and 81 per cent of daily actives have no login.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board meets at ten on Monday 19 October 2026. The FY27 covenant is net revenue of ₹340 crore. The bridge from Exhibit 1 runs: gross billings ₹78.91 crore, less the Bazm share of ₹7.69 crore, less agency commission of ₹5.73 crore, 15 per cent on the ₹38.22 crore that is neither the ₹27.46 crore sold through Bazm nor the ₹13.23 crore taken on the self-serve platform, and is treated as all agency-booked — giving Q2 net revenue of ₹65.49 crore. With Q1 at ₹55.71 crore, H1 net revenue is ₹121.20 crore. At the 1.5 times H2-to-H1 ratio of the last two years, FY27 lands at ₹303.00 crore.

Cash was ₹286 crore on 30 September against an operating burn of ₹31 crore a quarter. The Bazm agreement runs to 31 March 2028 and terminates for convenience at the greater of ₹24 crore or the average partner share of the preceding two quarters, which on Q1's ₹6.95 crore and Q2's ₹7.69 crore is ₹7.32 crore. The Pune ad-experience pod is nine engineers, two of them committed to the self-serve migration until 31 December; seven engineers over the ten working weeks to 31 December is 70 engineer-weeks. Counsel's May 2027 reading of the DPDP transition sits outside FY27.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibit 1, describe what Bijuli sells and to whom. Which unit — a request, an impression, a click, a minute — would you put at the centre of its pricing?
  2. Exhibit 2 reports a fortnight in August; Exhibit 1 the quarter containing it. What would have to be true of that fortnight for Exhibit 2's revenue column to hold across a year, and how would you find out?
  3. Exhibit 4 gives two impression counts for the same inventory. Which should Bijuli price against, what happens to Exhibit 1's eCPM column if the other is used, and what does Rajkakoti's email imply about re-basing?
  4. Exhibit 5 gives two age distributions. Work out Bijuli's exposure under each, stating your assumption about how heavily under-18 users consume relative to everyone else. What evidence would move you from one to the other?
  5. Take the five options in turn. For each, say who bears the cost, in what currency, over what period, and who inside Bijuli is measured on the result.
  6. What should Ramchiary do on Monday morning, and what should she say to the board about the covenant? If the two differ, say why.

Sunday, 11:20 p.m.

The dhaak had stopped. Ramchiary gathered the four pages into one pile and separated them again; they would not sit in any order. Her phone showed eleven unread messages on the product channel. Downstairs a delivery rider waited under the streetlight with his phone held close to his face, watching something in portrait, and she found herself counting the cards before the advertisement came.
case20v1-bm.ads:
Alokit: Whose Attention Is for Sale

A decision case in advertising business models

1. Opening

At 8.30 on the evening of Monday, 5 October 2026, Ishtuti Pyne, chief product officer of Alokit, sat in the Bengaluru office with a note from the chief executive and a deadline. By Friday, 16 October, Alokit had to tell its advertising agencies what the Puja-to-Diwali rate card would be: how many ad breaks a listener would be offered each hour, and at what price. The agencies were holding festive budgets and would commit to whichever platform fixed its terms first.

Indrasish Patowary, the founder, wanted ad revenue raised by a quarter. Ishtuti had a test result on the obvious way to do it. She had eleven days, a team spread across four time zones, and one question the dashboard could not answer: who, exactly, was Alokit's customer?

2. Company background

Indrasish, a former radio producer from Guwahati, founded Alokit in 2021 in Kolkata's Salt Lake, to sell audio stories in Bengali, Assamese and Hindi to listeners who found English-first apps thin on their languages. By September 2026 it had 50 lakh listeners active in a four-week period and a catalogue of 1,200 titles: serialised thrillers, folk tales and Puja-special radio plays. Engineers worked in Bengaluru and Pune. The Puja-to-Diwali quarter was the busiest of the year: families travelled home, listening rose, and agencies booked festive budgets early, which is why rate cards were fixed in October.

The app was free. Alokit earned from audio ads played between episodes, sold two ways: direct, by a small sales team dealing with brands and agencies, and programmatic, through automated auctions. Three terms recur in this case. An impression is one ad played. An ad break is one slot, whether or not it is sold. Fill rate is the share of available ad slots that were sold. The effective rate, eCPM, is revenue per 1,000 filled impressions.

Rivals pulled in different directions. Pocket FM and Kuku FM sell paid access to episodes; JioSaavn and YouTube Music carry advertising beside far larger catalogues. Alokit's edge was depth in Bengali and Assamese. Content rules came from the Advertising Standards Council of India, and because targeting individuals needs consent under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, Alokit targeted by language and city only.

3. The situation

Exhibit 1 shows the four weeks to 27 September. Listeners were offered 2.5 ad breaks an hour, 60 per cent of slots were sold, and revenue was ₹36 lakh. Direct buyers paid ₹150 per 1,000 impressions and programmatic buyers ₹50, so the smaller direct share earned as much as the larger programmatic one. Indrasish wanted ₹45 lakh for the period ending 20 December, ahead of a fundraising round in January.

The simplest lever was more breaks. In August Imanta Pegu, the data scientist in Toronto, ran a four-week test (Exhibit 2) on two random arms of 2,00,000 listeners each. He presented it on Monday, 14 September, and the dates are on the timeline in Figure 1. Imanta cautioned that it measured five weeks and a single change. Ishtuti's difficulty was that both stories were partly true. Ads were Alokit's only revenue, which gave Indrasish's ₹45 lakh target its weight; yet nobody in the company could say what a listener who left would otherwise have been worth.

The team saw it from where they sat. The designer in Berlin said that a slot offered every 17 minutes was the point at which she would stop listening herself. The customer-success lead in Singapore reported that complaints about ads had risen in the test arm. In Edison, New Jersey, Ibrar Palchaudhuri, the sales head, argued the opposite. A Dubai jewellery group, his largest direct buyer, wanted Puja-season reach among Gulf listeners, and he believed new slots would sell as readily as the old.

Ishtuti scheduled a call for 8.30 pm IST on Tuesday, 6 October: 11.00 am in Toronto and New Jersey, 5.00 pm in Berlin and 11.00 pm in Singapore.

4. The people

Ishtuti Pyne, chief product officer, Bengaluru, owns the decision. She wants a rate card she can defend with evidence from the test rather than with the revenue target.

Indrasish Patowary, founder and chief executive, Kolkata, wants ₹45 lakh a period by 20 December. He reads the test as five weeks of data on a business that needs revenue now.

Ibrar Palchaudhuri, head of sales, Edison, New Jersey, is paid on direct bookings. He wants more inventory to sell and holds that extra breaks would fill at the existing 60 per cent.

Imanta Pegu, data scientist, Toronto, ran the test. He wants the result described for what it measured, which was five weeks, one load change and a random split.

6. The options

Option 1: raise the load. From 16 October every free listener is offered 3.5 breaks an hour instead of 2.5. In the test, revenue per listener rose from ₹0.7200 to ₹0.7302, which at 50 lakh listeners is ₹36.51 lakh a period. Option 2: add an ad-free tier. Alokit keeps 2.5 breaks for free listeners and sells ad-free listening at ₹79 per 28-day cycle, billed through UPI AutoPay. Pune estimates six weeks of work to build billing and the new tier, so, counting from today, the first revenue would arrive after Diwali on 8 November. Exhibit 3 assumes 0.6 per cent of listeners subscribe. Subscribers stop generating ad revenue, which Exhibit 3 deducts.

Option 3: sell premium only. Alokit stops programmatic sales and runs 1.5 breaks an hour, sold directly. Direct buyers earn ₹18.00 lakh in Exhibit 1, so the programmatic ₹18.00 lakh is given up; at 320 lakh hours and 1.5 breaks, 480 lakh slots would carry 120 lakh sold impressions, a fill rate of 25 per cent. Free listeners would hear a quieter app; Exhibit 2 does not cover that load.

7. Questions for discussion

1. In Exhibit 1, who pays Alokit, what does each buyer type buy, and what does ₹0.72 per listener say about what a listener is worth to the business?

2. In Exhibit 2, follow the move from breaks per hour to revenue per listener, one row at a time. What changed at each step, and what would you want to know before trusting the result beyond five weeks?

3. Ibrar expects new slots to fill at 60 per cent; Indrasish needs ₹45 lakh. What does each option do to slots, fill rate and eCPM, and what does Exhibit 3 show for each?

4. What should Ishtuti tell the agencies on 16 October, and what would she test first?

8. A note for the learner

An advertising business sells attention, and the listener supplies it. Ad load is the price listeners pay in attention, so raising it adds supply while testing the patience of the people who provide it. In the test, available slots rose 29.1 per cent (16.00 to 20.65) but filled impressions only 11.9 per cent (9.600 to 10.738), because fill fell from 60 to 52 per cent; eCPM fell from ₹75 to ₹68 as well, so revenue per listener rose just 1.4 per cent. A well-reasoned answer asks what a change does to every step of the chain, then asks whose money it is.

One defensible path: keep 2.5 breaks through the festive quarter and tell agencies so; protect the direct buyers, who pay three times the programmatic eCPM; and build the ad-free tier for mid-November. Under the stated assumptions it adds ₹23.33 lakh a period, 64.8 per cent of today's revenue. About 655 subscribers (0.013 per cent of listeners) match Option 1's gross gain before payment fees, since each nets ₹77.76 after forgone ads. The 0.6 per cent is untested, so a two-week price pilot should follow the build and precede any commitment to ₹45 lakh; if take-up falls below 0.6 per cent, the target would be reset downward openly with Indrasish, not met by trading away listeners.

Advertising Business Models

When attention is the inventory, who is the customer?

1. The board paper

On Monday 14 September 2026, Varalakshmi Ellappan, head of product at Lokam, opened a spreadsheet she had been dreading. Lokam is a free Hyderabad-based app carrying cricket scores and Telugu and Tamil news. It averaged 12 lakh daily active users (distinct people opening the app on a given day, abbreviated DAU) in August and earned ₹90.72 lakh a month from advertising. The board's plan assumed ₹1 crore (100 lakh) a month by Diwali, which fell on 8 November.

Her chief financial officer, Vedagiri Eswaramurthy, proposed a one-line fix: raise ad slots per session from three to five. Slots rise by two-thirds, so revenue rises by two-thirds, and the target is passed with room to spare. He was not careless. He was applying the arithmetic most people apply to an ad-funded product, and it is correct as far as it goes.

Ellappan had a four-week split test behind her, run from 17 August to 13 September, in which separate groups of about a tenth of users saw three, four or five slots. The five-slot group opened the app less often, and some of it had stopped. She had until the board on Tuesday 15 September. If she backed the two-thirds arithmetic and it was wrong, Lokam would spend its best trading quarter shrinking the audience it was selling.

2. The idea

An advertising business model is one in which the product is free to users and the money comes from third parties who pay to put messages in front of them. What advertisers buy is attention: a measured moment in which a particular kind of person looks at a screen. The firm's inventory, the stock it sells, is the supply of such moments. Unlike unsold shoes, an unsold slot cannot be sold next week; it expires when the user closes the app.

The model predates the internet. In 1833 Benjamin Day's New York Sun sold for a penny, below its cost, and lived on advertisers who wanted its readers. Broadcasting measured the same trade in CPM, cost per mille, the price of one thousand exposures. Search added a second unit in the late 1990s, when Bill Gross's GoTo.com, later Overture, charged per click, and Google's AdWords, launched in 2000, moved to an auction in 2002. CPC, cost per click, answered advertisers' complaint that they paid for people who looked and did nothing.

The sentence Ellappan could say in the meeting without sounding glib: "We sell our users' attention, so every extra ad is revenue today borrowed against attention tomorrow." It answers the topic's question. The user consumes the product, the advertiser pays for it, and the firm must keep both in view.

3. How it works

Figure 1 shows the loop. Users give Lokam sessions (one visit, from open to close). Each session offers ad slots, the positions where an advertisement could appear, and each slot sends an ad request to the systems that sell it. Advertisers, directly or through an automated auction, bid; Lokam shows the winner and is paid. The user gets free content and pays only in time and patience.

Three conversions sit inside the loop, and practitioners leave them implicit. First, a slot is not an impression: an impression is one displayed advertisement, and only a slot an advertiser has bought becomes one. Filled slots divided by offered slots is the fill rate. Second, an impression is not a payment. Under CPM the advertiser pays per thousand impressions whatever happens; under CPC Lokam earns CTR × CPC per impression, where CTR, click-through rate, is clicks divided by impressions. Third, to compare the two, the industry converts everything to eCPM, effective revenue per thousand impressions.

In a 30-day month at August's volumes, a 0.8% click-through rate and a ₹5 click give 0.008 × 5 = ₹0.04 per impression, or ₹40 per thousand. A flat ₹40 CPM costs the advertiser the same, and Lokam is indifferent while the 0.8% holds. Under CPC, Lokam carries the risk of a weak creative.

4. A worked example

Table 1 walks the August baseline. Each line states its base, because impressions, sessions, users and slots are four different denominators.

Table 1. Baseline month: 30 days, three slots per session

ARPDAU, revenue per daily user per day, is ₹7.56 ÷ 30 = ₹0.252. Check: 22.68 crore × 0.8% = 18,14,400 clicks, × ₹5 = ₹90,72,000.

Figure 2 shows where the 32.4 crore slots go: 30% never sell, 70% become impressions, and clicks are 0.56% of slots on the same scale. The whole revenue rests on that sliver.

Now change inputs. Table 2 sets the baseline beside three versions of the plan. In the finance view only slots change, impressions per session rise from 2.10 to 3.50, and revenue rises 66.7%. The measured five-slot column uses the split test, scaled to the full base: demand did not grow with supply, so fill fell to 60% and eCPM to ₹34; users opened the app 2.8 times a day, not 3.0; and 5% of daily users were gone. Revenue rose only 7.7%. The four-slot arm reached ₹100.28 lakh.

The finance view was right about its arithmetic and wrong about the system: slot count, fill, price, frequency and audience all moved together. Four slots out-earned five in the arms, though by a gap the test may not resolve, because more supply sold into the same demand lowers its price, and each extra slot pushes some users away.

5. Nuances

CPM, CPC and CPA are prices, not outcomes

CPA, cost per acquisition, is paid only when a click becomes a purchase or install. The three allocate risk: under CPM Lokam bears none of the response risk, under CPA all of it. Convert to eCPM before comparing. If one click in forty became an install, the ₹5 click is a ₹200 acquisition, the figure the advertiser's finance team judges Lokam by.

Fill rate measures demand, and price falls with volume

A low fill rate says advertisers did not want the slots at the offered price; more sales staff rarely raises it. Marginal slots sell to cheaper bidders and sit lower on the screen, so eCPM is a function of volume: ₹40 at three slots, ₹34 at five.

An impression is counted, not necessarily seen

An ad can load below the fold. Viewability standards count an impression as seen only when a set share of its pixels was visible for a set time. Ask whether 22.68 crore means loaded or viewable.

The user-cost of ads has three channels

Ads cost attention at once (sessions), loyalty over weeks (retention, the share of users who return) and goodwill (the belief that the product is worth opening). A 28-day test sees the first reliably, the second partially and the third poorly.

Targeting is regulated

Personalised advertising uses personal data. In India that means the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, which requires lawful grounds and consent. An eCPM lifted by personalisation may be partly rented from a consent flow that can shrink.

Advertisers care about incrementality, which you cannot see

The advertiser wants to know which sales happened because of the advertisement. Lokam sees clicks, not whether the viewer would have bought anyway. A buyer who cannot prove incrementality eventually cuts budgets, and Lokam sees the cut, not the reason.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace

In consumer products such as Lokam, attention is a by-product and ad load is a dial. In B2B software advertising is usually a poor fit: the buyer pays a subscription, and an ad in a work tool is an irritant a procurement team can veto. B2B firms more often sell sponsored content and events, priced per lead.

In a marketplace, sponsored listings raise a seller's product in search results. The advertiser is also a supplier the marketplace needs, so heavy promotion raises sellers' costs and weakens the buyer's results; returns tend to be strong because the click sits next to the purchase.

An early-stage company has little traffic, sells through a network at low, volatile eCPM and treats a light ad load as an investment in audience. A large firm has direct-sold campaigns, its own auction and the data to test.

7. Common mistakes

Multiplying slots instead of modelling the system

Symptom: a forecast moving in lockstep with ad load. Misunderstanding: fill, price and users are constants. Diagnostic: rerun it with fill and eCPM falling, as Table 2 does.

Mixing bases

Symptom: two teams quote different ARPDAU for one month. Misunderstanding: one divides by sessions, another by registered users. Diagnostic: write the denominator beside every number, as Table 1 does.

Reading a four-week test as permanent

Symptom: a launch justified by revenue up in week four. Misunderstanding: the test saw session losses but not slow loyalty loss. Diagnostic: keep a holdout at the old ad load running.

Confusing the payer with the customer

Symptom: reviews written for advertisers, users unmentioned. Misunderstanding: the advertiser pays, so only the advertiser matters. Diagnostic: ask who would leave if the product got worse. Both groups would, at different speeds.

8. What good looks like

A good team sets ad load against retention, not revenue alone, reports revenue per DAU, per session and per thousand impressions with each base stated, and keeps a holdout at the old load. It picks the load where an extra slot stops adding revenue net of lost users. Table 3 shows the test when the first month's loss recurs.

Losses: 5.0% a month for five slots, 1.67% (11.80 against 12.00 lakh) for four. Revenue per DAU-month: ₹8.568 and ₹8.498. The recurrence is an assumption, and months 4 to 6 ignore the trip-wire described in section 9.

9. The decision, and what to learn next

On 15 September Ellappan took four slots to the board, not five. She said which columns of Table 2 were measured and which assumed, and agreed with Eswaramurthy a launch on Monday 21 September. She attached two conditions: a 5% holdout on three slots, and a trip-wire that would restore the old load if daily users fell below 11.4 lakh, the loss the five-slot arm showed. On the measured numbers four slots cleared the ₹100 lakh target in month one, by a margin (₹0.28 lakh) smaller than arms of this size can resolve, at ₹100.28 lakh; five did not clear it, at ₹97.68 lakh, and Table 3 shows that if the loss recurred, four slots would stay ahead of the old load through month six. Her trip-wire would fire first, in month 4, when DAU fell to about 11.2 lakh; the month 4 to 6 figures are what would happen if the rule were suspended.

Next, study unit economics and pricing, where the same logic returns as lifetime value against acquisition cost, and then ad-supported consumer products, where the audience becomes the asset.

Two questions. If Lokam's retention loss were 10% a month rather than 5%, what ad load would you choose, and which input of Table 2 would you most want to remeasure? If a rival offered a flat ₹1 crore a month for Lokam's top slot, who would then be the customer?

Advertising business models: attention as inventory, and the question of who the customer is

CPM, CPC, fill rate and the user cost of advertising, argued through three firms that had to price attention in the first quarter of 2026.

1Two decisions, four weeks apart

On Wednesday 14 January 2026 Yazhisai Gurusamy, who runs monetisation at Mazhai Audio Networks, put a recommendation to the executive committee carrying a number she did not believe. Mazhai streams Tamil, Telugu and Bhojpuri audio to 38.0 lakh daily active users on an ad-supported free tier. Her four-arm ad-load test closed on 29 November 2025, and the arm she designed to be rejected had won: three requests a session to four lifted revenue per daily active user from ₹0.2143 to ₹0.2385, up 11.3 per cent, and cut day-28 active share from 41.2 to 39.4 per cent. Finance annualised the first figure and wrote ₹3.36 crore into a board deck. Gurusamy's estimate was a little over half that.

Twenty-eight days later, on Wednesday 11 February 2026, Yogambal Gudivada met the same identity from the other side at Muthira Commerce Cloud, an ordering platform used by 86,000 kirana retailers. Muthira takes 2.30 per cent of gross merchandise value: at ₹22,400 of GMV per retailer-month, ₹192.64 crore of GMV and ₹4.43 crore of commission a month. Yuvamani Gannavarapu, her brand-partnerships lead, wanted sponsored slots on category pages sold to the 38 packaged-goods brands already buying trade promotion: ₹74.21 lakh a year against a three-engineer build. Gudivada's question was whether a slot that pushes an organic result down the page costs more commission than it earns, and whether a 21-day holdout could tell her.

Both instincts are the same: distrust a figure whose base is not the base of what it is compared with.

2The idea, and the four positions people hold

An advertising business model gives a product to a user below its cost of production and recovers that cost by selling the user's attention to a third party. Four definitions must be fixed. An opportunity is a moment the product could show an ad — an ad request. An impression is an opportunity filled with a paid ad; fill rate is impressions over opportunities. CPM is cost per mille, the price of a thousand impressions, so a ₹48.00 CPM is ₹0.048 an impression; eCPM is realised revenue over impressions times a thousand, an outcome rather than a price. CPC is price per click, and eCPM equals CPC times click-through rate times a thousand.

It was invented to solve a distribution problem: how to sell to people who will not pay cost. Benjamin Day's New York Sun, launched in 1833, sold at a penny against a six-cent field by selling readers to advertisers rather than papers to readers. Herbert Simon's 1971 observation that an abundance of information produces a poverty of attention supplied the scarcity argument. Dallas Smythe's 1977 essay on the audience commodity made the uncomfortable reading explicit; Vickrey's 1961 auction work and the generalised second-price mechanism analysed by Edelman, Ostrovsky and Schwartz and by Varian in 2007 turned ad pricing into clearing; Rochet and Tirole's 2003 two-sided markets gave the cross-subsidy its shape.

Four positions are live, each with propositions it will and will not sign. The yield school treats attention as perishable stock: it signs "an unfilled opportunity is spoiled inventory", not "the ads team should set ad load". The attention-price school holds every ad to be a price increase denominated in the user's seconds: it signs "ad load belongs with pricing", not "fill rate is a performance indicator". The two-sided-market school signs "price the user side below cost as the more elastic side", not "the advertiser is the customer", since both sides are customers and neither is the product. The governance school, almost wholly practitioner, signs "ad load is settled by whoever owns the revenue line", not "there is a single optimum a firm can hold".

3Mechanics: the identity, its degrees of freedom, and the two instruments

A display or audio advertising business reduces to one identity: daily revenue equals daily active users, times sessions per user per day, times ad requests per session, times fill rate, times eCPM over a thousand. Mazhai's control arm: 38.0 lakh daily actives at 2.40 sessions gives 91.20 lakh sessions a day; at 3.0 requests a session, 2.74 crore requests (27,360,000); at 62.0 per cent fill, 1.70 crore impressions (16,963,200); at a ₹48.00 eCPM, ₹8,14,234 a day — ₹0.2143 per daily active user, ₹29.72 crore over 365 days.

Six quantities, one identity: five degrees of freedom, not two. Any five can be set and the sixth follows. The useful correction is to separate degrees of freedom from instruments. Mazhai has two instruments — requests issued per session, and the price floor below which it will not clear a bid. Fill and eCPM are then set by the auction; sessions and daily actives respond to the first with a lag. Five quantities free, two under control, and many bad forecasts live in that gap.

The gap is visible in Mazhai's ladder. Four arms — 2, 3, 4 and 5 requests a session — ran on 96,000 users each, randomised from the active base on 2 November 2025 and followed 28 days. Rows 1 and 6 are fitted, not measured.

Three second-order effects do the work. Fill falls as requests rise, because extra requests chase demand already met: one-third more requests at row 4, 58.0 rather than 62.0 per cent filled. Price falls as supply rises: the auction cleared at ₹44.50, not ₹48.00. Sessions fall: 2.31 against 2.40, down 3.75 per cent. So a 33.3 per cent rise in nominal ad load becomes an 11.3 per cent rise in revenue per active user — and a fourth effect, outside the identity, removes part of that again.

4When the inventory frame applies, and when it misleads

The frame — attention is perishable stock, so maximise revenue per unit — holds under three testable conditions. One: the opportunity base is fixed inside the window. If more ads reduce opportunities you are consuming inventory, not filling it. Mazhai fails: sessions per user fell 3.75 per cent and active days 4.40 per cent in 28 days. Muthira would pass only if the orders effect were zero, and its own holdout's interval excludes zero.

Two: the ad does not compete with the firm's own transaction. A Mazhai spot competes with music, which Mazhai does not sell; a Muthira slot competes with an organic result on which Muthira earns a 2.30 per cent take. ₹6,18,432 of monthly ad revenue against ₹4.43 crore of monthly commission makes the ad business 1.396 per cent of the commission it can damage, so any GMV loss above that turns it negative before a rupee of build cost.

Three: demand depth exceeds supply at the target load. Fill rate is the test, and it reads backwards from how it is quoted. Mazhai at 62.0 per cent has thin demand against supply; Muthira's plan assumes 41.0 per cent fill on 59.86 lakh slots a month from 38 bidding brands, at a ₹252.00 eCPM because the few brands that bid buy unusually high intent. The frame misleads wherever fill is a performance measure: cutting opportunities raises fill, buying fill with a lower floor lowers eCPM. Neither means anything beside revenue per opportunity — ₹29.76 per thousand requests, measured, at Mazhai; ₹103.32 per thousand slots, planned, at Muthira.

5Hard edge cases, and the organisational seams

Multi-product and two-sided. Muthira is the general case: ad business and core business share one surface, so ad revenue must be weighed against the cross-elasticity with the core, not against its own cost. Mature marketplaces cap sponsored density per page by policy and review the cap beside commission rates rather than optimising a blended objective, because the exchange rate between ad revenue and commission is itself contested.

Regulated. India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 prohibits behavioural advertising directed at children, and Mazhai's counsel has treated the restriction as binding since 2025. Some 14.2 per cent of Mazhai's daily actives self-declare as under eighteen. That slice fills at 48.0 per cent and clears at a ₹31.00 eCPM — ₹14.88 per thousand opportunities — against 64.32 per cent fill and ₹50.10 on the rest, or ₹32.22. Because an eCPM is weighted by impressions rather than opportunities, that slice is 11.0 per cent of impressions, and 0.110 × ₹31.00 + 0.890 × ₹50.10 returns the blended ₹48.00.

Hardware plus software. As at 30 September 2025 Munnodi Devices had sold 14.20 lakh connected-television units cumulatively and had 6.11 lakh monthly active devices, 43.0 per cent of them; its crisis was which of those numbers reached a sales deck. AI-native. Mozhi Assist carries 7.40 lakh daily actives at 1.8 sessions each — 13.32 lakh sessions a day, 5.1 turns a session — at a marginal inference cost of ₹0.41 a session. One sponsored suggestion a session at 34.0 per cent fill and a ₹96.00 eCPM earns ₹0.0326, covering 7.96 per cent of marginal compute. Break-even on compute alone needs ₹0.41 ÷ 0.34 × 1,000, an eCPM of ₹1,205.88, twelve and a half times what the market pays; Yegavalli Gummadavelli at Mozhi has said so since the first unit-economics review.

The seams are organisational: an ads team builds, measures and reviews ad load against a revenue line, while a growth team measures its cost against a retention target. At Mazhai those sat in separate reviews until Gurusamy's test forced them together.

6Eight distinctions an expert makes

One: fill rate is a demand statistic in a supply statistic's clothes. The tell is a quarter in which fill improves and revenue does not. A reliable way to raise fill is to issue fewer requests, so fill read as efficiency fails: it has no fixed denominator.

Two: eCPM is an outcome, not a price. The tell is an eCPM moving with no change in floors, formats or demand. Mazhai's blended ₹48.00 averages populations clearing at ₹31.00 and ₹50.10, weighted by impressions, so an age-mix shift moves it with nobody repricing.

Three: the ad load you set is not the load users receive. The tell is a request-based load figure in a user-experience discussion. Between rows 5 and 6 of Exhibit A, Mazhai issues 20 per cent more requests and shows 0.70 per cent more ads at an eCPM 11.25 per cent lower.

Four: user cost shows in sessions before retention. The tell is a flat retention chart in week one. Sessions per user can be read daily, where a day-28 figure needs a month; Mazhai's moved 2.40 to 2.31.

Five: revenue per active user and revenue per enrolled user answer different questions. Revenue per daily active user holds the population fixed by construction, so an 11.3 per cent lift in it is not an 11.3 per cent lift in revenue when the population moved. The tell is a forecast multiplying a per-active-user lift by an unchanged user count.

Six: the unit of sale and the unit of delivery must be one unit. Munnodi guaranteed viewable impressions but sized the guarantee from gross home-screen loads. A credit proportional to the shortfall silently converts a gross contract into a net-viewable one at the original CPM: Munnodi's realised ₹37.02 lakh over 336.54 lakh viewable impressions is ₹110.00 per thousand.

Seven: the marginal advertiser sets the clearing price, so the last tranche of demand prices the book. The tell is a bid-concentration table few firms keep. With 38 bidding brands at 41.0 per cent fill, Muthira's eCPM is set by whichever brand clears last, so one large brand withdrawing moves the price on every impression, not its own share alone.

Eight: in a marketplace, ad revenue is the budget for the damage ads may do. The tell is an ad business sized against its own cost, not against core revenue on the same surface: Muthira's ₹74.21 lakh a year is a 1.396 per cent tolerance on commission.

7How the picture changes by product type and stage

The identity does not change across product types; which term binds does, and much of what is written here invents differences that are not there. In consumer products the binding term sits outside the identity — sessions and retention — because the opportunity base is endogenous. In business-to-business and enterprise products it is demand depth: 38 possible buyers give high intent, high eCPM and low fill, and more inventory does not help. In platforms and marketplaces it is cannibalisation of the firm's own take; in hardware, the installed base; in AI products, marginal cost.

Stage changes the question, not the arithmetic. At seed the ad business proves demand exists and fill of any kind is informative. At growth the instrument is live and user cost is invisible because growth swamps it — which is how Mazhai's load reached three without a decision being taken. At scale the user-cost term dominates. The one real discontinuity is a paid tier: from that day every ad also advertises it, and the ad business carries a shadow cost in suppressed conversions.

8Three worked cases, one of them a failure

Mazhai: the right lift on the wrong base. Finance's ₹3.36 crore was ₹29.72 crore times 11.3 per cent — a per-active-user lift on an unchanged user count. The experiment randomised users, not user-days: on that base revenue per randomised user over 28 days rose from ₹3.90 to ₹4.15, up 6.4 per cent, and the decomposition is exact, 1.113 × 0.956 = 1.064 — an 11.3 per cent gain per active user against a 4.4 per cent loss of active days. On the randomised-user base the run rate is ₹29.72 crore × 1.064 = ₹31.62 crore, a gain of ₹1.90 crore against the deck’s ₹3.36 crore — high by roughly three-quarters. The window's own annualisation factor is 365 ÷ 28 = 13.036, turning ₹3.90 into ₹50.84 a year and ₹4.15 into ₹54.10. The retention gap is not noise: at 96,000 users an arm, the square root of (0.412 × 0.588 ÷ 96,000 + 0.394 × 0.606 ÷ 96,000) is 0.224 points, making 1.8 points 8.04 standard errors.

Muthira: an ad business inside its own measurement error. The holdout ran 21 days from 12 January to 1 February 2026, splitting the entire active base at 43,000 retailers an arm. Orders per retailer were 8.10 without sponsored slots and 8.01 with them, at a standard deviation of 6.4 orders in both arms; 6.4 × the square root of (2 ÷ 43,000) is 0.0436, so t = 2.06, the point estimate is a 1.111 per cent fall, and the 95 per cent interval runs from 0.055 to 2.167 per cent — with the 1.396 per cent break-even inside it. At the point estimate the slots cost ₹59.08 lakh of commission a year against ₹74.21 lakh of ad revenue, a net ₹15.13 lakh before build cost; at the adverse end they cost ₹1.15 crore, a net loss of ₹41.02 lakh. Against three engineers at ₹38.00 lakh fully loaded per person per year — ₹1.14 crore for the team — fill of 63.0 per cent, or 59 bidding brands at unchanged demand per brand, would cover the build alone; covering the point estimate's commission loss as well needs about 96 per cent fill and 89 brands, and the adverse end needs fill above 100 per cent. All three commission figures convert an orders effect into a GMV effect at constant basket size; sponsored slots can shift basket mix, and the sign and size of that shift are unmeasured. One trap sat in the first memo: 8.10 orders in 21 days annualised by twelve gives 97.20, where the window's own factor is 365 ÷ 21 = 17.381 and the answer is 140.79, so the convention understated the base by 31.0 per cent.

Munnodi: the failure, and the recovery. From October 2025 Munnodi sold its home-screen masthead on a guarantee of 5.50 crore viewable impressions a month at a ₹110.00 CPM, billing ₹60.50 lakh. The sales model took 14.20 lakh units sold at 3.4 home-screen loads a device a day. The deliverable base was different three times over: 6.11 lakh devices were monthly active, not 14.20 lakh sold; 3.4 loads a day on those devices over a 30-day month gives 623.22 lakh loads; and 54.0 per cent of loads held the masthead on screen for the two seconds the contract defined as viewable, leaving 336.54 lakh viewable impressions. That is a shortfall of 2.13 crore against the guarantee, 38.81 per cent, and a make-good credit of ₹23.48 lakh cut realised revenue to ₹37.02 lakh a month. Yogapriya Ganesamoorthy, who took over platform revenue in February 2026, rewrote the contract from 2 March 2026 to guarantee 3.00 crore viewable impressions at a ₹178.00 CPM: ₹53.40 lakh a month, covered 1.12 times by the 336.54 lakh of viewable supply. Billed revenue fell 11.74 per cent; realised revenue rose 44.25 per cent.

9Five failure modes and the cost of late diagnosis

The wrong installed base. Early sign: a sales deck and an engineering dashboard quoting different audience sizes, unreconciled. Diagnostic: what is the denominator, and when was it measured? Munnodi caught it in the fifth month, by which time ₹117.40 lakh of credits had been issued across five months at ₹23.48 lakh each.

Ad load set by the revenue owner. Early sign: load changes in release notes rather than review minutes. Diagnostic: who would have to approve taking it back down? Caught late, the firm holds a load it cannot reverse without visibly losing revenue in a quarter.

Annualising by convention. Early sign: a factor of twelve, four or fifty-two on a window that is not a month, quarter or week. Diagnostic: how many days are in the window, and what is 365 over that? Muthira's draft was out by 31.0 per cent on orders per retailer-year, which understates annual commission and so makes the ad tolerance look larger than it is.

Guaranteeing unmeasured supply. Early sign: a contract defining impressions one way and the ad server counting them another. Diagnostic: can we reproduce last month's delivery in the contract's unit? The cost lands as make-goods, invisible in billed revenue and brutal in realised revenue.

Reading a flat revenue curve as a plateau. Early sign: a recommendation to go one step past the revenue maximum because the curve looks flat. Moving Mazhai from four requests to five costs 3.10 per cent of revenue per active user but about 9.2 per cent of revenue per randomised user, because the active-day term falls on after the revenue term stops. Diagnostic: which terms still move at the margin?

10Where competent people disagree

Whether user cost is measurable at decision-relevant precision. The experimentalist: user cost is an elasticity, elasticities are estimable, and an 8.04-standard-error retention difference shows a 28-day test resolving effects well inside the range that changes a decision. The sceptic: the damage advertising does is a slow change in what a product is for, and 28 days catches the transient and misses the regime. The experimentalist is wrong if the 28-day elasticity differs in sign or magnitude from the 24-month one; The sceptic is wrong if a long-horizon holdout reproduces the 28-day elasticity. Mazhai can run neither test on the data it holds, and Yezhilan Gajapathi, who runs growth there, says so in every review.

Whether advertising is terminal or transitional. The terminal position: where median willingness to pay for an entertainment service is a few hundred rupees a month, advertising is, on this view, the structure that reaches the whole market, and a product reaching a tenth of it at ten times the price is no larger. The transitional position: an advertising model permanently misaligns the firm's objective from the user's, so it caps quality and invites regulation. The first falls if paid conversion at low price points beats ad revenue per user on the same cohort; the second falls if a mature ad-funded product sustains both high load and rising satisfaction over years.

Whether first-party targeting pays for its compliance cost. The optimist rests on eCPM lift: Mazhai's behaviourally targetable base clears ₹50.10 against ₹31.00 on the slice the statute protects, a 61.6 per cent premium. The sceptic notes the premium is confounded with age — advertisers pay more for adults whether or not they are targeted — and that consent funnels shrink the base faster than they raise its price. The optimist is wrong if an adults-only, consent-off cell clears close to ₹50.10. Nobody on this page has run that cell.

11What mastery looks like

Four observable differences. Someone who has internalised this states the denominator before the number, and will not let a rate into a document without the date its base was measured. They ask what the firm's instruments are before what its targets are, unembarrassed that the answer is two rather than five. They treat every ad-load change as a price change and route it through whoever owns pricing. And they will call a decision undecidable on available evidence, as Gudivada's interval leaves hers, rather than reporting a point estimate and letting the interval vanish into a footnote. Someone who has merely studied the topic can recite the identity and will still multiply a per-active-user lift by an unchanged user count.

12What each of them did

Gurusamy recommended four requests a session, with the forecast restated at ₹31.62 crore rather than ₹33.08 crore and revenue per randomised user replacing revenue per active user as the reported series from the first quarter of 2026. She also proposed a ceiling: no further increase without a fresh randomised arm, since the 10.15 per cent tolerance in active user-days at four requests would be far smaller at five. Gudivada did not build the retail-media product. A ₹74.21 lakh line whose break-even sits inside the interval of what it damages was, in her reading, a bet on measurement rather than a business decision; the cheaper move was to sell the 38 brands a fixed placement fee on a capped number of slots, which prices the inventory without an auction that rewards density. Gannavarapu disagreed, recording that 21 days was too short to see a habit effect either way.

Discussion questions.

  1. Mazhai's board deck and Gurusamy's memo describe one experiment. Identify the base each figure sits on, say which series a board should see quarterly, and what it loses by seeing only that one.
  2. Muthira's break-even GMV loss lies inside the interval its holdout produced. What change of sample, duration or outcome measure would narrow that interval enough to decide, and what would it cost in time and foregone revenue?
  3. Munnodi's billed revenue fell 11.74 per cent while its realised revenue rose 44.25 per cent. What explains the rise, and what would you require before signing any impression guarantee?

13Going deeper

  • Revenue models. The comparison works once each model's base is stated; it unlocks asking who pays before how much.
  • Ad-supported consumer products. The sequel: formats, placements and ad-load conventions built on this identity.
  • What a business model is. The vocabulary that keeps "who is the customer" from staying rhetorical.
  • Business Model and Lean Canvas. Forces the two-sided structure onto one page, where a second customer appears.
  • Subscription economics. The alternative competing for the same user; prices the conversions an ad suppresses.
  • Marketplace economics. Where Muthira's cannibalisation question belongs, take rate and basket effects together.
  • Freemium as a business model. The hybrid in which ad load drives paid conversion as well as revenue.
  • Hardware business models. Munnodi generalises: activation discipline decides whether the ad business exists.

Rupak Messaging: Pricing by the Message

1. Opening

At 7:40 on Thursday morning, 22 October 2026, Chiranjiv Javadekar sat in Rupak Messaging's Baner office in Pune, reading an email from a customer in Dubai. The customer, a remittance company that sends transaction alerts to recipients across India, had asked a courteous question: if Rupak charged by the message, what would its September volume cost? Javadekar, Rupak's chief product officer, could not yet answer it. He was also unsure whether Rupak should make the move at all. Customer contracts demanded sixty days' written notice of any price change, so a price list for 1 January 2027 had to reach customers by Monday 2 November. The leadership team would decide on Friday 30 October (Figure 1).

Figure 1. The days that remain

Distances are drawn to scale in days from 22 October.

2. Company background

Founded in 2017, Rupak sells cloud messaging: an API and dashboard through which businesses send WhatsApp Business, SMS and one-time-password messages to their own customers. Growth came with the UPI-era boom in fintech lending and online retail, taking it from a few start-up accounts to 240 paying ones, which include direct-to-consumer brands, NBFCs and edtech firms, and it now bills ₹112.50 lakh a month, or ₹13.5 crore a year, before 18 per cent GST. Gupshup, Route Mobile and Kaleyra compete for the larger accounts, MSG91 and Interakt for the smaller, and Twilio for any buyer who already uses it elsewhere. SMS in India must pass through TRAI's DLT registry, and WhatsApp charges are set by Meta, so each message carries a real cost, and under the DPDP Act its customers must also be able to prove consent for what they send. Rupak's cost per message is about ₹0.09 on a blended basis, once operator, Meta and infrastructure charges are counted.

Rupak sells three annual plans, billed monthly in advance: Starter at ₹15,000, Growth at ₹60,000 and Scale at ₹2.4 lakh. Each is unmetered within fair use. Rupak counts every message internally, but no customer is billed by that count.

3. The situation

Three things changed in 2026. Tender documents, particularly from NBFCs, began asking for a rate per message, which the flat plans could answer only by dividing a fee by a guess. Chiranjiv had asked each colleague for the one number that worried them most, and the answers pulled in different directions. Rivals publish per-message rates, and Meta itself now prices WhatsApp by the message. In conversations over the past quarter, several Starter customers told the sales team that they paid the same fee in months when they sent almost nothing. Rupak's costs followed volume while its revenue did not. And Chitrangada Jalgaonkar, the finance head, was preparing the company for a funding round in the new year, at which investors would ask for a revenue forecast.

A product designer in Berlin, 3.5 hours behind Pune until 25 October and 4.5 after, had already mocked up a usage dashboard and a metered invoice. A data scientist in Toronto assembled the evidence. Exhibit 1 shows September 2026, the most recent full month. "Consumed" there means messages sent through Rupak's gateway between 1 and 30 September. Because usage is uneven, the exhibit shows the median and the p90, the volume that nine accounts in ten stay below, beside the mean. Exhibit 2 gives twelve months of volume for the 240 accounts live throughout. Anyone quoting revenue per message must say which messages: sent messages, as in Exhibit 1; billed messages, which today are none; or committed messages, which exist only if Rupak asks customers to commit.

The team saw it from different places. Conrad Jejurkar, in Edison, New Jersey, found that American buyers comparing Rupak with Twilio wanted a rate per message in a spreadsheet, and feared that a surprise at renewal would cost him a deal already in negotiation. Chayanika Jangale, in Singapore, managed the largest accounts, including the Dubai remittance company, and heard from its procurement head that its September volume was 71 lakh messages against a fee of ₹2.4 lakh.

4. The people

Chiranjiv Javadekar, chief product officer, Pune, owns the price list and must recommend a course. Chitrangada Jalgaonkar, finance head, Mumbai, wants a revenue number she can defend to investors and a margin that does not shrink when customers send more. Conrad Jejurkar, head of sales, Edison, joins an 8:00 p.m. Pune meeting at 10:30 a.m. his time until 1 November; he wants quotes that buyers can compare and a change that does not stall deals in his pipeline. Chayanika Jangale, customer-success lead, Singapore, two and a half hours ahead of Pune, answers to the large accounts and fears a bill that surprises them. She is also the one who would have to explain a changed invoice to a Dubai finance team that thinks in dirhams and reads Rupak's price list as a cost line it must budget a year ahead.

5. The options

Exhibit 3 sets out the terms. Costs below use September's 685 lakh messages.

Option A drops the fee and bills every message at ₹0.16. September would have billed ₹109.60 lakh against ₹112.50 lakh today. Each customer's bill then moves with its own volume, and Rupak needs invoices that customers can check against their own logs. Option B keeps a floor. Each account commits to a monthly volume at ₹0.15, so 481 lakh committed messages bring ₹72.15 lakh a month whatever volume does, and messages beyond the commitment cost ₹0.17. Customers must forecast their own volumes, Rupak must negotiate each commitment, and a shortfall month is billed at the commitment regardless of what was sent. Option C leaves the plans as they are and raises each fee 10 per cent. On the 240 accounts that is ₹123.75 lakh, if none leaves. It needs no new metering and leaves price unconnected to volume.

6. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibit 1, compute the revenue per message sent for each plan. How far should the means be trusted, given the medians and p90s?
  2. Using Exhibit 2, convert the twelve months into revenue under Option A and compare the range with today's flat figure. What would you need to know before promising investors a number for January to March 2027?
  3. Compare the Dubai company's monthly bill with a typical Starter account's under each option. Who has reason to resist each option, and what might they do?
  4. Which option would you take to the 30 October meeting, and what would you do between 2 November and 1 January to learn whether you were wrong?

7. A note for the learner

Usage-based pricing is subscription with a variable meter. It aligns price with value, since the customer who sends more pays more, and it removes the barrier of a fixed fee for the small. But it moves volume risk from the customer to the vendor, so forecasting changes: the question is no longer how many accounts renew but how many messages they send.

One defensible path is Option B. First, September is the third-highest of the twelve months, at 6.85 crore against a mean of 6.43, so any bill priced on it flatters the vendor. Then the percentile. Growth and Scale commitments sit at their plan's median and Starter's slightly above it, so half or more of the accounts will sit below them and pay the commitment, while the rest pay overage. The overage bound is therefore a floor: 685 lakh sent less 481 lakh committed leaves at least 204 lakh messages at ₹0.17, or ₹34.68 lakh, for at least ₹106.83 lakh in all. The true figure is higher, because the shortfalls of low accounts are not netted against the excess of high ones.

Option A's monthly range follows volume: twelve months give a mean of 6.43 crore and a standard deviation of 0.66 crore, so one standard deviation is about ₹10.5 lakh of revenue, on twelve observations. Most of that spread is one month: October 2025 carried Diwali (20 October), and without it the mean is 6.28 crore and the SD 0.42 crore, about ₹6.7 lakh. Seasonality is therefore part of any forecast. Option B's committed revenue is ₹72.15 lakh whatever volume does, 64 per cent of today's ₹112.50 lakh, and that share is what a forecast can rest on. Before 2 November, test the commitments on the twenty Scale accounts, where Chayanika's relationships are deepest, since they carry 48.00 of the 112.50 lakh. Keep Option C as the fallback if few will sign, and after 1 January compare each month's committed share and overage against these figures, so that the choice is judged on data rather than argument.

Strategy & Business · Business Models

Usage-based and consumption models

A meter aligns price to value and destroys the predictability a subscription was built to deliver. Two product leaders, one October week, and the arithmetic that frames the trade.

1. Two decisions, one week

On Thursday 1 October 2026 Narmada Yashwante read the September close her chief financial officer had already circulated. Gavaksha, the Bengaluru company where she runs product, sells a document-extraction API: insurers and lenders post scanned files, Gavaksha returns structured fields, and the bill is a count of pages. September revenue was ₹5.00 crore from 412 paying accounts and 41,61,200 pages. The CFO's note said the company earned ₹12.25 a page; Narmada's dashboard said ₹12.02. Neither was wrong — the CFO divided by billed pages, Narmada by every page the meter counted. The two bases differ by 1.95 per cent, and that morning's decision, whether to floor the meter by pushing annual commitments, moved either way depending on which number the board heard.

Four days later, on Monday 5 October, Nishita Yeldurkar argued the opposite case in Pune. Gatipath Systems puts a telematics device in a commercial vehicle and sells a platform on top, at ₹340 per vehicle per month across 2,64,000 vehicles and 1,240 fleet customers — ₹8.98 crore a month, ₹107.71 crore annualised. Her largest customer had spent the quarter asking why it paid for 1,900 vehicles when 1,500 moved. Across the base, 45,000 of the 2,64,000 vehicles logged no trip in September: 17.05 per cent of the fleet, billed and idle. A per-trip meter would answer that honestly. It would also hand back ₹1.53 crore a month, ₹18.36 crore a year, against costs that do not move, because a parked lorry still carries its SIM and its device.

2. The idea, and who disputes it

A usage-based model prices by a measured quantity of consumption rather than by access, seats or time. Four elements define one: a meter the customer can audit, a tariff mapping quantity to money, a period over which the meter resets, and an entitlement fixing what may be consumed free. Change one and the model changes under the same name.

The invention is not software's. Samuel Insull's Chicago electricity business settled the structure in the 1890s, and settled it correctly: a demand charge recovering reserved capacity plus an energy charge recovering what is drawn. Measured telephone service followed, then time-sharing bureaux billing CPU-seconds, then telecom's long detour through unlimited bundles; cloud re-established the meter after 2006.

The problem is distributional. Under one flat fee serving a heterogeneous population, light users overpay and leave, heavy users are subsidised and stay, and neither end is served profitably. Gavaksha's heaviest 22 accounts, 5.34 per cent of the list, generate 54.44 per cent of its pages; its lightest 289, 70.15 per cent, generate 9.26 per cent.

Four schools disagree. Value-alignment signs that a customer getting twice the value should pay twice as much, and refuses that predictability is a first-order design goal. Predictability, largely finance, signs that a rupee of committed recurring revenue beats a rupee of metered revenue of equal expected value, and refuses the meter as sole billing instrument. Cost-pass-through signs that any unit carrying material marginal cost must be metered or capped, and refuses a meter chosen for communicating value. Adoption-friction signs that the first unit cost nothing and the second be computable without a salesperson, and refuses commitments as the default.

3. Mechanics, worked through

Experts separate two decisions amateurs run together: the meter, and the rate. The meter shapes roadmap, invoice, sales conversation and data model, and is picked on five tests — correlation with value, controllability, auditability, correlation with marginal cost, resistance to gaming. Rates change yearly; meters almost never.

Gavaksha's tariff is graduated: each band's rate applies only to pages inside it, so the bill is continuous in volume. Stair-step volume pricing applies one rate to the whole quantity, so a customer at 2,501 pages pays less in total than one at 2,499.

Exhibit 1 — Gavaksha list tariff, graduated bands, in force from 1 May 2026
