Tier 2: 55,000 + 17,500 × 16.00. Tier 3: 3,35,000 + 80,000 × 11.50. Tier 4 at 2,00,000: 12,55,000 + 1,00,000 × 8.40. Blended rate is cumulative bill over volume; 20,95,000 / 2,00,000 = ₹10.475, rounded. The 200-page allowance sits outside this tariff. Tier 3 was ₹12.80 before 1 May 2026.

Now the second-order effects. The first is three denominators, decomposed in Figure 3. Consumed pages are what the meter counted; billed pages are consumed less the 79,600 given away under the allowance, since 371 accounts exhausted it and 41 more consumed 5,400 pages between them without reaching it. Committed pages are the pro-rata entitlement of the 86 accounts on annual drawdowns, 25,20,000, against which they consumed 22,47,800 — 89.20 per cent utilisation, 2,72,200 unused. Revenue per unit means nothing until you name which of the three you divided by.

The second is volatility that will not diversify away. Gavaksha's median account has a monthly coefficient of variation of 0.38 over the twelve months to September 2026, and the seductive inference is that 412 accounts smooth this to 0.38 / √412 = 1.9 per cent. Two corrections kill it. The accounts are not equally weighted: taking pages as spread evenly within each band, the Herfindahl index of page share is 0.0208, so the effective count is at most about 48, and independence gives 0.38 / √48 = 5.5 per cent. And the observed aggregate figure is 9.4 per cent. Solving 0.094 = 0.38 × √((1 + 47ρ) / 48) gives an average pairwise correlation ρ = 0.041, whose asymptotic floor is 0.38 × √0.041 = 7.7 per cent. The formula assumes one common σ across accounts, so ρ is an order of magnitude.

The third is the break-even identity. A revenue-neutral per-unit price is revenue over units; the usage at which a customer pays the same either way is the old fee divided by that price, which reduces to units over billed accounts. Break-even is the mean usage per billed unit, always. Since usage is right-skewed the mean sits above the median, so a neutral conversion leaves most customers paying less and a minority far more.

4. When it applies, stated as tests

One: spread, and two: controllability. Does usage per billed unit vary by close to an order of magnitude at equal willingness to pay, and can the customer set the meter's level? Gavaksha's median account sits in band two of Figure 1 and its p90 account in band four, a ratio near ten, and its customers call the API deliberately. Gatipath's p90 active vehicle runs 141 trips against a median of 44, a ratio of 3.2, and its fleets do not choose their trips — their shippers do. A meter the buyer cannot control is felt as a tax.

Three: marginal cost. Is marginal cost per metered unit material? Gavaksha's is — inference is bought by the page. Gatipath's is not: cost of service is ₹118 per vehicle per month, or ₹3,11,52,000 a month, 34.71 per cent of revenue, at a 65.29 per cent gross margin. Under a meter that hands idle fees back, the 45,000 idle vehicles still cost ₹53,10,000 a month, 5.92 per cent of September's ₹8.98 crore, against nothing. Revenue falls 17.05 per cent, cost falls nothing, gross margin goes to 58.16 per cent — 7.13 points for a fairer-looking invoice.

Four: the buyer's own revenue. Does the customer earn in the unit it is billed in? Here Gatipath passes and the tests disagree: fleets are paid per trip, so a per-trip fee is countercyclical to their distress where a per-vehicle fee is not, which is why her fleets will keep asking. The page leaves it unresolved because practitioners do.

The idea actively misleads in three cases: when usage measures a customer cost it is trying to eliminate, so revenue falls as the product succeeds; when procurement cannot approve an uncapped variable line; and when usage is bimodal, so tiers calibrated to the mean misprice both modes.

5. Hard edge cases

Multi-product. One universal credit spendable anywhere is elegant, and hands the margin mix to the customer. If a Gavaksha page credit bought either extraction or classification, whose cost per page is an eighth, every rupee of shift is margin nobody priced. Firms weight their credits; customers read that as a hidden rise.

Two-sided. A take rate is a meter, and metering the inelastic side maximises short-run revenue while starving liquidity on the other — which is why marketplaces usually meter the seller.

Regulated. A filed tariff cannot be personalised, so the discrimination tiers deliver quietly becomes public. India's sharpest case is the zero merchant-discount-rate mandate on UPI and RuPay debit, which set a meter's rate to nil by statute. A unit price that is a policy variable is regulatory risk.

Hardware plus software. Gatipath's seam, and Insull answered it: a demand charge per connected vehicle for device, SIM and support, plus an energy charge per trip for the platform. The fight is internal, because whether capital recovery sits in revenue or against cost of goods moves reported gross margin without moving cash.

AI-native. Consumption per task is non-deterministic, so a customer cannot forecast its own bill even in full control of its behaviour; one action can trigger two hundred model calls. And unit costs fall steeply year on year, so a token meter is a deflating revenue line where an outcome meter is not.

The seams, and what firms actually do. Sales is paid on bookings and revenue arrives on consumption, a gap of a quarter. An engineer raising a rate limit at 2 a.m. is making a revenue decision with no mandate to. And mature companies say they sell pure consumption while selling discounted annual commitments, booking them as recurring revenue, and staffing a function whose job is preventing breakage.

6. Eight things that separate an expert

The meter is not the price. Two decisions, different reversibility. The tell is a team arguing rupees per unit before it has agreed the unit. A rate is a spreadsheet; a meter is a migration.

Revenue per unit is three numbers. Gavaksha's September figure is ₹12.25 over billed pages and ₹12.02 over consumed; committed units give a third. The tell is an average revenue per unit that moves between months with no change in customer behaviour: somebody switched denominators.

Diversification does almost nothing. A small common factor dominates a large account count, and the effective count is set by concentration, not logos. The tell is a forecast whose error does not shrink as the book grows. Experts compute the floor, 7.7 per cent here, and stop promising scale fixes it.

Break-even usage is a mean, so conversion redistributes. The obvious reading of a revenue-neutral conversion is that nothing happens; in fact between 35 and 37 per cent of Gatipath's vehicles pay more and the rest less. The tell is a conversion the field loves and the top twenty accounts escalate in week two.

A commitment discount buys variance, not volume. It is a risk transfer priced as a quantity discount, which is why schedules keyed to size rather than term and take-or-pay leak money. Gandaki Health Claims pays ₹10.20 a page against a ₹12.81 list blended rate at its committed 80,000 pages a month: 20.39 per cent off, the question being whether that fairly prices twelve months of certainty.

Breakage is a forward liability. An account that consumes 89 per cent of its entitlement renews near 89 per cent of it, so unused entitlement is next year's price cut, not a windfall. Gandaki has drawn 4,36,800 of 9,60,000 pages in six months, 45.50 per cent against a 50.00 per cent pace, and 61,200 in September alone; six more months at that rate finishes at 8,04,000, leaving 1,56,000 unused — 16.25 per cent of the commitment, ₹15.91 lakh of a ₹97.92 lakh contract.

Your efficiency roadmap is an undecided price cut. Caching, batching, deduplication and smaller models all reduce the meter. The tell is a product council approving a thirty per cent cost reduction with no pricing paper attached.

Net revenue retention flatters a meter. A customer halving its usage appears as negative expansion rather than churn, and cohort retention silently mixes price, volume and mix. The tell is strong retention alongside flat consumed units: the number is measuring the tariff, not the customer.

7. How it differs, and where it does not

Consumer. Mostly the difference is not real: freemium does the discrimination a meter would, without a running total. The exception is where consumers already think in units, as Indian mobile buyers did with data packs — and that market moved to unlimited bundles, because meter anxiety suppresses the usage the vendor wants.

B2B and enterprise. The pricing logic is identical; only the contract shape differs. Mid-market buys pay-as-you-go, enterprise buys a commitment with a cap, and that commitment serves the buyer's budget process as much as the vendor's forecast.

Platform, hardware, AI. On a platform the live choice is the unit, not whether to meter: transaction value inherits the customer's price inflation, while count is stable and drifts from value as baskets grow. On hardware a physical unit is an unavoidable demand charge, so pure consumption pricing is a lease dressed as a subscription. AI products are the one category where the tariff must be reset annually, because unit cost falls faster than willingness to pay.

By stage. Seed-stage firms meter to learn which unit correlates with value. Growth-stage firms meter because in-account expansion is the cheapest revenue there is. Pre-listing firms convert metered revenue into commitments, because public markets pay for a forecast.

8. Three worked examples

A. Gavaksha cuts tier 3, and reads its own result twice

On 1 May 2026 Gavaksha cut tier 3 from ₹12.80 to ₹11.50, holding a randomly assigned cohort at the old rate. Tier-3 pages in the treated cohort went from 8,91,000 in April to 10,42,000 in August: by the midpoint arc form, 1,51,000 / 9,66,500 = +15.62 per cent against a price change of −1.30 / 12.15 = −10.70 per cent, an elasticity of −1.46. The holdout, priced identically on both dates, went from 2,96,000 to 3,18,000; the same arc form gives +7.17 per cent. Difference-in-differences is 8.46 points, and 8.46 / −10.70 gives −0.79 — little more than half the naive figure, the gap being whatever the holdout saw too. Use one formula on both sides, every time.

B. Gatipath prices a trip, and finds out who pays

September trips were 1,40,16,000: 64.00 per active vehicle but 53.09 per subscribed vehicle — 64.00 being 20.55 per cent above 53.09. Revenue-neutral is ₹8,97,60,000 / 1,40,16,000 = ₹6.4041, and break-even is ₹340 / ₹6.4041 = 53.09 trips. The active-vehicle distribution has a median of 44, a p75 of 88 and a p90 of 141. Interpolating inside the median-to-p75 band puts 44.8 per cent of active vehicles above break-even — 37.2 per cent of subscribed vehicles, once the 17.05 per cent that never moved are counted; a lognormal fitted to the median and p90 gives σ = 0.909 and 34.7 per cent. So between 35 and 37 per cent pay more, and the honest answer is a range. The fit implies a mean of 66.5 trips against an actual 64.0, so the real upper tail is lighter than the fit.

C. Granula Health Cloud: a meter that failed, and a floor that half-worked

Granula Health Cloud, in Hyderabad, sold a hospital platform at ₹1,250 per bed per month across 18,400 beds — ₹2.30 crore a month. From January 2025 it charged ₹46 per patient encounter, set off 2024's mean of 5,00,000 encounters a month. That mean was the error. The twelve 2024 monthly totals, in lakh, were 4.52, 4.38, 4.71, 4.60, 4.95, 4.41, 4.66, 5.08, 5.21, 6.44, 6.12 and 4.92: mean 5.00, median 4.815, two surgical-season months carrying the average. Four of the twelve months reached the mean, which sat near the sixty-seventh percentile of Granula's history. January to June 2025 averaged 4,12,000 encounters and ₹1.90 crore — short ₹40.48 lakh a month, 17.60 per cent, ₹2.43 crore over the half-year.

Exhibit 2 — Granula: the ₹40.48 lakh monthly shortfall, January to June 2025

H1 2024 averaged 4,59,500 encounters a month; at that volume the tariff yields ₹2.11 crore, still ₹18.63 lakh short of ₹2.30 crore — 8.10 per cent of old revenue. H1 2025 ran 47,500 encounters lower, 10.34 per cent, worth ₹21.85 lakh at ₹46, or 9.50 per cent. The two sum to 17.60 per cent, on unchanged beds.

The recovery, from July 2025, was a floor: each hospital committed to 85 per cent of its own trailing median monthly encounters, billed whether consumed or not, encounters above it at ₹46 and shortfalls forgiven. The floors summed to 3,86,000 encounters a month. Second-half consumption averaged 4,34,000, of which 61,000 sat above individual floors while 13,000 of floor went unused, so 4,47,000 encounter-equivalents were billed: ₹2.06 crore a month, 8.50 per cent above the trough and 10.60 per cent below the old per-bed line. The floor itself added 13,000 billed encounters, ₹5.98 lakh a month, 2.60 of the 17.60 points; the other 4.40 came from H2 volume rising to 4,34,000 from H1's 4,12,000, which no tariff delivers.

9. Failure modes and their diagnostics

Pricing off a mean. Warning: forecast misses in the same direction for three months running. Diagnostic: at which percentile of our own monthly history is this price revenue-neutral? Granula's answer was the sixty-seventh, and finding out took six months and ₹2.43 crore.

No cap and no credit policy. Warning: a disputed invoice larger than the account's own monthly revenue. Diagnostic: what is the largest bill one misconfiguration can generate in a day? The late cost is not the write-off but the cap every later prospect demands.

Bookings pay on a consumption meter. Warning: commitment utilisation below 70 per cent at month six. Diagnostic: what share of last year's committed units was consumed? Gavaksha's September pro-rata 89.20 per cent is healthy; a book at 60 per cent has sold next year's revenue at this year's price.

Reporting committed revenue as recurring. Warning: reported recurring revenue growing while consumed units are flat. Diagnostic: reconcile it to last quarter's recognised usage revenue. Caught late, this is restated in public.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Does a meter raise or lower lifetime revenue? The expansion case rests on net revenue retention in cloud and API cohorts running well above seat-based comparables, and on a meter capturing growth without renegotiation. The leakage case holds that the same figure is a composition artefact — metered books over-weight fast-growing customers — and that flat-fee incumbents realise more revenue per unit of value because they never price at marginal cost. The expansion case fails if matched cohorts show equal retention; the leakage case fails if metered accounts show lower revenue per unit of value at equal growth.

Should the meter track value or cost? The value camp notes that a cost-based meter dies the moment costs fall, as token prices are falling now. The cost camp notes that a value-based meter with uncoupled costs inverts gross margin under exactly the usage spike the vendor hoped for. The value camp is wrong once marginal cost exceeds roughly a fifth of price; the cost camp is wrong if the customer cannot connect the unit to anything it values.

Is a commitment a feature or a defeat? One side says it is the demand charge, legitimate since Insull, and buyers want a budgetable ceiling. The other says every commitment is a vendor confessing its meter does not forecast. The second weakens if commitment accounts expand faster than pay-as-you-go accounts at equal size and tenure.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this argues about rates. Someone who has internalised it writes down the meter, the period, the entitlement and the audit path before discussing money, and never states a per-unit figure without naming its denominator and date. They compute the standard error before calling a cohort gap a lesson: Gavaksha's commitment-calculator cohort of 118 accounts averaged 6,420 pages in September against 5,556 for 191 matched controls, a gap of 864 against a standard error of 1,335 on a pooled standard deviation of 11,400 — 0.65 standard errors, interval −1,752 to +3,480. They call that noise. And they treat rate limits and sales comp as parts of the pricing model.

12. The decisions

  1. Gavaksha's effective account count is at most 48 and its volatility floor 7.7 per cent. What should it tell its board about a forecast it cannot improve by selling more?
  2. Gatipath's third test says do not meter; its fourth says its customers will force one. Which should carry more weight, and what evidence would settle it?
  3. Granula's floor itself added 2.60 of the 7.00 points recovered, leaving 10.60 outstanding. Was the floor the wrong instrument, or the right one applied well?

Narmada chose a two-part tariff over a commitment push: a platform fee per connected environment, sized to Gavaksha's fixed cost, with the page meter above it unchanged. The volatility she wanted to fix is structural at ρ = 0.041, so a commitment campaign buys a forecast at a 20 per cent discount and gives it back as breakage, where a demand charge buys the same stability without mortgaging the renewal. Nishita declined the per-trip meter and shipped a device activation state: a parked vehicle drops to ₹118 a month, exactly her cost of service, and resumes at ₹340 when it moves. It gives back only ₹99.90 lakh of the ₹1.53 crore, protecting 2.79 of the 7.13 margin points, and leaves the meter available if her fleets insist.

13. Going deeper

Usage-based and consumption models

Strategy & Business, Business Models: what happens to forecasting and adoption when price tracks usage?

1. The September board pack

On Monday 14 September 2026, Manaswi Vengurlekar, co-founder and chief product officer of Eltara Cloud, sat down in Pune with the company's finance lead, Madhukar Velhal, and the August numbers. Eltara sells an interface that reads invoices and bank statements into structured data. It served 172 accounts, mostly lenders and accounting firms, and had parsed 9.6 million pages that month. Revenue was ₹2,88,000, because every account paid one of three flat monthly plans: Starter at ₹700, Growth at ₹3,000 and Scale at ₹7,000.

The problem sat in one line of the table. Twelve Scale accounts averaged 320,000 pages each and paid the same ₹7,000 they had paid when they parsed a fraction of that. Eltara's inference bill rose with every page, but its revenue did not. Velhal proposed to the board, meeting on Friday 25 September, that Eltara charge by the page.

His first sheet rated every account at its band's average consumption and arrived at ₹3,21,200, an increase of ₹33,200 or 11.5 per cent over the flat plans, and at most that, as a later exhibit explains. The increase was not spread evenly. A Starter account would pay ₹720 instead of ₹700, a Growth account ₹3,200 instead of ₹3,000, and a Scale account ₹8,900 instead of ₹7,000, 27.1 per cent more. The accounts that would pay most were the ones with the most bargaining power.

Vengurlekar saw the logic and the trap together. Maitreyee Vazarkar, head of finance operations at a Thane lender and a Growth customer, had told her she would not sign a bill she could not estimate before the month began. If Eltara chose badly, it would lose its largest accounts to a rival with flat prices, or win a model whose revenue its own finance team could no longer forecast.

2. The idea

A usage-based (or consumption) model charges a rate for each unit of something the customer actually uses, measured after the fact, instead of a fixed fee for access. The measured thing is the meter; the unit should be the one in which the customer receives value. It was invented to fix a mismatch: when usage varies widely across customers, a flat price overcharges light users, undercharges heavy ones, and taxes the first purchase, since a customer must pay in full before learning whether the product works for them.

The idea is old. Utilities billed by metered electricity and gas from the late nineteenth century, and telephone companies billed by the minute. Software adopted it when Amazon launched S3 in March 2006, pricing storage per gigabyte-month, and interface companies such as Twilio, from 2008, priced per minute and later per message. In the vocabulary of the previous topic, it is subscription economics with a variable meter: the recurring relationship survives, but the amount charged in each period is no longer known in advance. That single change is what makes forecasting and adoption behave differently, and it is the thread this page follows.

The sentence Vengurlekar could repeat in the boardroom: “We charge for the unit in which customers receive value, and we forecast the units before we forecast the rupees.”

3. How it actually works

A metered bill is produced in four steps, and the second and third are where practitioners leave things implicit.

The first step defines the unit and logs an event each time it occurs. Eltara chose the page. The second step, metering, turns raw events into a billable quantity: it removes duplicates when a client retries, drops pages that failed to parse, and fixes the instant at which a month ends, including the time zone in which it ends. Customers dispute bills about retries and cut-offs far more often than about rates. The third, rating, applies the price schedule to the quantity. The fourth issues the invoice and, less visibly, feeds the finance team's forecast. Because the quantity is known only when the month closes, the forecast has to be built from consumption, never read off a contract.

Velhal's draft schedule was graduated: each band of pages is charged at its own rate, and only the pages inside a band pay that band's rate. The rates fall as volume rises, which rewards heavy use and keeps the largest customers from looking elsewhere.

4. A worked example

Take a mid-sized customer that parsed 190,000 pages in a month. Rating proceeds tier by tier.

Velhal also drafted a commitment plan: ₹4,800 a month buys 150,000 pages, and pages beyond that cost ₹32 per 1,000. Plotting both bills against pages shows something the board had not expected.

The graduated bill is 500 + 30 × pages (in thousands) between 50,000 and 200,000 pages, so it equals the commitment bill of ₹4,800 at 143,333 pages. Beyond 150,000 pages the commitment plan climbs at ₹32 against ₹30, then ₹20 above 200,000, so the graduated line overtakes it again at 208,333 pages. Usage fell 36.8 per cent. The graduated bill fell 33.9 per cent, because the marginal pages were the cheap ones. The commitment bill fell only 21.1 per cent, because 30,000 of the missing pages were paid for anyway. Revenue that is partly committed is steadier than revenue that is fully metered. The customer pays for that steadiness with a premium at low volume, which at 120,000 pages is ₹700 over the graduated bill. A commitment is a trade of price against predictability, and Vazarkar's complaint was about predictability.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

Three denominators, never one

Revenue per unit has at least three bases, each measured when the month closes: units consumed, units billed and units committed. In Exhibit 4 the same ₹4,800 bill is ₹40.00 per thousand consumed, ₹32.00 per thousand billed and ₹32.00 per thousand committed. Quote a rate without naming its base and two colleagues will argue about a number on which they agree.

Graduated is not volume pricing

In graduated pricing each band pays its own rate. In volume pricing the whole quantity pays the rate of the band it reaches. Under volume pricing at the same rates, a customer at 199,000 pages would pay ₹5,970 and at 201,000 pages ₹4,020, a bill that falls as use rises. Graduated schedules have no such cliff.

The mean account is not the typical account

Usage is skewed, which is why the model exists. Exhibit 5 rates each band at its average consumption. Because 120 of 172 accounts are Starter accounts, the median account sits in the smallest band, while the 12 Scale accounts, fewer than one in ten, supply a third of the metered revenue (₹1,06,800 of ₹3,21,200).

A bound sits on a percentile

Among Growth accounts, the 75th percentile of monthly pages is 120,000 and the 90th is 160,000. The share above a 150,000-page commitment is therefore at least 10 per cent and at most 25 per cent, so between 4 and 10 of 40 accounts. That is a range, not an estimate; the percentiles alone cannot say where in it the truth lies.

A gap inside noise is not a finding

Eltara piloted metered billing on 30 new accounts beside 30 on flat plans. Over the 60 days, the metered cohort averaged 21,400 pages per account in total (standard deviation 18,000) and the flat cohort 17,900 (15,000). The 3,500-page gap carries a standard error of about 4,280, so it is 0.8 standard errors. It does not show that metering raises usage, and it could not show it with 30 accounts a side.

Revenue moves less than usage, and also less in your favour

Were one Scale account to cut usage 40 per cent, from 320,000 to 192,000 pages, its bill would fall from ₹8,900 to ₹6,260, or 29.7 per cent. The same cheap upper tiers that cushion a fall flatten growth. Forecasting therefore has two stages: forecast pages by band, then rate them.

What the model cannot tell you

It cannot tell you whether the page is the right unit. A one-line receipt and a forty-line statement both count as one page, and customers who notice will arbitrage. Nor does it tell you what a customer would pay for the result. Ask first whether usage tracks value, and whether the customer can predict it.

6. Consumer, B2B, marketplace; early and late

Consumers accept meters for electricity and mobile data but dislike bill shock, so consumer products often prepay in packs. B2B buyers have procurement departments, which is why enterprise contracts pair a commitment with overage. A marketplace's take rate is a usage price on transaction value, so its revenue swings with the season in which sellers transact. An early-stage company has no history from which to forecast and benefits from low entry cost. A large one needs commitments to plan capacity and to satisfy its buyers' budgets.

7. Common mistakes

Quoting the average rate. Sales say ₹33.46 per thousand and a Scale customer sees ₹27.81. The misunderstanding is that a pooled rate describes any account. Diagnostic: re-rate three real accounts by hand.

Forecasting from the mean account. The forecast misses in the months a large account moves. Diagnostic: forecast each band separately from its percentiles and back-test six months.

Billing a unit nobody can check. The symptom is a rise in disputes after the first invoice. The misunderstanding is that the meter is the customer's record too. Diagnostic: reconcile fifty invoices to the customer's own logs before launch.

Reading a pilot gap as an adoption effect. The symptom is a slide claiming uplift from 60 accounts. Diagnostic: compute the standard error before the meeting.

8. What good looks like

A well-handled version publishes the rate card on one page, shows each customer a running bill preview, and reports revenue to the board on all three denominators, labelled. Forecasts carry ranges drawn from named percentiles. Failed pages are never billed, and a customer can see before the month ends which side of a commitment she is on. Above all, the team can say, for any rate it quotes, which units it divides by and when they were counted.

9. Closing

On 25 September Vengurlekar put one proposal to the board: the graduated schedule for every account, plus the commitment plan offered only to accounts whose trailing usage sits inside the window in Exhibit 3, which on the percentiles above is at most ten of the 40 Growth accounts, and possibly none. Most Scale accounts, averaging 320,000 pages, stay on graduated rates, since above 208,333 pages the commitment costs them more. She reasoned that the schedule fixes the cost mismatch, while the commitment gives Vazarkar the predictability she demanded. Next, read the topic on forecasting usage-based revenue, because the first question that follows any such decision is how wide the range is.

Two questions to sit with. If a customer's usage falls for three months, is that churn or a quiet month, and what would you measure to decide? Which unit would you choose for a product whose value is not tied to anything countable?

Srote Systems: What the Meter Would Have Said

An observability company has spent four months shadow-metering its own customers. On Sunday night its chief product officer has six exhibits, four options and a board meeting.

1. The night before

At twenty past nine on Sunday 15 November 2026, Dipannita Khanolkar was the only person on the fourth floor of Srote Systems' office in HSR Layout, Bengaluru. The air conditioning had gone off at eight. On the table were six printed exhibits and the agenda for the ten o'clock board meeting: Item 3 — pricing basis, FY28. Decision requested.

She had asked for that wording in September, when it still felt like a question with an answer. Srote billed for every server, container host and Kubernetes node its agent watched: a flat licence per host per year, three bands, no meter on the invoice. Since June the platform team had run a silent second calculation beside the real one — what each account would have paid had Srote billed by the volume of log data it ingested. The numbers came back and did not agree.

Not in doubt was the calendar (Figure 1). Every contract required sixty days' written notice of a price change. The effective date sales had been told to plan for was Monday 1 February 2027, putting the last day for notices eighteen days away, on Thursday 3 December.

Figure 1. The 137 days from tonight to FY28, drawn to scale at four pixels to the day, day 0 at the left tick.

2. How Srote came to charge for hosts

Srote was founded in 2016 by Dhairyashil Kanetkar and two colleagues from a Pune infrastructure team, to collect logs, metrics and traces from Indian engineering teams and make them searchable fast enough to be useful during an incident. Revenue for the year ended 31 March 2026 was ₹131 crore. It employs 486 people across Bengaluru, Baner in Pune, Mumbai, Singapore, Berlin, Toronto, Princeton and Dubai.

The decision that shapes tonight was made in 2019 and was not thought of as a pricing decision. Srote's first large customer, the Mumbai non-banking finance company Stambh Credit Services, was offered two price lists: one per gigabyte ingested, one per monitored host. Stambh's chief technology officer refused the meter — he could not forecast gigabytes, could not explain a variable line to his audit committee, and would not sign something his own engineers could make dearer by changing a log level. Srote took the host licence, won the account, and built the agent, the order form and the commission plan on it.

In 2023 the pattern hardened. To win three large accounts against Datadog — among them Safinah Freight Systems FZE, a Dubai logistics group that remains Srote's largest contract — Srote signed five-year agreements carrying what its lawyers call the basis clause: the commercial basis may not change during the term, and the per-host price at renewal is capped at prevailing list. Thirty-five contracts still carry it (Exhibit 6). Srote built its metering pipeline in 2024 for capacity planning rather than billing, which is why raw usage events are discarded after thirty days.

3. The industry

Observability is sold in India against the global incumbents — Datadog, New Relic, Dynatrace, Splunk, Grafana Labs and Elastic — all of whom publish volume- or consumption-based price lists, most in dollars. Zoho's Site24x7 competes from the other end on price. Srote's pitch has been latency, rupee billing and Indian data residency.

Demand is not Srote's problem. UPI volumes reported by NPCI have made every lender, broker and payment processor a heavy log producer; quick commerce did the same for retail, and ONDC added another layer of traffic. Regulation pushed harder still. CERT-In's April 2022 directions require regulated entities to keep ICT system logs for a rolling 180 days within Indian jurisdiction, so Srote's bank, NBFC and broking customers cannot cut log volume to cut a bill. The DPDP Act of 2023 governs personal data arriving in those logs, SEBI's cyber-security framework does the same for broking accounts, and GST of 18 per cent sits on the invoice either way.

Srote's Dubai, Singapore and United States customers hold ₹29.55 crore of the ₹155.53 crore book, 19 per cent, and are the likeliest to arrive at a renewal holding a competitor's per-gigabyte price list. Kanetkar is in diligence on a ₹340 crore Series D whose term sheet expires on 31 January 2027.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

Exhibit 1 is the contract book at 30 September 2026, and the first place the story goes wrong. Srote sells an entitlement to monitored hosts; the agent reports how many appeared. The gap between 50,730 and 57,480 is not evenly spread: Enterprise reported 27.4 per cent more hosts than it had bought, Mid-market 7.4 per cent more, Growth 17.5 per cent fewer.

Through 2024 the host count was believed to track value, and for a time it did. In March 2025 two large Enterprise accounts containerised, their host counts tripled, and sales recorded the windfall as proof the model worked. By January 2026 the same two had consolidated onto a quarter as many larger hosts, cut their entitlement at renewal, and raised the volume they sent by roughly half. Finance treated it as a one-off; it is now standard consultant advice.

On Monday 1 June 2026 Dhrumil Kharade's team began shadow-metering 41 accounts. On Friday 14 August, Safinah's procurement office in Dubai asked in writing for a per-gigabyte quotation at its 2028 renewal. On Friday 18 September the Toronto pricing team delivered the tier card. The two numbers meant to settle the question — Exhibits 4 and 5 — arrived in the first week of November and did not agree on how large the change would be.

5. The people

  • Dhairyashil Kanetkar, co-founder and chief executive, Bengaluru. Wants the meter announced before the Series D closes: every comparable company bills by volume. His round is priced on growth. He has not said the lead investor's draft term sheet carries a revenue-quality covenant.
  • Durgaprasad Kashalkar, chief financial officer, Mumbai. Against: a meter turns a forecastable line into a weather report. He has guided the board to ₹198 crore for FY28. He has not said his own model applies the pilot's headline percentage to the whole book in one step.
  • Darshak Kelekar, senior vice-president, sales, Princeton, New Jersey. For commitments with overage: his buyers sign numbers, not meters. His quota credit is earned on committed value. He has not disclosed that three FY27 deals in his pipeline are already quoted per gigabyte.
  • Dhrumil Kharade, vice-president, engineering (metering), Pune. Can meter precisely forward and not at all backward. His fourteen engineers are committed to the Hyderabad build until 31 March 2027. He has not mentioned the eleven-day gap in the rollup store in March 2026, after a region migration.
  • Devarati Kakodkar, lead data scientist, pricing, Toronto. Argues the distribution, not the average, must set the tiers. She wrote the Exhibit 3 card and her objectives name its adoption. She has not said she fitted the breakpoints to the 41 pilot accounts rather than all 573.
  • Dhanisha Khambete, head of customer success, Asia-Pacific, Singapore. Expects the smallest accounts to leave. Her bonus is a gross renewal rate. She has not told anyone that in August she assured eleven Growth accounts their price would not change in FY28.
  • Dheemant Kelaskar, principal designer, Berlin. Holds that a customer must see consumption in the product before it reaches an invoice — "if the invoice is the first place a customer sees their own volume, we have shipped a dispute, not a price" — and wants the usage dashboard funded alongside the meter. He has not said the dashboard reads the same rollup store, and would show customers the March gap.

7. Voices

"Every company we are benchmarked against bills by volume. Walk into the Series D holding a per-host licence and I spend the first hour explaining why."

"The pilot says minus 7.6 per cent. On a 155.53 crore book that is 11.8 crore a year, and I have guided the board to 198 for FY28. I am not carrying that into Monday on a four-month read of 41 accounts."

8. The options as Khanolkar sees them

She wrote four on the back of Exhibit 6 on Saturday. Options 1 to 3 meter gigabytes ingested; Kharade's platform also counts indexed events and retained gigabyte-days.

  1. List price only. Publish the Exhibit 3 card as list price for new business from 1 February 2027. Existing contracts stay on the host licence until their renewal quarter. Cost: ₹1.40 crore in Q4 FY27 and Q1 FY28 — six of Kharade's Pune engineers for two quarters at a loaded ₹38 lakh a year, plus ₹26 lakh of billing changes. Leaves untouched: the basis-clause contracts and the host entitlement.
  2. Platform fee plus meter. Keep the host licence at 60 per cent of today's list as a platform fee and meter volume above an allowance set account by account at the trailing three-month mean from the daily rollup store. Cost: ₹2.10 crore. Leaves untouched: the entitled-host count and the commission plan.
  3. Commitment and overage. Customers commit an annual rupee value against the Exhibit 3 card; consumption beyond it bills at the tier rate times 1.35. Cost: ₹1.75 crore, plus ₹90 lakh to redesign sales compensation, which today pays on licensed hosts. Leaves untouched: the agent and the entitlement register. The host count stops being a billable unit.
  4. Enforce what was sold. No change of basis. From 1 April 2027 the agent refuses to report above the entitled count, so every host above an account's own entitlement must be licensed or stop reporting. Cost: ₹35 lakh. Leaves untouched: the tier card, the pilot, and Safinah's Q4 FY28 renewal.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board meets at ten on Monday 16 November 2026 in Bengaluru. Legal requires ten working days between approval and the issue of notices, and Srote's draft holiday calendar lists Tuesday 24 November for Guru Nanak Jayanti and Wednesday 25 November for a Pune office closure; neither is confirmed in writing for 2026. Counting from Tuesday 17 November and assuming both are non-working days in both offices, the tenth working day is Wednesday 2 December, one day inside the 3 December deadline; if they are working days it is Monday 30 November.

The rest is fixed. Sixty days' notice is contractual for all 573 accounts. Thirty-five contracts cannot change basis before their term ends, and the largest, Safinah at ₹10.14 crore of annual value, renews in Q4 FY28. The ₹340 crore term sheet lapses on 31 January 2027. Kharade's fourteen engineers are committed to Hyderabad until 31 March 2027 and there is no second metering team. CERT-In's 180-day retention duty and the residency requirement bind Srote's regulated customers whatever the price list says. GST at 18 per cent applies either way. And ₹198 crore of FY28 revenue is already with the board.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Exhibit 1 puts revenue at ₹2,555 a month per entitled host. Compute the same figure per reporting host. Which denominator belongs in a price per host, and why do the two diverge in opposite directions across the segments?
  2. Using Exhibit 2's percentiles and the Exhibit 3 card, find the monthly volume at which the card's effective rate per gigabyte crosses Srote's blended revenue per gigabyte. Where does that volume sit in the distribution, and which accounts is the card repricing?

  5. Exhibit 4's eight accounts were modelled by hand; the other 565 were not. State what must be true of those 565 for Exhibit 4's pattern to hold, and which of the four options still stands if it is not.
  6. What should Khanolkar do on Monday morning, 16 November 2026 — and what should she say to the board about forecasting a revenue line that will move with her customers' log volume rather than her own sales plan?

11. Sunday night

At a quarter past eleven Khanolkar put the six exhibits back in order, then out of order again, Exhibit 5 on Exhibit 4 and then Exhibit 4 on Exhibit 5. Her phone held a message from Kharade sent at 23:04: agent build is green, say the word by Tuesday or it slips past the Hyderabad freeze. Below it, unanswered since August, was Safinah's procurement note and its single courteous question. In under eleven hours she would have ten minutes and a slide, and she had not decided what the slide should say.

Nivaan Reads: The Diwali Budget

A decision case in subscription economics

1. Opening

At 5:30 pm on Tuesday 27 October 2026, Anuja Honrao, chief product officer of Nivaan Reads, sat in the company's Baner office in Pune with a spreadsheet and a deadline. By Friday 30 October the media agency needed a signed plan for Diwali, which fell on Sunday 8 November, and the board had set aside ₹60 lakh for it. The money could buy new subscribers, repair the way new subscribers were looked after, or fund an offer to hold the ones already paying. Three colleagues, in Pune, Toronto and Singapore, were about to join a video call, at 8:00 am in Toronto and 8:00 pm in Singapore, each carrying a different answer. Anuja's own view was less settled than she had let on at the last board meeting, where she had promised the directors a recommendation, not a menu. Whatever she chose would shape the November renewals, the December board pack and the first half of 2027. Figure 1 shows the days that remained.

2. Company background

Nivaan Reads, founded in Pune in 2020, sells audiobooks and serialised stories in Marathi, Hindi, Tamil and Bengali, mostly to first-time paying listeners in smaller cities who play them on phones during commutes. It was free and advertising-funded until March 2024, when it introduced one paid plan at ₹149 a month before GST. Payments run mainly through UPI AutoPay mandates under the NPCI and RBI e-mandate framework, with cards as fallback. Its rivals are Kuku FM and Pratilipi in regional audio and stories, Audible and Amazon's Kindle at the premium end, and free YouTube. About 140 people work for it, most in Pune and Bengaluru. It has ₹360 lakh in the bank and a net monthly burn of ₹40 lakh. Growth has come mainly from paid social media, from referrals inside Marathi and Hindi reading groups on WhatsApp, and from two festival campaigns. The company thinks of itself as a habit business: a listener who has finished three serials rarely leaves, while one who never starts a second title often does. The board, led by an investor who also backs a Bengaluru software-as-a-service firm, reads the company through the metrics of that world: MRR, churn and cohort retention.

3. The situation

Exhibit 1 sets out September. Nivaan ended the month with 1,29,120 paying subscribers and a monthly recurring revenue (MRR) of ₹192.4 lakh, an annualised run-rate of about ₹23.1 crore; that is MRR times twelve, not booked revenue. The subscriber count grew by 9,120 because 18,000 joined and 8,880 left (Exhibit 2).

Anay Hatkar, the data scientist in Toronto, has shown that leaving is concentrated early. In the first two months a subscriber is far likelier to stop than later. In August he ran a randomised test of a new onboarding sequence: a starter shelf in the subscriber's own language, a WhatsApp nudge on day three and offline downloads. Among 6,000 people who joined between 3 and 16 August, 3,000 got the sequence and 3,000 did not; all first renewals were known by 16 September. Last Diwali's cohort looked worse than usual: of 11,000 festival joiners in October and November 2025, 3,300 failed their first renewal. Exhibit 3 turns these rates into survival curves.

Not everything fits a spreadsheet. In September Alka's team phoned 40 lapsed subscribers from the 2025 festival cohort, and 26 said they had joined for the festival price and never formed a listening habit. Those 40 were simply the people who picked up. The Bengaluru engineering team has confirmed that the onboarding sequence, already built for the test, can be switched on for every joiner from 1 November. Atharva, meanwhile, has pointed out that Nivaan's cash would last nine months at the current burn, and that investors in this market now ask about payback before they ask about growth.

4. The people

Atharva Hajare, chief financial officer in Pune, applies one rule: money spent must come back as contribution within twelve months. He is drawn to cash now, because a Series B is at least a year away.

Anay Hatkar, in Toronto, wants the onboarding result extended, and warns that it was measured on one renewal only. Because his morning is Anuja's evening, he sends his analyses overnight and rarely speaks live; he has asked that any conclusion drawn from the test be described as what it is, one renewal on 6,000 people.

Alka Hende, customer-success lead in Singapore, speaks to subscribers every week. The long-standing ones, she says, are the ones who write in about price and who notice when newcomers get discounts they never did. She is based in Singapore, serves Tamil and Bengali listeners abroad, including a large group in Dubai, as well as readers in India, and is unconvinced that a festival price travels well across them.

Anuja Honrao must decide, then defend the choice to a board that approved last year's festival push and expects to see it either repeated or explained. She prefers evidence to instinct, but accepts that a ₹60 lakh decision must be taken before most of the evidence exists.

5. The options

Option A: buy the festival (₹60 lakh). The whole budget goes to Meta, YouTube and regional-language creators at an expected ₹600 per paying subscriber, adding 10,000 joiners to September's 18,000-a-month pace. They are assumed to behave like the 2025 festival cohort, and none is assumed to have joined anyway. The onboarding sequence stays off for everyone, and the spend is committed in full on Friday.

Option B: fix the front door (₹15 lakh). The tested sequence goes to every joiner from 1 November to 30 April, six monthly cohorts of 18,000 each. The cost covers the starter shelves in four languages, WhatsApp messaging charges and an analyst's time. It assumes regular joiners, that the August effect on first renewal (20% to 16%) holds at full scale, and that second-month churn stays at 20%. ₹45 lakh of the budget stays unspent. No subscriber is added.

Option C: lock in the loyal (no budget). An annual plan at ₹999, or ₹83.25 a month, is offered to the 66,000 subscribers in month 6 or later on 1 September, with 20% assumed to accept (13,200). Cash rises by ₹131.9 lakh and MRR falls by ₹8.68 lakh. Left monthly, such a payer would yield about ₹1,521 (months 6–11) or ₹1,648 (month 12 onward) over the next year, if each band's current churn held for all twelve months. First-month leavers are untouched, and the offer carries no ad spend. Finance would need to confirm GST invoicing on a year's payment.

6. Questions for discussion

  1. What was September's blended monthly churn, over which base, and why can it not simply be multiplied by twelve to give an annual figure?
  2. If joiners stayed at 18,000 a month and that blended rate held, where would the base level off, and why might that figure mislead?
  3. Using Exhibits 1 to 3, how does each option fare against Atharva's twelve-month rule, and which assumption carries each one?
  4. Which option would you lead with on Friday, what would you tell Atharva and Alka, and what evidence would make you change course?

7. A note for the learner

The lens is that retention compounds unevenly. Exhibit 2 shows churn falling from 20% to 1.5% as tenure grows, so a subscriber kept past month three is worth far more than a headline count suggests, and a blended rate is a statement about the current mix as much as about the product. September's 8,880 leavers over a 1,20,000 opening base is 7.4% a month, about a 60% loss over a year when compounded, and an 18,000 inflow at that rate would level at roughly 2.4 lakh. A base this young will probably settle higher, because a maturing base has more of its members in the low-churn months.

One defensible path is Option B. Its 4.0-point gain adds 0.30 paid months per joiner, so 1,08,000 joiners yield 32,451 extra paid months, ₹29.9 lakh of contribution at ₹92 against ₹15 lakh spent, about twice. Option A buys 10,000 joiners worth 6.26 paid months each, ₹57.6 lakh against ₹60 lakh, which misses the rule inside twelve months though later retention could redeem it. Option C, whose annual payers carry twelve months of variable cost (₹684, leaving ₹315 of contribution), gives up about ₹88 lakh of contribution, or ₹78 lakh of revenue, for cash it can wait for, with nine months of runway.

Hold the other ₹45 lakh. Every joiner then receives the sequence, so compare the November cohort's first-renewal churn, complete on 30 December, with the old 20%; if it exceeds 18%, stop, and revisit acquisition with a lifetime view in January. The evidence is one month of one test on 6,000 people, which is why the path is staged.

Subscription Economics

Why retention compounds, and where it stops

1. A slide for the board

On 14 October 2026, Ketki Sawardekar, chief product officer of Candor Desk, carried one slide into a board meeting in Pune. Candor sold a shared-inbox and ticketing tool to small Indian businesses at an average of ₹4,000 per account per month, collected through UPI AutoPay mandates. On 1 September it had 1,000 paying accounts and monthly recurring revenue (MRR, the subscription fees the company expects to bill in a month) of ₹40.00 lakh. The first table shows what September did to that figure.

Table 1. Candor Desk, September 2026: MRR movement (₹ lakh)

Rates quoted from this table are measured on the opening base: 1,000 accounts, ₹40.00 lakh.

Chief executive Kamlakar Supekar had ₹60 lakh to spend over the next twelve months and two proposals. Growth wanted new paying accounts raised from 50 a month to 70 by buying more leads (Option A). Kaveesh Sahasrabudhe, who ran customer success, wanted to rebuild onboarding so that the share of accounts lost each month fell from 3 per cent to 2 (Option B). Each cost the same, and each promised more revenue. Supekar asked which of them would still be paying Candor in three years, and which would stop working the day the money stopped.

Sawardekar's difficulty was that September argued both ways. The company had added ₹2.00 lakh of new MRR and still grown only 3.25 per cent. If she backed the wrong lever, Candor would spend a year of runway on a business that could not grow beyond a size she could already compute.

2. The idea

Subscription economics starts from one change: a customer pays repeatedly for continued access, so a customer is worth a stream of payments rather than a single sale. Churn is the share of customers, or of revenue, present at the start of a period that has gone by its end. Retention is one minus churn, and because it applies again every period it compounds: after t months a cohort (a group that joined together) keeps (1 − churn)t of its members.

The problem it was invented to solve was a measurement gap. Software moved from licences sold once to fees billed monthly during the 2000s, a shift Tien Tzuo, who founded Zuora in 2007, named the subscription economy. Investors then needed to know whether money spent winning a customer came back before the customer left. David Skok's widely read writing from around 2009 popularised the answer: compare a customer's lifetime value (LTV, the gross profit a customer is expected to yield before leaving) with the cost of acquiring them (CAC).

The consequence Sawardekar needed is the churn ceiling. If a company adds n accounts a month and loses a fraction c of its base, the base stops growing when losses equal arrivals, at n divided by c. The sentence she could repeat without sounding glib: "Every month we lose 3 per cent of what we have and add 50, so however hard we run, we converge on 1,667 accounts."

3. How it works

The mechanics have four steps. Fix a period, here a month. Apply churn to the opening base. Add that month's arrivals. Repeat. For Candor, each month's base is 0.97 times the previous month's plus 50. Two conventions stay implicit. Churn is charged only to accounts that were present on the first day, so a new account cannot leave in its month of joining; and every rate here is measured on the opening base, a choice that changes the answer.

The ceiling is 50 ÷ 0.03 = 1,667 accounts, or about ₹66.7 lakh of MRR at ₹4,000 each. The company does not jump there. The gap between today's base and the ceiling shrinks by 3 per cent a month: 667 accounts now, and 667 × 0.9712 = 463 after a year, which puts the base at 1,667 − 463 = 1,204. The gap halves only after about 23 months, because 0.9723 is 0.496.

A cohort tells the same story from the customer's side. A customer who leaves at 3 per cent a month stays on average 1 ÷ 0.03 = 33.3 months, so at 75 per cent gross margin LTV is ₹4,000 × 0.75 ÷ 0.03 = ₹1,00,000. This is undiscounted, and it is only as good as the margin and the constant churn behind it.

Read the figure by its gap. Early on the curves are nearly indistinguishable, which is why a retention programme looks unconvincing in its first quarter. By month 36 the 2 per cent cohort holds 48.3 accounts against 33.4, nearly half as many again. That divergence is what "retention compounds" means.

4. A worked example

Start every projection from a round base of 1,000 accounts (September's opening count; the true 1 November base is about 4 per cent higher, which lifts every figure but not the ranking). Hold the average bill at ₹4,000 and gross margin at 75 per cent, so each account yields ₹3,000 a month, and leave expansion out of both options. Option A costs ₹60 lakh a year, every year, buying 20 extra accounts a month from November, 240 a year, each billed ₹4,000 and leaving at 3 per cent: ₹25,000 per extra account, or LTV ÷ CAC of 1,00,000 ÷ 25,000 = 4.0, with payback of 25,000 ÷ 3,000 = 8.3 months. Option B costs ₹60 lakh once. Its churn does not reach 2 per cent at once: the monthly rate runs 2.75, 2.50 and 2.25 per cent in November to January and 2.00 from February, as the playbooks reach each support pod.

B trails at month 24 and leads at month 36. That is the first pass. For the second, change one input: Kaveesh delivers half the promised cut, so churn settles at 2.5 per cent, reached by the same staged path (2.875, 2.75 and 2.625 per cent first). Accounts at month 36 are 1,595, extra gross profit is ₹85.5 lakh, and net is 85.5 − 60 = ₹25.5 lakh, far below A's 109.3. B's whole case rests on a churn number nobody has yet observed.

5. Nuances a learner must absorb

Logo churn is not revenue churn.

September lost 3.0 per cent of accounts, but the accounts lost were small, so churned MRR was only 0.90 ÷ 40.00 = 2.25 per cent. Add contraction and gross revenue churn is 1.40 ÷ 40.00 = 3.5 per cent. Net revenue retention (NRR, opening MRR after churn, contraction and expansion, excluding new accounts) was 39.30 ÷ 40.00 = 98.25 per cent. Four measures, four answers.

Monthly and annual churn do not convert by multiplying.

Three per cent monthly is 1 − 0.9712 = 30.6 per cent a year, not 36; 2 per cent is 21.5, not 24. Compare only like with like.

The denominator is a decision.

Candor divides by the opening base. Dividing 30 losses by the average of 1,000 and 1,020 gives 2.97 per cent; including free trials in the base would dilute it further. Name the base and its date.

The ceiling assumes constant churn.

Real cohorts usually lose customers fastest early, so churn blended across an ageing base falls without any programme. Read cohort curves before trusting a single rate.

Expansion can remove the ceiling.

The formula counts accounts. If surviving accounts spend more each month than leavers take away, so NRR exceeds 100 per cent, a cohort's revenue grows indefinitely. Candor's 98.25 per cent sits below that line.

Not every loss is a decision.

A failed mandate debit is involuntary churn, caused by expired cards or low balances rather than dissatisfaction. Its fix, retry and reminder logic, is cheaper than redesigning onboarding. Candor had not yet separated the two.

LTV is hypersensitive to churn.

Lifetime is 1 ÷ c: 28.6 months at 3.5 per cent, 33.3 at 3.0, 40.0 at 2.5. A half-point error moves LTV by 14 to 20 per cent, and none of this says why customers leave.

Questions before relying on a churn figure.

Ask which base, which window, which cohort, whether the programme's effect was measured or assumed, and whether leavers were bounced or decided.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace

Consumer subscriptions, such as music or fitness apps billed monthly, face low switching costs and steep early churn, so the ceiling sits low and acquisition cost dominates. B2B products like Candor's can add seats and tiers, so expansion matters and NRR above 100 per cent is achievable. Annual contracts turn churn into lumpy renewal events, so a quiet month proves little. In a marketplace the paying side may not be the side that is scarce, and retention of suppliers often matters more than of subscribers.

Size changes the reading. An early-stage company has two or three cohorts, so a rate is noisy and the ceiling is a rough warning. A large one has cohort curves years deep, but its blended churn hides segments whose economics differ, and its ceiling is high enough that expansion must carry growth.

7. Common mistakes

Annualising by multiplication. The symptom is a deck quoting 36 per cent annual churn while Table 2 shows 69.4 of every 100 accounts still paying after a year, a 30.6 per cent loss. The misunderstanding is treating compounding as addition. The cheapest diagnostic is to recompute (1 − c)12 from the monthly rate.

Mixing bases. The symptom is an average revenue per account that falls when free trials are counted, then used to size the paying accounts needed to close a gap. The misunderstanding is that a rate belongs to its denominator. The diagnostic is to write the denominator beside every ratio.

Booking the end state. The symptom is a plan crediting 2 per cent churn from the first month. Option B then shows 1,323 accounts at month 12 against the staged 1,311, and gross profit of ₹23.3 lakh rather than ₹18.6 lakh, an overstatement of a quarter. The diagnostic is to integrate over the stages.

8. What good looks like

A well-handled decision starts by naming the denominator. The analyst prints the opening base, the four churn measures and the cohort table, so every rate can be recomputed. She shows both options at 12, 24 and 36 months, with the ceiling beside each, and discloses margin and discounting. She also states the single input on which the choice turns, here the churn Option B will actually deliver, and proposes a cheap way to learn it before the money is gone.

9. The decision

Sawardekar recommended Option B, paced: half of the ₹60 lakh released at once and the rest after the churn reading for February 2027, available in early March; the staged path above presumes full release, so paced release delays the ramp. If churn was still above 2.5 per cent, the unspent half would go to acquisition. Her reasoning was that A pays only while it is paid for, whereas B raises the ceiling itself, from 1,667 to a promised 2,500, and the second pass had shown her the one number to measure before the money was gone. Supekar approved it.

The next topics to learn are expansion revenue and net revenue retention, which decide whether the ceiling binds at all, then freemium and usage-based pricing, which change what a "customer" and a "churn event" even are.

Two questions to sit with. First, suppose Candor's cohort curves showed early churn of 6 per cent a month falling to 1.5 after the third month: which number would you use for the ceiling, and why? Second, if Option B worked, what would you expect to happen to the case for Option A?

Pranaali Technologies: the churn ceiling

Pune, Sunday 18 October 2026. A board meeting on Thursday, a renewal run that locks on the 30th, and four numbers that all answer to the name of retention.

1. The night before

At twenty to eleven on the night of Sunday 18 October 2026, Bhimsen Idate sat at the dining table of his flat in Aundh, Pune, with two printouts before him and a third he had not opened. The first two were the billing extract of 2 October and the board pack Bibhuti Iglekar had circulated on Thursday 15 October, one line of which read Legacy migration: ₹37.80 lakh, year one, no engineering dependency. The third was a memo from Toronto he had asked for himself and now suspected he did not want.

Pranaali Technologies Private Limited closed September 2026 with ₹39.74 crore of annual recurring revenue, up 21.5 per cent on the ₹32.71 crore of a year before. The board met on Thursday 22 October; the tables feeding the November renewal run locked on Friday 30 October. Between Monday morning and that lock lay twelve days, nine of them working, and five things Bhimsen could put his name to. What there was not, after four weeks of asking, was agreement about what Pranaali's retention number was.

2. How Pranaali got here

Baldeep Ingalhalikar and two colleagues from a Pune accounting software firm founded Pranaali in March 2017, four months before the Goods and Services Tax arrived. The first product typed a return for a distributor who had typed it himself. The second, in 2018, was a subscription: Lite, at ₹13,200 a year billed annually, for the single-godown trader with one accountant and no patience.

Lite sold. The order form used from November 2018 carried a clause the founders wrote themselves and were proud of: the price of your Lite plan will not be increased for as long as your subscription runs without a break. It left the form in November 2019, by which point some fourteen hundred accounts had signed with it. Lite closed to new sign-ups on 1 April 2021 and became Legacy Lite. Nine hundred were still paying in September 2026, and 612 of the 900 — 68.0 per cent — hold the 2018 form.

Starter replaced Lite on 1 April 2021 at ₹999 a month, moved to ₹1,250 on 1 April 2024 and to ₹1,450 on 1 July 2025. Growth followed in 2022 for multi-branch firms, Scale in 2023 with implementation. Figure 1 sets out the sequence.

3. The market Pranaali sells into

India's accounting software market is not an empty field. Tally Solutions sits on a very large share of the country's distributor desktops and is what a customer means when he says he already has software. Zoho Books, Vyapar, Busy and Marg ERP compete for the same trader; Clear built a business on e-invoicing compliance. Freshworks and Zoho are the comparables Pranaali's investors reach for.

Two pieces of regulation bear directly on how Pranaali may price. The GSTN extended the e-invoicing mandate to firms with turnover above ₹5 crore from 1 August 2023, turning the product from a convenience into an obligation. And the Reserve Bank's framework for recurring e-mandates caps each mandate, requires fresh authentication whenever the amount changes, and requires notice twenty-four hours before each debit: Pranaali cannot raise a monthly price by editing a table, but must ask several thousand customers to tap approve again. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 governs what it keeps of the invoice data.

The UAE's phased e-invoicing programme opened a Gulf market Pranaali entered through one large Dubai group; Singapore's InvoiceNow network gave Benita Ikolkar's team a second country.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

Through 2025 the company held three beliefs. That Starter was the funnel: cheap, self-serve, the source of the accounts that became Growth. That Legacy Lite was a rounding error. That retention was improving, because the cancellation count had stopped rising while the base grew.

The first survived in a form nobody planned: of the 303 new Growth accounts won in the twelve months to 30 September 2026, 148 arrived by upgrade from Starter, which billing books as a Starter cancellation and a new Growth account the same day. The second was put to the test in the board pack, where Exhibit 4 acquired a number. The third is where the company disagrees with itself: Exhibit 1, its own note and Exhibit 5 each describe how fast Starter accounts stop paying. Of the 1,650 Starter cancellations, 1,502 left the platform altogether; a cancellation-reason picklist has existed only since 1 April 2026, so the 718 of them falling before that date were hand-recoded from support notes in July 2026, and 194 of the 718 carry no reason at all. Then on 7 October, five days after the extract behind Exhibits 1 and 4, Benita Ikolkar's team granted 61 Legacy Lite accounts a written one-year price extension, by email, outside billing.

5. Exhibits

B — Close Starter to new sign-ups. New small firms route to the free tier, whose cap rises from 50 e-invoices a month to 150; the 4,800 existing Starter accounts keep their plan and price. The calendar is its own constraint, because the 2026 festival list was not fixed when the board pack went out. This case assumes Vijayadashami falls on Tuesday 20 October 2026, with the Pune and Bengaluru offices closed, and Lakshmi Puja on Sunday 8 November, with Pune closed on Monday 9 and Tuesday 10 November — the second week of the November run, when any re-authorisation would be chased. Reconstruct his arithmetic, list every assumption this case gives you reason to examine, and say what you would put to the board instead.
  5. Exhibit 2 reports 93.4 per cent net revenue retention on the 1 October 2025 cohort; Exhibit 3's note gives new Starter MRR added in each of the last six months. If neither changes, what size does Starter settle at, and the company — against ₹60 crore of ARR by 31 March 2028 and ₹48 crore by 30 June 2027?
  6. It is Monday morning, 19 October 2026. What does Bhimsen Idate do before the board meets, what does he say to it, and what does he decline to say? Which option or combination would you commit Pranaali to, and what would make that wrong?

11. Monday morning is nine hours away

At a quarter to midnight Bhimsen opened the Toronto memo and read it twice. Then he turned the board pack over and wrote one sentence on the back of it. He read that too, and could not decide whether it belonged in Thursday's deck or in a different conversation with Baldeep Ingalhalikar. Outside, the lane had gone quiet.
