Subscription economics

Why retention compounds, what the churn ceiling is, and why two experts read one cohort table to opposite conclusions.

1. Two decisions, taken three months apart

On 14 May 2026, in a converted bungalow off Senapati Bapat Road in Pune, Lipanshu Tilekar, chief product officer of Deepstambh Systems, had a single engineering team-year to allocate. Deepstambh sold laboratory-information and billing software to independent diagnostic-lab chains: 461 paying accounts, ₹46.20 crore of ARR at the close of FY26, priced at ₹4,800 per collection centre per month plus modules. The board wanted ₹60.00 crore by 31 March 2027, a rise of 29.9 per cent. One roadmap, pressed by the finance lead Lakshmesh Tungarkar, would build NABL-accreditation reporting and instrument integrations to stop accounts leaving. The other, which sales wanted, would build a patient-app and home-collection module for accounts already won. Both cost the same team.

Three months later, on 11 August in Bengaluru, Lamiksha Tonape faced a harder version of the same question. Tonape had co-founded Dhoop, a Marathi, Hindi and Kannada spoken-word and audiobook subscription at ₹149 a month or ₹999 a year: 8.10 lakh paying subscribers, gross additions of about 60,000 a month, blended monthly churn of 6.2 per cent. At a mix of 82 per cent monthly and 18 per cent annual the blended gross price was ₹137.17 a subscriber-month, so ₹11.11 crore a month of gross billings before store commission. The plan promised 15 lakh subscribers by March 2027. Her board member Lahanu Tarkhad, who had run subscriptions at a listed Indian media group, asked what nobody could answer: at 6.2 per cent a month, what does this business converge to if nothing improves? Lohadri Tengse, who ran analytics, had the table, and the answer was not 15 lakh.

2. The idea, and the four schools that read it differently

A subscription business is one whose revenue in any period is mostly the consequence of decisions taken earlier: the base is a stock, not a flow, and growth is the gap between the rate at which the firm adds to it and the rate at which it decays. Retention compounds because retained revenue is the base on which next period's retention and expansion both operate. The identity is multiplicative —

ARR(t+1) = ARR(t) × (1 − logo churn rate) × (1 + net expansion on the retained base)

— so a point of churn and a point of expansion are not interchangeable. It also explains the costliest routine error: rates compound, they do not add. Two per cent monthly churn is 21.5 per cent over twelve months of exposure, because 0.9812 = 0.785, not 24 per cent.

The apparatus is borrowed. Survival curves and hazard rates come from the actuarial tradition — Halley's Breslau life table of 1693, Gompertz's mortality law of 1825 — a subscriber base being a population with births and deaths. Cohort accounting came from mail-order: the negative-option book clubs of the 1920s valued a member before knowing how long she would stay. Cable and mobile telephony made churn and ARPU managerial words by the 1980s; hosted software after 1999 added expansion inside a retained account; and the repricing of 2022 made net revenue retention software's headline retention figure.

Four schools disagree, and it pays to know which proposition each signs. The actuarial school signs "a single churn rate is a category error; the object is a survival curve with heterogeneity" and refuses "cutting churn two points raises the ceiling proportionally". The cohort school signs "never compute lifetime value from a blended rate" and refuses an infinite horizon. The net-retention school signs "above 100 per cent a company grows with no new logos" and denies that cohort lifetime value is measurable in enterprise. The payback school signs "months to payback is the only retention statistic you can act on", refusing every lifetime-value multiple.

3. Mechanics: the two decompositions experts actually run

The first is a revenue-retention decomposition on a fixed cohort. Deepstambh held 412 paying accounts on 1 April 2025 carrying ₹3,708 lakh of ARR; 46 free pilots are excluded, which matters: revenue per account averages ₹9.00 lakh over the 412, ₹8.10 lakh over all 458. Every rate below is measured on the 412 as constituted that day.

Read it as a bridge. Thirty-seven accounts of 412 left — 9.0 per cent by logo count — but destroyed only 7.8 per cent of revenue, because leavers averaged ₹7.81 lakh against the cohort's ₹9.00 lakh: small accounts churn more, so logo and revenue churn are different measures.

In multiplicative form the bridge reads 0.9221 × 1.1892 = 1.0966: retention of 92.21 per cent of revenue against logo loss, then net expansion of 18.92 per cent on the ₹3,419 lakh retained. Those are the two dials. The second decomposition is a cohort survival curve.

The hazard falls monotonically, 28.0 per cent to 4.3 per cent, which destroys most uses of a blended rate and is itself the mechanism of compounding: survivors are better than the cohort they came from. Summing the survival column gives expected paying months, 5.716 in year one. At ₹149 a month, less 15 per cent store commission, an 18 per cent content royalty and ₹6.40 of delivery and support, contribution is ₹93.43 a paying month, a 62.7 per cent margin. First-year contribution is ₹534.05 undiscounted, ₹504.46 discounting each month at 1.3888 per cent (18 per cent a year, month 1 undiscounted). Against acquisition cost of ₹360 — ₹2.16 crore over 60,000 first payments — that is 1.48 and 1.40, with payback between month 6 (₹347.09) and month 7 (₹383.16): about 6.4 months.

4. When the standard treatment applies, and when it misleads

Four testable claims, applied to both companies. Churn is observable as a discrete event. True at Deepstambh, where a renewal is signed or not; only partly at Dhoop, where a lapse, a cancellation and a declined mandate arrive as one ledger status. The hazard is stationary within a cohort. False at both, decisively at Dhoop. Expansion headroom exists and can be measured. True at Deepstambh, where 318 of 375 retained accounts had unsold sites or modules; false at Dhoop, which sells one tier in two durations, so its net revenue retention cannot exceed its retention rate times any price rise it imposes. Acquisition cost attributes to a cohort. True at Dhoop, weak at Deepstambh, whose sales cycle runs two quarters.

The claim that fails outright is Tarkhad's. The standard answer is that a base with gross additions A and churn c converges to A/c: 60,000 ÷ 0.062 = 9.68 lakh, putting Dhoop at 83.7 per cent of its ceiling. That assumes a constant hazard, and Exhibit 3 refutes it. Properly, the steady-state base is A times expected lifetime on the monthly-plan curve, the sum of the survival column: 5.716 observed months plus a tail which, at the last observed step of 3.4 per cent, adds 0.282 ÷ 0.034 = 8.294 months — 14.010 months, a ceiling of 8.41 lakh. Dhoop sat at 96.4 per cent of that, not 83.7. The honest statement is a range on the same basis: a tail hazard of 4.0 per cent gives 7.66 lakh, 2.0 per cent gives 11.89 lakh. The plan's 15 lakh lies above that range, needing a steady-state tail hazard of 1.46 per cent a month.

5. Hard edge cases, and what happens at the seams

Multi-product. Drop one of three products and the logo is retained while revenue contracts, so gross revenue retention falls with logo retention untouched; cross-sell raises net revenue retention while making each account more fragile, since more of it is cancellable at once. Two-sided. Where only one side pays, its churn follows liquidity on the free side, so a subscription metric is measuring a marketplace problem. Regulated. The Reserve Bank of India's e-mandate framework requires an additional factor of authentication above ₹15,000 for recurring card debits, pushing volume onto UPI AutoPay on NPCI's rails: involuntary churn in India is a payments-infrastructure variable, not a product one. Annual plans collect cash in advance against revenue recognised monthly, so deferred revenue diverges from the cohort's cash. Hardware-attached. Capital sits in the customer's home, so the governing statistic is months to recover it. AI-native. Cost of service scales with use: a subscriber at ₹499 a month with ₹210 of inference cost contributes ₹289, while a heavy user at ₹640 of inference loses ₹141, so retention and margin stop pointing the same way.

At the organisational seam, expansion belongs to sales, renewal to customer success, engagement to product, deferred revenue to finance. Mature companies say they are retention-first; what they do is set separate gross-retention and expansion targets with separate owners, review cohorts monthly, and pay commission on expansion — which is why expansion moves first.

6. Eight distinctions that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

The falling hazard is mostly sorting, not growing loyalty. Fader and Hardie's shifted-beta-geometric result shows that subscribers with constant but heterogeneous hazards produce a declining aggregate hazard with nobody changing behaviour. The tell is a hazard falling identically in cohorts where the product did not change. If it is sorting, the lever is acquisition quality, not onboarding.

Blended churn and cohort churn are different objects. Dhoop's 6.2 per cent is a property of today's tenure mix; its own cohort implies a steady state of 1 ÷ 14.010 = 7.1 per cent — higher, because the blended figure mixes in annual plans facing one renewal a year. The tell is blended churn improving when growth slows.

Net revenue retention above 100 per cent can sit on a rotting logo base. Deepstambh's 109.7 per cent coexists with 9.0 per cent logo churn. The tell is net revenue retention rising while logo retention and the eligible-to-expand count both fall. The obvious reading, that the product is getting more valuable, fits the opposite equally well.

Expansion headroom is finite and has a half-life. Deepstambh's 318 eligible accounts carried ₹7.10 lakh of average unsold capacity at 1 April 2025, ₹2,258 lakh in all; FY26 consumed ₹803 lakh, leaving ₹1,455 lakh, or 1.8 more years at that pace. The tell is total expansion rising while expansion per eligible account falls.

Involuntary churn is an operations number in product clothing. Of Dhoop's 28.0-point month-one churn, 6.3 points were declined mandates, 22.5 per cent of month-one exits, extrapolated from the 71 per cent classified. The tell is churn clustering on mandate anniversaries, not usage decline. Recovering half lifts month-one survival to 75.15 per cent and, if later hazards hold, first-year contribution to ₹553.33, up 3.6 per cent.

An annual plan does not reduce churn; it defers the measurement and builds a cliff. It also turns a price into a bet: ₹999 against ₹149 a month is a 44.1 per cent discount, and whether it pays depends on how long the monthly subscriber would have stayed. The tell is an annual discount defended by "cash and retention" with no monthly-survival counterfactual.

The lifetime-value horizon is the decision, not an input to it. Dhoop's twelve-month contribution is ₹534.05; extrapolate the 3.4 per cent tail hazard to infinity and the same cohort is worth 14.010 × ₹93.43 = ₹1,308.95, two and a half times as much. The tell is two teams with identical data differing by a multiple; set the horizon to the funding horizon and say so.

Gross margin is not a constant, so the same churn number means different things. A 62.7 per cent contribution margin and an 85 per cent one imply different tolerable churn at one acquisition cost. The tell is a lifetime-value figure quoted without its margin and discount.

7. How it differs by product type and company stage

In consumer subscriptions expansion is near zero, so the ceiling binds, price is almost the only lever, and involuntary churn is large and fixable. In small-business software account mortality dominates and the curves look consumer-like. In enterprise, gross retention sits in the nineties and churn is a renewal event rather than a rate, so cohort lifetime value is barely estimable and net revenue retention does the work. On platforms a subscription rides on a take rate, and volume-linked tiers turn churn into contraction, flattering logo retention. Hardware turns on months to recover capital, AI products on cost of service moving with usage.

By stage: before product-market fit the curves are too short to extrapolate and the only honest output is a bounded range. Between roughly ₹50 crore and ₹150 crore of ARR the installed base starts to dominate new business — Deepstambh's supplies ₹5,302 lakh of a ₹6,000 lakh target — and at scale the tenure mix makes a blended rate uninformative. What does not change is the arithmetic; what changes is observability and the expansion term.

8. Three worked examples

Deepstambh's two roadmaps. The retention roadmap cuts revenue churn from 7.79 to 3.50 per cent: 0.9650 × 1.1892 = 114.8 per cent. The expansion roadmap lifts net expansion on the retained base from 18.92 to 24.70 per cent: 0.9221 × 1.2470 = 115.0 per cent. On the ₹4,620 lakh base they yield ₹5,302 lakh and ₹5,312 lakh in FY27, needing 109 and 107 new accounts at the new-account average of ₹6.44 lakh — FY26's ₹554 lakh of new business over 86 accounts, which with the cohort's ₹4,066 lakh gives the ₹4,620 lakh base. Over three years, if headroom held: ₹6,982 lakh and ₹7,024 lakh, 0.6 per cent apart.

Dhoop's annual push, priced twice. An annual subscriber yields ₹592.53 of first-year contribution — ₹999 less commission, royalty and twelve months of delivery cost, a 59.3 per cent margin — against the monthly cohort's ₹534.05: ₹58.48 more despite the 44.1 per cent headline discount, because the monthly subscriber pays only 5.716 months. Finance valued the shift at 55 per cent of 7.20 lakh new subscriptions all year, 2.66 lakh incremental annual plans over an 18 per cent baseline, and called the resulting ₹155.79 lakh conservative.

But the mix only reaches 55 per cent in the fourth quarter. Integrated over its own ramp of 26, 37, 48 and 55 per cent against 1,80,000 new subscriptions a quarter, annual plans run 46,800, 66,600, 86,400 and 99,000 — 2,98,800 in all, an average share of 41.5 per cent, and 1,69,200 above the baseline of 32,400 a quarter. At ₹58.48 each that is ₹98.95 lakh: the conservative figure overstated the gain by 57.4 per cent, and the error ran the way the case being made needed. Tengse caught a second. Mandate recovery had been valued at ₹19.28 across all 7.20 lakh new subscriptions, ₹138.82 lakh — but 2,98,800 are annual plans with one mandate event, not twelve. Over the 4,21,200 monthly subscriptions it is ₹81.21 lakh. The levers sit on disjoint populations, so they add to ₹180.16 lakh; and the second shrinks exactly as the first succeeds.

Devrai Pure, where the approach failed. The Pune company rented water purifiers at ₹449 a month and in FY25 valued a subscriber off a 34-month average lifetime from a book nine months old — a survivorship-biased extrapolation, not a mean. Net of ₹103.33 of monthly servicing (₹1,240 a year) contribution was ₹345.67. Against ₹6,850 of hardware placed at install, less expected recovery of ₹1,643 — 62 per cent of units retrieved, each worth ₹4,100 refurbished less ₹1,450 of refurbishment — net hardware was ₹5,207; with ₹2,100 of acquisition cost a subscriber had to pay 21.1 months to break even. The cohort stayed 16.8, so each of the 14,200 added in FY25 destroyed ₹1,499.74, ₹212.96 lakh in all.

The recovery was not a retention programme. A ₹4,999 refundable deposit cut gross additions by 41 per cent but lifted retrieval to 94 per cent, so recovery rose to ₹2,491 and net hardware fell to ₹4,359, while acquisition cost fell to ₹1,450. At a repriced ₹349 a month — contribution ₹245.67, break-even 23.6 months — projected lifetime rose 75 per cent to 29.4 months, turning ₹1,499.74 of loss into ₹1,413.70 of surplus, because the deposit selected for intent. All figures are undiscounted contribution less upfront cost, on FY25's completed and FY26's projected lifetimes.

9. Failure modes and their early diagnostics

Planning off a blended rate. Early sign: gross additions must grow faster than the budget. Diagnostic: what base does your cohort curve converge to? Cost: a year of spend against an unreachable number — Dhoop's 15 lakh against a ceiling of 7.66 to 11.89 lakh.

A lifetime longer than the data. Early sign: a lifetime exceeding the oldest cohort's age. Diagnostic: what did your oldest completed cohort do? Cost: Devrai's ₹212.96 lakh.

Pricing a ramp at its end state. Early sign: a mix shift modelled as a step change. Diagnostic: integrate over the quarters and check direction. Cost: a 57.4 per cent overstatement inside a board-approved plan.

Reading a segment gap as a lesson. Early sign: a strategy resting on under 150 accounts. Diagnostic: what is the standard error? Cost: an engineering year aimed at noise.

Treating expansion as repeatable. Early sign: expansion per eligible account falling while total expansion rises. Diagnostic: what is unsold in the base, in rupees? Cost: a net-retention cliff once headroom is gone.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Is the falling hazard loyalty or sorting? The sorting camp rests on the shifted-beta-geometric result: heterogeneity alone reproduces the curve, so month-two engagement spending buys a statistical artefact. The loyalty camp rests on habit formation and switching costs visible in usage logs. Sorting fails if a randomised onboarding change moves the month-three hazard within a cohort; loyalty fails if hazard curves are identical across channels of differing intent.

Is net revenue retention a sufficient statistic? Defenders note that a company above 100 per cent grows without new logos while gross retention is mechanically capped, so the marginal rupee belongs in expansion. Critics answer that 2022 showed net retention collapsing as customers cut headcount, so seat-based net retention measured customers' growth, not the product's value. Defenders fail if net retention cannot predict next year's gross retention; critics fail if the collapse was confined to seat-priced products.

Is lifetime value a decision statistic at all? The payback school argues that every estimate embeds a horizon, a discount rate and a margin forecast, none observable, so months to payback is the only number a board can govern. The cohort school answers that payback is a truncated lifetime value with an implicit horizon of zero, underfunding products whose hazard falls steeply. Payback fails if month-six estimates prove stable to month thirty-six; the cohort school fails if they do not.

Four questions stay open: whether consumer hazards reach a true floor; whether net retention is a property of the product or of the contract, once multi-year ramps and escalators are stripped out; how to state a ceiling when cost of service rises with usage; and whether consumption pricing improves retention or just relabels churn.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this asks for the cohort before accepting the rate, and names the denominator and its measurement date unprompted. They will not state a lifetime longer than their oldest completed cohort. They report gross retention and expansion separately: two dials. They know the standard error of their own segment story before telling it. They price a ramp by integrating over its stages and check which way a bound points. They treat involuntary churn as an operations queue with an owner. And they set the valuation horizon to the funding horizon, refusing any ratio whose margin and discount assumptions are unwritten.

12. The decisions, and three questions

Tilekar chose the retention roadmap, and rejected Tungarkar's argument for it. Tungarkar's case was that tier-2 chains churned at 13.5 per cent by logo against 7.6 per cent in the metros; that gap of 5.9 points carries a standard error of 3.80 points on bases of 96 and 316 accounts, so it is 1.6 standard errors, not yet a finding. He chose on headroom instead: with three-year outcomes 0.6 per cent apart if headroom held, the tie-breaker was that expansion at FY26's pace exhausts unsold capacity in 1.8 years, while lower churn preserves both. Tonape approved the annual push at ₹98.95 lakh rather than ₹155.79 lakh, funded mandate recovery at ₹81.21 lakh, and told the board 15 lakh by March 2027 was unreachable at any tail hazard her cohort supported.

  1. If Dhoop's falling hazard is mostly sorting, what should change about its ₹2.16 crore a month of acquisition spend, and how would you test that first?
  2. Deepstambh's roadmaps differ by 0.6 per cent over three years. What evidence would reorder them, and could it be collected before the FY27 commit?
  3. Devrai's deposit cut gross additions 41 per cent to raise lifetime 75 per cent. Under what market conditions is that the wrong trade?

13. Going deeper

exp20v2-bm.ai.economics:
The Economics of AI-Native Products

Strategy & Business Models — reconciling variable inference cost with subscription pricing

1. A board meeting in two weeks

On 3 March 2025, Priya Nandakumar, VP of Product at a Berlin-based startup called Aldea, opened the finance dashboard she now checked every morning instead of once a week. Aldea's product, Fieldglass AI, is a research-and-writing assistant that analysts and consultants use inside their browser: it drafts memos, summarizes documents, and — since a January launch — runs a "Deep Research" feature that autonomously searches, reads, and synthesizes dozens of sources before answering a single question. Subscriptions are priced flat, at $20 per user per month, in the familiar SaaS style Priya had used at two previous companies.

The dashboard told her something a flat-price SaaS business is not supposed to have to think about: her gross margin — revenue minus the direct cost of serving each customer — had fallen from 78% in December to 41% in February, and the trend line was still pointed down. Nothing about her pricing had changed. What had changed was that a growing minority of users had discovered Deep Research and were hammering it: fifteen, twenty, even forty invocations a month, each one triggering a chain of calls to a large language model that cost real money every single time it ran. Aldea's board meets on 17 March, and the lead investor has already asked, over email, whether Fieldglass "has normal software margins or whether it's secretly a services business wearing a SaaS multiple." Priya has twelve days to build a pricing and packaging model that answers that question honestly — and to decide, concretely, what she is going to cap, charge for, or redirect to cheaper technology before the meeting.

2. The idea, precisely

Token economics is the study of how the cost of running a large language model — measured in "tokens," the word-and-punctuation fragments a model reads and generates — scales with usage. Every prompt sent to a model and every word it generates in reply has a price attached, set by whichever lab supplies the model (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, or an open-weight model Aldea hosts itself). Subscription economics is the older, well-understood discipline of pricing a product as a flat recurring fee, which works beautifully when the cost of serving one more customer action is close to zero — adding a row to a database, rendering a web page. The economics of AI-native products is what happens when those two disciplines collide: a subscription business whose marginal cost — the extra cost incurred by one more unit of use — is neither zero nor fixed, but varies with how a customer actually uses the product.

No single person invented this field; it crystallized between 2022 and 2024 as product and finance teams at companies such as Jasper, Notion, and GitHub (with Copilot) discovered, usually the hard way, that a customer who used their AI feature heavily could cost the company more in a single month than that customer paid in a year. The problem it solves is specific: how do you design pricing, packaging, and technical routing so that a product with real, variable, per-use cost still produces a gross margin a software investor would recognize as a software margin, rather than the margin of a consulting firm? The sentence Priya can say in the boardroom without sounding glib is this:

"Every feature we ship has a unit cost attached to it, and our subscription price only protects margin if usage stays inside the line we've actually drawn — so the job is to draw that line deliberately, not discover it on a finance dashboard."

Figure 1. In traditional SaaS, serving one more click costs almost nothing. In an AI-native product, each additional model call carries a real token cost, so the cost curve climbs with usage rather than staying flat.

3. How it actually works, step by step

The mechanics are not exotic, but they involve several steps practitioners skip under deadline pressure. First, identify the cost driver precisely: for an LLM feature, cost equals (input tokens × price per input token) plus (output tokens × price per output token), summed across every call a user makes in a billing period. Input and output are usually priced differently — output tokens, the ones the model generates, typically cost three to five times more than input tokens, the ones you feed it — and teams that model "tokens" as one undifferentiated number get the arithmetic wrong before they start.

Second — and this is the step most often left implicit — build a distribution of usage, not an average user. A mean cost-per-user figure hides the fact that a small share of users drive a large share of cost. Third, compute the cost of serving each segment of that distribution against the price they pay, which yields a contribution margin per segment, not just a single company-wide number. Fourth, identify the tail: the 90th or 99th percentile user, because that is where an AI-native business actually loses money, often invisibly, for months. Fifth, design the levers available to manage that tail: a usage cap (a hard limit on calls included in a plan, with overage priced separately), and routing (automatically sending a request to a cheaper, smaller model when the task is simple, and reserving the expensive, more capable model for requests that need it). Sixth — again often skipped — stress-test the whole model against a future state: what happens to margin if the expensive feature's adoption triples, or if the model provider halves its token price next quarter. Treating today's usage pattern as permanent is the single most common error in this discipline.

4. Worked example: Fieldglass AI, line by line

Priya starts with three user segments she can already see in the data, weighted by share of the user base.

SegmentShareBasic queries/moDeep Research/moCost/moRevenueMargin
Light10%5 × $0.020$0.10$2099.5%
Typical80%40 × $0.022 × $4.00$8.80$2056.0%
Power10%80 × $0.0215 × $4.00$61.60$20−208%

Basic queries cost two cents each — cheap enough to ignore. Deep Research is the problem: at roughly $4.00 per invocation (several tool calls and a long context window, each burning tokens), a Typical user costs the business $8.80 against $20 of revenue, a 56% margin — tolerable, if below the 70%+ a SaaS board expects. A Power user, however, runs Deep Research fifteen times a month and costs $61.60 — a loss of $41.60 on every such customer, every month. Blending the three segments by their share of the base (0.10×$0.10 + 0.80×$8.80 + 0.10×$61.60 = $13.21 average cost) against $20 of revenue gives a company-wide gross margin of 34% — the number the dashboard was showing Priya, and the number that will worry the board on the 17th.

Figure 2. Green bars are flat revenue ($20). Red bars are variable cost. The Power segment alone flips the business from profitable to loss-making on that cohort.

Now change one input: suppose Priya introduces a cap of five included Deep Research calls per month on the $20 plan, with overage billed at $5 per extra call, and adds routing — a lightweight classifier that detects when a Deep Research request is actually simple (roughly 60% of them, her data suggests) and sends those to a smaller model costing $1.20 per call instead of $4.00, reserving the $4.00 model for the genuinely complex 40%.

SegmentCost (routed)Overage revenueTotal revenueMargin
Light$0.10$0$2099.5%
Typical (within cap)$5.44$0$2072.8%
Power (10 overage calls)$36.40$50$7048.0%

For a Typical user, routing alone cuts Deep Research cost from $8.00 to $4.64 (60%×2×$1.20 + 40%×2×$4.00), lifting margin to 73%. For a Power user, the cap converts ten of their fifteen monthly calls into billed overage — $50 of additional revenue — while routing trims the underlying cost to $36.40; the segment now generates $70 of revenue against $36.40 of cost, a 48% margin instead of a 208% loss. Blended across the same 10/80/10 split, revenue rises to $25 per user on average and cost falls to $8.00, for a company-wide gross margin of 68% — close to the board's target, and achieved without banning the feature that makes the product worth $20 a month in the first place.

5. The nuances that separate understanding from vocabulary

Mean versus tail

The most common analytical error is building the entire pricing model around an average user. The average told Priya the business was fine at 56% margin; the tail told her it was dying at 34%. Any AI-native margin model that reports a single number without showing the distribution behind it should be treated as unfinished work.

Contribution margin is not gross margin is not net margin

The $8.80 and $61.60 figures above are direct inference cost only — they exclude hosting, support, R&D, and sales cost. That is deliberate: this exercise is about contribution margin per unit of use, the cleanest signal of whether usage itself is profitable. Blending in fixed costs too early obscures exactly the signal the model exists to surface.

Routing is not free, and it is not invisible

The classifier that decides whether a query is "simple" has its own cost and latency, and it makes mistakes — sending a genuinely hard question to the cheap model produces a worse answer, silently, on the company's own instruction. Routing is a quality decision disguised as a cost decision, and a thoughtful team discloses it rather than hiding it.

Caps can suppress the exact behavior that creates retention

Deep Research is Fieldglass's strongest retention driver — the users who run it most are the users least likely to churn. A cap set too tight protects margin while quietly deleting the product's main source of stickiness. The right question is never "what cap maximizes margin this month" but "what cap preserves the behavior we're trying to encourage, while pricing the tail that behavior creates."

Token prices are not static

Inference prices per token have fallen roughly tenfold over periods of twelve to eighteen months as model providers compete and hardware improves. A margin crisis diagnosed in March may partly resolve itself by September — but only partly, because usage growth and adoption of more capable (and more expensive) models tend to offset falling unit prices. A model built on this quarter's token price alone will be wrong within two quarters.

"COGS" now includes inference, and many teams still don't book it that way

Software finance teams raised on hosting-as-COGS often under-classify model inference spend, burying it in a generic cloud line. If inference is not broken out as its own cost-of-goods line, the margin dashboard a VP sees will lag reality by months, exactly as it did for Priya in January and February.

This model does not tell you the right price

Everything above answers "is this margin acceptable at this price," not "is $20 the right price." That second question belongs to value-based pricing — what the feature is worth to the user — a separate exercise this one must feed, not replace.

It does not account for competitors

A rival offering unlimited Deep Research at $15 can force Priya to match a price her unit economics say she cannot afford, regardless of how correct her model is. Unit economics describe what is sustainable in isolation; they do not describe what the market will let you charge.

6. How the picture changes by product type and by stage

In consumer products, price sensitivity is high and visible usage caps provoke churn, so companies often subsidize margin deliberately during a land-grab phase — ChatGPT Plus ran at a loss per heavy user for a long stretch by design, treating the gap as a customer-acquisition cost rather than a pricing failure. In B2B products, buyers are more tolerant of usage-based add-ons and seat-based plus metered pricing, because a finance department, not an individual, absorbs the line item, and enterprise contracts can carry custom caps negotiated per account. In marketplaces, the AI cost often sits on the platform's side of a two-sided transaction — powering both a buyer's and a seller's experience — and margin logic shifts from "subscription minus inference cost" to "take rate minus inference cost," a materially different equation. Early-stage companies frequently run usage cost-negative on purpose, to learn real usage distributions before building routing infrastructure; large companies cannot, because board-level scrutiny treats gross margin as a direct comparable to SaaS peers, and a 68% margin, however improved, still invites the question a pure-software company never has to answer.

7. Common mistakes

Forecasting margin from launch-week data. Symptom: a confident margin projection that collapses within two months. Underlying error: early adopters are atypical, often enthusiasts who do not represent the steady-state power-user tail. Cheapest diagnostic: compare usage curves across a 90-day cohort window before committing to a pricing structure, not a seven-day one.

Treating all tokens as equal. Symptom: a cost model that is consistently wrong by a fixed-seeming multiple. Underlying error: ignoring the three-to-five-times price gap between input and output tokens. Cheapest diagnostic: split the cost formula into input and output lines before trusting any total.

Announcing caps reactively, after a margin crisis. Symptom: a support ticket spike and public backlash the week a cap ships. Underlying error: caps bolted onto pricing after the fact read as a broken promise, not a design choice. Cheapest diagnostic: before shipping a cap, ask what share of current users would hit it today — above roughly 15%, it is a repricing event, not a cap, and should be communicated as one.

Shipping routing silently. Symptom: a rise in quality complaints that doesn't track any model change the support team is aware of. Underlying error: assuming a cost optimization has no user-facing effect. Cheapest diagnostic: A/B test output quality by route, not only the cost savings, before calling routing a win.

8. What good looks like

A well-handled version of Priya's decision does three things at once. It makes the segmentation explicit in every board document — light, typical, power, with real counts and real costs, not a single blended margin figure that hides the tail. It treats the cap and the routing as product decisions communicated to users in plain language ("Fieldglass automatically chooses the right model for your request to keep answers fast and included in your plan") rather than as quiet engineering changes discovered through a support channel. And it commits to revisiting the model quarterly, because both token prices and usage patterns will have moved by the next board meeting — the number on the slide is a snapshot of a moving system, not a settled fact.

9. The decision, and what to carry forward

Priya takes the second model into the 17 March meeting: a five-call included cap on Deep Research, $5 overage pricing, and complexity-based routing to a cheaper model for roughly 60% of requests. It lifts blended gross margin from 34% to 68%, close to the board's target, while leaving the feature that drives retention fully available to anyone willing to pay for extra use of it. She also brings the sensitivity table, so the board sees the model's assumptions, not just its conclusion — because the honest answer to "do we have normal software margins" is "we can, at this usage mix and this routing split, and here is what breaks that."

What Priya should study next is value-based pricing — the separate question of whether $20 captures what Deep Research is actually worth to a user, which this model never answered — and the operational discipline some teams now call FinOps for AI, the ongoing practice of monitoring inference spend with the same rigor finance teams apply to cloud infrastructure. Two questions are worth sitting with before the next cycle: what is the actual shape of your usage distribution, and have you modeled its tail rather than its mean; and what happens to this entire model twelve months from now, when your cheapest model's token price has likely halved but your most engaged users have, just as likely, moved on to the next, more expensive model.
